name: ATSAME51J18A-AUT
title: SAM D5x/E5x family: Arm Cortex-M4F microcontrollers, 120 MHz, 256 KB to 1 MB Flash, 128 to 256 KB SRAM, 1 Msps 12-bit ADC, QSPI, USB, Ethernet, CAN-FD, PTC
summary: A family of 32-bit microcontrollers on an Arm Cortex-M4 core with floating-point unit, running up to 120 MHz (100 MHz in the 125 °C grade) from one 1.71 V to 3.63 V supply, with 256 KB, 512 KB or 1 MB of dual-bank ECC Flash, 128 to 256 KB of SRAM plus 8 KB of backup SRAM, and a 4 KB cache that can be turned into tightly coupled memory. The D51 members carry USB full-speed host and device, QSPI with execute-in-place, SD/MMC hosts, up to eight SERCOMs, two 12-bit 1 Msps ADCs, a two-channel 12-bit DAC, capacitive touch, AES, a TRNG and a public-key accelerator; the E51 adds two CAN-FD controllers (one on the E51G), the E53 an Ethernet MAC and the E54 both. Packages run from 48 to 128 pins. The ATSAMD51J19A-AUT is the 64-pin TQFP member with 512 KB Flash and 192 KB SRAM, industrial grade (-40 °C to +85 °C), on tape and reel.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M4F, 120 MHz (-40 °C to +85 °C and +105 °C grades), 100 MHz (+125 °C grade)
512 KB, ECC, dual bank read-while-write, SmartEEPROM
4 KB combined instruction and data cache, usable as up to 4 KB TCM
TQFP64, 10 x 10 x 1.2 mm, 0.5 mm pitch
2 x 12-bit, 1 Msps; 16 channels on ADC0 and 8 on ADC1 in the SAMD51J

tables.title: SERCOM SPI timing characteristics and requirements
notes: (1) From simulation with a load of 5 pF to 20 pF; not covered by production test limits.
(2) Rise and fall times follow the I/O pin characteristics.
(3) tCLIENT_OUT is the output response time of the external client device, normally tEXT_SOV + tLINE_DELAY.
(4) tCLIENT_IN is the input constraint of the external client device, normally tEXT_SIS + tLINE_DELAY.
(5) tHOST_OUT is the output response time of the external host device, normally tEXT_MOV + tLINE_DELAY.
(6) tHOST_IN is the input constraint of the external host device, normally tEXT_MIS + tLINE_DELAY.
(7) tLINE_DELAY is the delay of the transmission line.
(8) tEXT_MIS is the input constraint of the external host device.
(9) tAPBC is the SERCOM's APB clock period.

(10) Where both directions must work, the SPI clock is held to the slower of the reception and transmission limits: for example reception tSCK = 2 × (tMIS + tCLIENT_OUT) = 2 × (18 + 8) = 52 ns and transmission tSCK = 2 × (tMOV + tCLIENT_IN) = 2 × (9 + 20) = 58 ns.

circuits.title: Power supply connection for linear mode only
circuits.description: One supply of 1.71 V to 3.63 V feeds VDDANA and VDDIO together, with a capacitor from that rail to ground. The internal regulator runs linear, so VDDCORE needs only its capacitor to ground and VSW stays open. GND and GNDANA both go to ground; VBAT (PB03) is left free.

circuits.title: Power supply connection for switching/linear mode
circuits.description: As in linear mode, but an inductor joins VSW to VDDCORE so firmware can move the main regulator into switching mode on the fly, the more efficient choice while the CPU and peripherals run. VDDCORE keeps its capacitor to ground; VBAT (PB03) is left free.

parts.note: regulator inductor, needed for switching mode

notes: The inductor is fitted only when switching mode is used.

circuits.title: Power supply connection for battery backup
circuits.description: The switching/linear arrangement with a backup battery from VBAT (PB03) to ground. The automatic power switch selects VDD or VBAT as the supply of the internal VSWOUT rail.

parts.note: regulator inductor, needed for switching mode

notes: The inductor is fitted only when switching mode is used.

circuits.title: Crystal on the XOSC oscillator
circuits.description: A crystal of 8 MHz to 48 MHz across XIN0 (PA14) and XOUT0 (PA15) of the multi-crystal oscillator, each pin carrying a load capacitor CLEXT to ground. CLEXT follows from the crystal's specified load capacitance, the pin capacitances and the board stray capacitance.

circuits.title: Crystal on the XOSC32K oscillator
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal across XIN32 (PA00) and XOUT32 (PA01), each pin carrying a load capacitor CLEXT to ground, sized from the crystal's load capacitance, the pin capacitances and the stray capacitance.

circuits.title: Supply connection for switching or linear mode
circuits.description: A separate IO supply feeds VDDIOB with 10 µF bulk and 100 nF at the pin. The main supply feeds VDDIO directly and VDDANA through a filter inductor, each with 10 µF and 100 nF. A 10 µH inductor runs from VSW to VDDCORE, which carries 4.7 µF and 100 nF, so the regulator can run either as buck or linear; GND and GNDANA share one ground and VBAT is left open.

parts.note: CIN4, VDDIO, close to the pin
filter between the main supply and VDDANA (inductor or ferrite bead)

notes: Values are typical examples; each 100 nF capacitor sits close to its pin.

circuits.title: Supply connection for linear mode only
circuits.description: As for switching mode but without the buck inductor: VSW is left open and VDDCORE carries only its 4.7 µF and 100 nF capacitors. The IO supply feeds VDDIOB, the main supply feeds VDDIO and, through a filter inductor, VDDANA, each with 10 µF and 100 nF; VBAT is left open.

parts.note: CIN4, VDDIO, close to the pin
filter between the main supply and VDDANA (inductor or ferrite bead)

notes: Values are typical examples; each 100 nF capacitor sits close to its pin.

circuits.title: Supply connection with battery backup
circuits.description: The supply network of the switching-mode connection with a battery on VBAT (PB03), its other terminal on ground, so the backup domain keeps running when the main supply is gone. The 10 µH inductor from VSW to VDDCORE is optional, fitted for buck operation.

parts.note: CIN4, VDDIO, close to the pin
filter between the main supply and VDDANA (inductor or ferrite bead)

notes: Values are typical examples; each 100 nF capacitor sits close to its pin.

circuits.title: Three external analog references
circuits.description: External references on VREFA, VREFB, VREFC, each decoupled by 4.7 µF and 100 nF to ground with the 100 nF close to the pin. On the TQFP64 VREFA is PA03, VREFB PA04 and VREFC PA06.
notes: Values are typical examples.

circuits.title: Two external analog references
circuits.description: External references on VREFA, VREFB, each decoupled by 4.7 µF and 100 nF to ground with the 100 nF close to the pin; the unused reference pins are left open. On the TQFP64 VREFA is PA03, VREFB PA04 and VREFC PA06.
notes: Values are typical examples.

circuits.title: One external analog reference
circuits.description: External references on VREFA, each decoupled by 4.7 µF and 100 nF to ground with the 100 nF close to the pin; the unused reference pins are left open. On the TQFP64 VREFA is PA03, VREFB PA04 and VREFC PA06.
notes: Values are typical examples.

circuits.title: External reset circuit
circuits.description: RESETN carries a 100 nF capacitor to ground and an optional 10 kΩ pull-up to VDD; a push-button through 330 Ω pulls it to ground for a manual reset, the resistor limiting the capacitor's discharge current.
notes: Values are typical examples.

circuits.title: External clock on XIN
circuits.description: An external clock signal drives XIN (PA14) of the XOSC; XOUT (PA15) is left unconnected or used as a GPIO.

circuits.title: Crystal oscillator with 26 pF load capacitors
circuits.description: A crystal of 8 MHz to 48 MHz across XIN (PA14) and XOUT (PA15) with a 26 pF load capacitor from each pin to ground, the crystal placed as close to the device as possible so long lines neither overload it nor couple into other circuits.
notes: Values are typical examples.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal without load capacitors
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal straight across XIN32 (PA00) and XOUT32 (PA01), its load supplied by the pin and board capacitance.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal with 18 pF load capacitors
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal across XIN32 (PA00) and XOUT32 (PA01) with an 18 pF capacitor from each pin to ground, as a crystal datasheet may ask for.
notes: Values are typical examples.

circuits.title: SWCLK pull-up
circuits.description: A 1 kΩ resistor pulls SWCLK (PA30) up to VDD.

circuits.title: Cortex Debug Connector (10-pin)
circuits.description: The 10-pin Cortex debug header wired for SWD: VTref (1) to VDD, GND (3, 5) to ground, SWDIO (2) to PA31, SWDCLK (4) to SWCLK on PA30 and RESET (10) to RESETN; pins 6 to 9 are not connected.

circuits.title: 20-pin IDC JTAG connector
circuits.description: The 20-pin IDC header (as on SAM-ICE) wired for SWD: VCC (1) to VDD, SWDIO (7) to PA31, SWDCLK (9) to SWCLK on PA30, RESET (15) to RESETN, the even pins 4 to 20 to ground; the GND* pins 14 to 20 are reserved and may also be left open.

circuits.title: QSPI serial flash
circuits.description: A quad-SPI flash on the QSPI pins: PA08 to PA11 to SIO0 to SIO3, PB10 to SCK and PB11 to CS, with a 100 kΩ pull-up holding CS high. The flash runs from VDDIO with 100 nF across its supply, and its VSS and exposed pad go to ground. Series resistors on each QSPI line, sized from the pin drive strength (PINCFGn.DRVSTR) and the trace impedance by IBIS simulation, can improve signal integrity.

circuits.title: SD card on the SDHC
circuits.description: An SD card socket on the SDHC signals: DAT0 to DAT3 (socket pins 7, 8, 9, 1) each pulled up by 100 kΩ, CMD (2) by 10 kΩ, card detect (10) and write protect (12) by 10 kΩ each, CLK (5) direct. The socket's VDD (4) has 100 nF and 10 µF to ground; VSS1, VSS2, the switch common and the shell pins go to ground.

operation.text: Every member runs from 1.71 V to 3.63 V. Clock limits by temperature: DC to 120 MHz from -40 °C to +85 °C, DC to 120 MHz up to +105 °C, and DC to 100 MHz up to +125 °C.

Arm Cortex-M4 at 120 MHz scoring 403 CoreMark, with floating-point unit, Thumb-2 instructions, an 8-zone MPU, a 4 KB cache shared by instructions and data, and trace through the ETM instruction stream, a CoreSight ETB and a TPIU.

Self-programmable Flash of 1 MB, 512 KB or 256 KB with ECC, two banks allowing read-while-write, and hardware EEPROM emulation (SmartEEPROM). Main SRAM of 256, 192 or 128 KB, of which 128, 96 or 64 KB can be used with ECC. Up to 4 KB of tightly coupled memory, up to 8 KB more SRAM that survives Backup mode, and eight 32-bit backup registers.

Power-on reset and brown-out detection, internal and external clock sources, an external interrupt controller with 16 lines plus one NMI, and a two-pin SWD port for programming, test and debug. Sleep modes are Idle, Standby, Hibernate, Backup and Off; SleepWalking peripherals and battery backup are supported. The embedded regulator works as buck or LDO and can change between them while running.

A 32-channel DMA controller with built-in CRC generation and memory CRC monitoring. Up to two SD/MMC hosts at up to 50 MHz, 4-bit or 1-bit, following SD/SDHC 3.01, SDIO 3.0 and e.MMC 4.51. One quad SPI with execute-in-place and its own AHB memory window. On the E53 and E54, a 10/100 Mbps Ethernet MAC in MII or RMII with its own DMA, IEEE 1588 PTP and time-stamping unit, 802.3az energy efficiency, 802.1AS support and wake on LAN. Up to two CAN controllers on the E51 and E54 (CAN 2.0A/B and CAN-FD to ISO 11898-1:2015). One full-speed (12 Mbps) USB 2.0 port, host and device, eight endpoints, transceiver on chip with series resistors built in.

A 32-channel event system. Up to eight SERCOMs, each one of: USART (full duplex or single-wire half duplex), ISO7816, I2C to 3.4 MHz, SPI, LIN host/client, RS485, or SPI with inter-byte space. Up to eight 16-bit TCs, each usable as a 16-bit or 8-bit counter with two compare/capture channels, or paired into a 32-bit counter.

Two 24-bit TCCs with up to six compare channels each, optional complementary outputs, synchronized PWM patterns across pins, deterministic fault protection, fast decay, programmable dead time and dithering adding up to 5 bits of resolution. Up to three 16-bit TCCs with up to three compare channels and optional complementary outputs. PWM channels: up to six per 24-bit TCC, three per 16-bit TCC and two per TC.

A 32-bit RTC with clock/calendar, as many as 5 wake-up pins that detect tampering, with debounce filtering, a windowed watchdog, a CRC-32 generator, a two-channel I2S, a position decoder, a frequency meter and a four-LUT configurable custom logic block.

Two 12-bit 1 Msps ADCs with up to 16 channels each, single-ended or differential, automatic offset and gain correction, and hardware oversampling and decimation to 13, 14, 15 or 16 bits. A two-channel 12-bit 1 Msps DAC. Two analog comparators with window compare. Two temperature sensors. A parallel capture controller up to 14 bits wide. A peripheral touch controller for buttons, sliders and wheels, with wake on touch and up to 32 self-capacitance or 256 mutual-capacitance channels.

AES with 256-bit keys at up to 2 MB/s, in ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB and CTR, plus CCM and GCM; a true random number generator; a public key accelerator (PUKCC) with its PUKCL library for RSA, DSA and elliptic curves over GF(2n) and GF(p); and an integrity check module for SHA1, SHA224 and SHA256 with DMA help.

A 32.768 kHz crystal oscillator (XOSC32K) and up to two 8 to 48 MHz crystal oscillators (XOSC), all with clock failure detection; a 32.768 kHz ultra-low-power internal oscillator; a 48 MHz digital frequency-locked loop (DFLL48M); and two fractional digital PLLs of 96 to 200 MHz (FDPLL200M).
Up to 99 programmable I/O pins. AEC-Q100 Grade 1 (-40 °C to 125 °C) parts exist.
Members differ in their numbers of SERCOM and TC instances, PTC signals and ADC signals.
On the VQFN packages the exposed pad is best tied to ground on the board.
Out of reset every pin is a general-purpose I/O under the PORT. Setting PINCFGn.PMUXEN hands a pin to a peripheral, and PMUXn.PMUXE/O picks which one of the functions A to N it gets.
The crystal oscillators sit outside the normal PORT multiplexing: their pins are claimed through registers of OSCCTRL and OSC32KCTRL.
SWCLK is the one SWD pin that goes through the normal PORT functions. SWDIO is switched to its debug role automatically when a debugger is detected by cold or hot plugging.
The ETM sends its trace out through the TPIU.

SUPC outputs and RTC tamper pins sit outside the PORT multiplexing and are set by SUPC and RTC registers. A tamper pin the RTC does not use can serve other I/O functions once its TAMPCTRL.INACT function is off.
Up to eight SERCOM instances; every instance supports USART (with RS485 and ISO7816), SPI and I2C.
Five TCC instances, TCC0 to TCC4.

Peripherals that appear at several pin locations group their pins in IOSETs; the signals one peripheral uses must all come from the same IOSET (PAD0 and PAD1 both from IOSETn, never PAD0 from one set and PAD1 from another).

The domains depend on one another. VDDCORE, VDDIO and VDDIOB return to GND, VDDANA to GNDANA. VDDANA and VDDIO must come from the same main supply, VDD. VDDCORE is only an output of the internal regulator for monitoring, never an input. VSWOUT, VSW and VDDBU are internal domains. The VSW pin is where the inductor connects for switching-mode operation of the main regulator.

VDDIO feeds the I/O lines, the XOSCn oscillators and the regulator for VDDCORE, 1.71 V to 3.63 V. VDDIOB feeds the I/O B lines, 1.71 V to 3.63 V, and must not exceed VDDIO. VDDANA feeds the I/O pins of its cluster, the automatic power switch, both ADCs, the AC, the DAC and the PTC, 1.71 V to 3.63 V. VBAT feeds the automatic power switch, 1.71 V to 3.63 V. VDDCORE, 1.2 V typical, is the regulator output in linear mode and powers the VSW core domain, the VDDBU backup domain, memories, peripherals, DFLL48M, the FDPLLs and the RAMs. VDDIO and VDDANA take the same voltage, called VDD.
A configurable switch picks VDD or VBAT to supply the internal VSWOUT rail.

The main regulator has three modes, set through the Power Manager. Linear is the default while CPU and peripherals run and needs no inductor. Switching is the most efficient while running, needs an inductor between VSW and VDDCORE, and can be selected by software at any time. In Backup sleep the regulator shuts down, the VSW core domain is off, and the backup regulator (LPVREG) keeps VDDBU alive.
VDDIO and VDDANA are joined and come up together. VDDIO must be present before XOSCn or any digital feature on a VDDIO pin is used; VDDIOB must be present before features on its pins are used.
One POR circuit on VDDANA needs a minimum rise rate, and no supply may rise faster than the maximum; both limits are in the supply characteristics.

After power-up the device is held in reset until VDDIO/VDDANA and the internal VDDCORE are stable. It then runs from a 48 MHz clock: DFLL48M in open loop, on by default after reset, drives generic clock generator 0, whose GCLK_MAIN feeds MCLK. The synchronous clocks that are on by default get this 48 MHz; other generic clocks are off.
All pins are tri-stated except PA24 and PA25, which are inputs with pull-down, and PA30, an input with pull-up so it can serve the debug interface.
Once reset is released the CPU loads its PC and SP from address 0x00000000, the start of internal Flash; code there sets up the clocks.

Three monitors: POR on VDD (VDDANA/VDDIO) and on VSWOUT; BOD33 on VDD or VBAT; and BOD12 inside the regulator for VDDCORE. BOD12 is calibrated in production with its values in the NVM User Row, which must be kept when the User Row is rewritten.
Always on, in start-up and every sleep mode; VSWOUT under its threshold resets the whole chip.
Always on, in start-up and every sleep mode; VDD under its threshold resets all the I/Os on VDDIO.
BOD33 watches VSWOUT or VBAT, as configured. BOD12 watches VDDCORE once the device has started.
High-speed Flash with read-while-write on part of the array, plus main RAM and backup RAM with single-cycle access at full speed. The bus matrix addresses are fixed and never remapped, boot included.
Flash pages are 512 bytes on every device; their number is the Flash size divided by 512.
In Standby or Hibernate the retained part of system RAM is chosen by STDBYCFG.RAMCFG and HIBCFG.RAMCFG in the Power Manager: all of it (the default), the lowest 32 KB, or none.

System RAM can carry ECC that corrects single-bit errors and detects double errors, chosen by the RAM ECCDIS bit of the NVM User Row. With ECC on, the upper half of system RAM holds the codes and is lost to the application, and full SRAM retention must be selected.
With the CoreSight ETB in use, the lowest 32 KB of system RAM is set aside for it; ECC and ETB can be used together.

512 bytes at 0x00804000. Its first eight 32-bit words hold calibration and configuration read automatically at power-on; the other 480 bytes are free for user data. It is written through NVMCTRL, and peripherals pick up new values only after a reset. Before erasing it, read the first 32 bytes and write them back unless the configuration is meant to change.
Production-test calibration values at 0x00800080, read-only, for software to copy into the matching peripheral registers. Temperature calibration parameters sit at 0x00800100, also read-only.
A 128-bit unique number made of four 32-bit words; only the full 128 bits are guaranteed unique.

Cortex-M4 revision r0p1: a 3-stage Harvard pipeline with IEEE 754 single-precision floating point, single-cycle and SIMD multiply and multiply-accumulate, saturating arithmetic and hardware divide, running the Thumb-2 instruction set. The NVIC is tightly coupled, with an NMI and up to 8 priority levels; registers are stacked in hardware, load/store-multiple can be interrupted, and tail-chaining shortens back-to-back interrupts. Deep sleep powers the device down quickly while keeping program state.
AMBA interfaces with unaligned access and atomic bit manipulation. The MPU separates code, data and stack by privilege level and task.

Debug runs over the 2-pin SWD port. Trace uses the ITM with data watchpoints and a profiling unit, and the ETM for instruction trace. Trace leaves the chip one of three ways: one pin (serial wire viewer, ITM trace only) through the TPIU, four pins through the TPIU with limited bandwidth, or into RAM through the CoreSight ETB with full bandwidth but little room. The Flash Patch and Breakpoint unit gives up to 8 hardware breakpoints and can remap up to 8 words of code.

NVIC for low-latency interrupts; the System Control Block for configuration and exception reporting; SysTick, a 24-bit down-counter on the processor clock that stops while the processor is halted for debug, usable as an RTOS tick; an MPU with up to eight regions and an optional background region; and an FPU for IEEE 754 single-precision operations.

138 interrupt lines at eight priority levels; interrupts must be enabled globally (__enable_irq()) before any fire. Each line belongs to one peripheral instance. A peripheral's flag in INTFLAG raises a request when the matching INTENSET bit is set (INTENCLR clears it); some peripherals OR their requests onto one line, others get a line per source. A request sets the pending bit (ISPR/ICPR); the NVIC acts once the line is enabled in ISER/ICER, and IPR0-IPR7 hold the priorities.

A symmetric crossbar with a 32-bit data path, running at the hosts' clock, letting different hosts reach different clients at the same time. The FlexRAM system memory is one area that several hosts can use at once, with privileged access for some hosts.

Each host reaching RAM has its own QoS level, passed with every access. DISABLE or LOW adds at least one cycle of latency. Concurrent accesses are ordered first by QoS, then by port ID, lowest ID first. The CPU level is at 0x4100C11C bits [1:0], reset 0x3; the ICM level at 0x4100C128 bits [1:0], reset 0x1; both take 32-bit access only. DSU, DMAC, CAN and USB set theirs in their own QoS registers.
The Cortex-M cache controller puts an L1 cache between the CPU and memory, transparent to software, talking to the CPU over AHB and configured over APB.

Physically addressed and tagged; 4 KB for data and instructions; 16-byte lines; a 32-bit host bus interface; one 4-way set-associative array for both; lock-down per way; write-through with read allocate; part can serve as data and instruction TCM; round-robin replacement; one programmable 32-bit event counter; cache maintenance registers.
Four ways, each 1 KB at base + 0x000, 0x400, 0x800 and 0xC00, each holding lines 0 to 63 of four 4-byte words.
The cache works while the CPU is awake and the CMCC is enabled. It halts when the CPU halts in debug, and debugger reads in cached areas are not cached.
After reset all entries are invalid and the cache is off. Check SR.CSTS shows it disabled, then write CTRL.CEN = 1; CTRL.CEN = 0 turns it off.
Disable (CTRL.CEN = 0), wait for SR.CSTS = 0, write the new CFG.CSIZESW, re-enable with CTRL.CEN = 1.
With the cache disabled and SR.CSTS confirmed 0, CFG.DCDIS = 1 leaves only instructions cached and CFG.ICDIS = 1 leaves only data cached; then set CTRL.CEN = 1.

A way locked through LCKWAY.LCKWAY is left alone by normal cache operation. To fill and lock one: disable the cache, invalidate the way line by line (which resets the round-robin for those lines), disable the instruction cache with the data cache on, enable the cache, load the wanted code or data (touching the first byte of a line refills the whole line), set LCKWAY.LCKWAY[3:0], and turn the instruction cache back on. The other ways stay usable as I- or D-cache.

Part of the cache can be used as TCM; CFG.CSIZESW sets the cache size and the rest is TCM. Cache comes first from the start address, TCM after it; way size is fixed and the way count follows the cache size. With the CMCC disabled the whole TCM is reachable, and TCM needs no lock. CPU writes into the DATA RAM can overwrite live cache lines, so DATA RAM is accessed only once it is set up as TCM.

By line: disable, check SR.CSTS, write {index, way} to MAINT1.INDEX and MAINT1.WAY, re-enable; the line's valid bit clears and the replacement counter points at it. All: disable, check SR.CSTS, write 1 to MAINT0.INVALL, re-enable.

One 32-bit counter counts clock cycles, data hits or instruction hits. The core fetches instructions 32 bits at a time, so two Thumb instructions (such as two NOPs) cost one bus access and one HIT count. Set MCFG.MODE (CYCLE_COUNT, IHIT_COUNT or DHIT_COUNT), enable with MEN.MENABLE, optionally reset with MCTRL.SWRST, and read MSR.EVENT_CNT.

With the CMCC disabled, a debugger reads and writes TAG and METADATA RAM over AHB; enabled, those blocks cannot be read. DATA RAM follows the CPU's rules. To reach the three RAMs: disable, check SR.CSTS, access CMCC_AHB_ADDR (DATA), CMCC_AHB_ADDR_TAG (TAG) or CMCC_AHB_ADDR_MTDATA (METADATA); after writing any of them in the cache section, invalidate before re-enabling.

The device service unit detects debug probes, gives the Arm DAP control of the debug pads and of CPU reset, holds a CoreSight ROM for device and debug component identification (Arm Peripheral Identification compliant), and offers system services such as memory tests used for IEC60730 Class B. It sits on the bus matrix, so debugger and CPU can use it at once. When the NVMCTRL security bit protects the device, some services are limited or absent.

CPU reset extension; probe detection by cold and hot plugging; chip erase with status; CRC32 of any memory the bus matrix reaches; CoreSight device identification; two debug communication channels with DMA; a DAP security filter; memory built-in self-test (MBIST).

SWCLK belongs to the DSU by default for probe detection and reset extension; if its PORT function is changed or PORT_MUX is disabled, hot plugging stays off until a power or external reset. The DSU keeps running in Idle. MCLK gates the CLK_DSU_APB and CLK_DSU_AHB clocks. DMA requests go to the DMAC, which must be set up first. The PAC can write-protect its registers except DCC0 and DCC1; that protection does not apply to an external debugger.

The CPU stays in reset after the external reset is released if SWCLK is low at that moment, so no code runs while a debugger connects. SWCLK has an internal pull-up at start-up so a floating pin is not taken for a debugger. STATUSA.CRSTEXT is set while the CPU is held; writing 1 releases it (writing 0 does nothing). On a protected device the release is refused and STATUSA.PERR is set.
Detection of a debugger while the system is in reset, by the reset extension request.

Detection of a probe outside reset, on a falling edge of SWCLK; not possible during reset since POR or RESET clears the detector. SWCLK must keep its default debug function; once changed, hot plugging is lost until a power or external reset. STATUSB.HPE shows whether it is available. Either kind of detection sets STATUSB.DBGPRES. A protected device offers only cold plugging, so the external reset must outlast POR; if reset is released before POR, retry until connected.

Erases all volatile memories and the Flash (SmartEEPROM area included) and clears the NVMCTRL security bit; the auxiliary rows, the User Row among them, are kept. Writing CTRL.CE = 1 starts it, unless the PAC protects the DSU or STATUSB.CELCK = 1. On a protected device the debugger resets it first to be detected. Recommended order: cold plug (probe detected, CPU held), write CTRL.CE, poll STATUSA.DONE, then reset so NVMCTRL reloads the fuses.

Possible only on an unprotected device. The debugger holds RESET low at power-up while POR and the regulator settle and the PM runs on the slow clock; it keeps SWCLK low while releasing RESET (cold plug), clocks SWCLK so the DAP runs, issues a chip erase, and programs through the AHB-AP. Afterwards the chip restarts on RESET or a power cycle, with SWCLK high at reset release so the CPU is not held.

Setting the NVMCTRL security bit limits external tools: AHB-AP accesses outside the DSU external range fail with an AHB-AP sticky error, and DSU commands are restricted. A chip erase removes the protection. The CPU uses the DSU without limits. The operating registers at 0x0000-0x00FF are mirrored at 0x0100-0x01FF; a protected device lets the DAP reach only 0x0100-0x2000.

A CoreSight ROM table, found through the MEM-AP BASE register, names the vendor and how the chip is identified; its 64-bit conceptual ID is assembled from PID0 to PID7. The DSU DID register then names the processor, product family, product series and device.

CRC32 and MBIST share ADDR, LENGTH and DATA; set them, then write the command to CTRL. Commands issued while one runs are ignored, so wait for STATUSA.DONE. The module is enabled by its clocks. Debug adapters use the external range 0x100-0x2000 (the first 0x100 bytes give an error on a protected device); the CPU should use 0x0-0x100.

Standard CRC32 with polynomial 0xEDB88320 (reversed), over Flash or AHB RAM; from the external range it is limited as AMOD sets. Write the word-aligned start address to ADDR and length to LENGTH, the seed to DATA (normally 0xFFFFFFFF, or an earlier result to chain blocks), then CTRL.CRC = 1. CTRL.SWRST cancels a running calculation. When STATUSA.DONE sets, check STATUSA.BERR, then read DATA: complement it for the standard CRC32, or keep it as the seed for the next block.

DCC0 and DCC1 are two registers with handshake that CPU and debugger can both use, also on a protected device, at run time or in debug, to build a custom debug protocol. A protected device cannot take a debugger while the CPU runs (CRSTEXT not writable, CPU held in reset). STATUSB.DCC0D and DCC1D set on a write and clear on a read. The registers are shared with MBIST and must not be used during it. Each channel has a DMA request, raised on register empty (CFG.DCCDMALEVELx = 0) or full (= 1).

A March LR memory test meant mainly for production: write all 0; bit by bit read 0 write 1 descending; read 1 write 0 read 0 write 1 ascending; read 1 write 0 ascending; read 0 write 1 read 1 write 0 ascending; read 0 everywhere ascending. Run time depends on CPU clock and the bytes tested. It finds address decoder, stuck-at, transition, coupling and linked coupling faults. From the external range on a protected device it is refused with STATUSA.PERR.

Write the memory start to ADDR.ADDR and its size to LENGTH; testing a whole physical block gives the best coverage. CTRL.MBIST = 1 starts, CTRL.SWRST cancels. With ADDR.AMOD = 0 (default) the test stops at the first fault or on success, setting STATUSA.DONE, and STATUSA.FAIL if it failed. With ADDR.AMOD = 1 it pauses on a fault with only STATUSA.FAIL set, and writing 1 to STATUSA.FAIL resumes. ADDR then holds the failing word and DATA the phase and bit index.

Clocks start at the sources (crystal oscillators XOSC0 and XOSC1, the DFLL48M and the FDPLL200M PLLs under OSCCTRL; XOSC32K and OSCULP32K under OSC32KCTRL). GCLK turns them into asynchronous clocks: each generator divides one source, and each peripheral channel takes one generator's output to one peripheral. Generator 0 drives GCLK_MAIN, the root that MCLK divides and gates into the synchronous CPU, AHB and APB clocks. RTC, WDT and EIC also take 32 kHz or 1 kHz clocks straight from OSC32KCTRL; USB takes its own generic clock line, and GMAC (GTXCK, GRXCK) and PCC (CLK) have their own clock pins.

To clock SERCOM0 from the DFLL48M: enable the DFLL48M, set generator 1's source to it (GENCTRL1.SRC), point peripheral channel 7 at generator 1 (PCHCTRL7.GEN) to make GCLK_SERCOM0_CORE, and unmask CLK_SERCOM0_APB in MCLK.APBCMASK. Each peripheral's channel number m is fixed; AHB clocks are gated in MCLK.AHBMASK and APB clocks in MCLK.APBxMASK.

Each peripheral has a bus interface clocked from the main clock domain and a core clocked from its generic clock, and hardware synchronizes between them even when both run from the same source. Bus-interface registers need no synchronization; core registers are synchronized on write, and some on read. Each such register has its own bit in SYNCBUSY (one shared bit when a register is synchronized both ways). After waking from Standby, wait for synchronization to finish before reading a read-synchronized register.

Writing a core register sets its SYNCBUSY bit until the write has crossed into the generic clock domain. Another write to the same register meanwhile is dropped and the PAC reports an error. Registers synchronize independently: two 8-bit registers at adjacent offsets can be written back to back, but a 16-bit register written as two 8-bit halves without waiting loses the second half. One 32-bit write covering several registers updates each of them on its own schedule.

A read-synchronized register is refreshed whenever its value changes, without setting SYNCBUSY, and a read returns the last synchronized value. On wake from sleep the SYNCBUSY bits of these registers set by themselves; reading before they clear gives the value from before sleep. A write to a register that is also write-synchronized succeeds while its SYNCBUSY bit is set; a read and write together discard the read and restart synchronization.

Poll SYNCBUSY, or use the Synchronization Ready interrupt where a peripheral has one; its flag sets when every SYNCBUSY bit is 0. Writing CTRLA.ENABLE sets SYNCBUSY.ENABLE, and CTRLA.ENABLE reads back its new value at once. Writing 1 to CTRLA.SWRST sets SYNCBUSY.SWRST; SWRST reads 1 at once and both clear when the reset is done. Writing 0 to SWRST does nothing. The ready interrupt is not usable for either ENABLE or SWRST synchronization; not every peripheral has SWRST.

A peripheral on a generic clock needs a running source, an enabled generator using it, its peripheral channel enabled on that generator, and its bus interface unmasked. With the interface masked its registers read 0 and writes are ignored.

Every clock source can run on demand: it stays stopped until a peripheral asks for it, the request travelling from the peripheral through its channel and generator to the source, and stops again once no request remains. The request only gets through if the peripheral, channel and generator are all enabled. Clearing a source's ONDEMAND bit keeps it always running, which removes its start-up time from the wake path at a cost in current. Setting RUNSTDBY in the modules lets requests work in Standby.
A slow peripheral clock lowers that peripheral's active current but lengthens synchronization with the CPU clock domain, so register access and response times get slower.

On every reset the DFLL48M is on at 48 MHz, generator 0 takes it as source and drives GCLK_MAIN, and CPU and bus clocks are undivided. A power-on reset also resets the 32 kHz sources and returns GCLK to its start state: all generators off except generator 0 (DFLL48M, 48 MHz) and all peripheral channels off. A user reset does the same except for generic clocks whose WRTLOCK was set before the reset.

Twelve generators (0 to 11), each fed by one of the external or internal oscillators and each with its own divider, drive up to 48 peripheral channels that deliver GCLK_PERIPH clocks to the peripherals. The number of channels follows the peripherals a device has. Generator 0 is always the source of GCLK_MAIN.

GCLK_IO pins must be set up in PORT. GCLK can run in sleep modes. Its bus clock CLK_GCLK_APB is gated in MCLK. It has no DMA, interrupts or events. It keeps running when the CPU halts in debug. Its writable registers can be write-protected by the PAC, which does not apply to an external debugger.

Enable the clock source first. Then write GENCTRLn once, as a single 32-bit write, with GENEN = 1 and the divider (DIVSEL, DIV); then write the peripheral's PCHCTRLm with that generator in GEN. Each generator has one GENCTRLn and each channel one PCHCTRLm. The module has no enable bit of its own. CTRLA.SWRST resets every register except write-locked channels and their generators.

Each generator selects one of eight sources (generator 1 one of seven) in GENCTRLn.SRC. Only generator 1 can be the source of other generators. Generator x has one pin, GCLK_IO[x], used either as its clock input or as its output. GENEN = 0 stops and gates the generator. Generator 0 feeds GCLK_MAIN to MCLK.

A generator can change source while running. If the new source is not yet ready it keeps using the old one, holding requests to both, and moves over when the new one is ready, then releases the old one. SYNCBUSY.GENCTRLn stays 1 until the switch is done.

The source is divided by the value in GENCTRLn.DIV, interpreted according to GENCTRLn.DIVSEL; DIVSEL = 0 with DIV = 0 or 1 passes the clock undivided. Generators do not all have the same number of DIV bits. An odd division gives an unequal duty cycle unless GENCTRLn.IDC is set, which makes it 50/50.

With GENCTRLn.OE = 1 and GENEN = 1 the generator requests its source and drives GCLK_IO[n], which must first be configured as an output in PORT. With OE = 0 the pin holds the level in GENCTRLn.OOV (0 low, 1 high). In Standby an output clock freezes at the OOV level unless GENCTRLn.RUNSTDBY = 1, which keeps it running.

With a generator enabled and chosen in PCHCTRLm.GEN, setting PCHCTRLm.CHEN = 1 enables the channel; CHEN = 0 disables and gates it. CHEN crosses into the generic clock domain and reads its old value until that is done. To change a channel's generator without glitches: write CHEN = 0, wait until it reads 0, write GEN, write CHEN = 1, and wait until it reads 1.

PCHCTRLm.WRTLOCK = 1 ignores every later write to that channel and also locks the GENCTRLn of its generator; only a power reset unlocks them, not CTRLA.SWRST. Generator 0, being GCLK_MAIN, is exempt from locking and returns to a known state on every reset. After an external reset (RESETN low) a locked channel's generator is disabled and its CHEN reads 0 until the generator is enabled again, when CHEN returns to 1.

operation.topic: GCLK after reset and in sleep
operation.text: Which generators and channels are running after reset depends on the device, since some peripherals need a clock straight away. GCLK supports SleepWalking: when a peripheral asks for its clock in a sleep mode where generic clocks are stopped, GCLK wakes the source and enables the generator and channel in turn. GENCTRLn.RUNSTDBY decides whether a generator's pin output continues in Standby. With RUNSTDBY = 0, entering Standby can take a little longer while GCLK checks that the generator has stopped, by a time that depends on its frequency.

GENCTRLn and CTRLA are write-synchronized. PCHCTRLm.CHEN is the exception: read it back after changing it to be sure the change has taken effect; changing it during synchronization does not raise an error.

MCLK takes GCLK_MAIN and makes the synchronous clocks for the CPU and for modules on the AHB and APB buses, with a prescaler dividing by 1 to 128, safe switching at run time, and a mask bit per module to stop clocks to unused ones.

CLK_MAIN feeds a common 8-bit prescaler. CLK_CPU goes to the CPU; stopping it stops execution. CLK_APBx and CLK_AHBx stay synchronous to the CPU clock and can keep running while the CPU clock is off in sleep; each module's bus clock passes through its own gate. There are two synchronous domains: the high-speed (HS) domain at fHS and the CPU domain at fCPU. The QSPI fast clock CLK_QSPI2X_AHB comes from fHS. CLK_MCLK_APB can be turned off, but then only a reset turns it on again.

MCLK runs in every sleep mode that needs a synchronous clock. Its interrupt goes to the NVIC. It has no DMA or events. It keeps running in debug halt, and in sleep its clocks keep running so a debugger can reach every module, which makes current measured under debug wrong. All writable registers except INTFLAG can be PAC write-protected, not against an external debugger.

After reset the GCLK_MAIN source is started and calibrated before the CPU runs, and it drives the main clock undivided with only the necessary module clocks on. MCLK is always enabled and cannot be reset. CPUDIV.DIV sets the CPU domain divider and can be written on the fly without stopping peripherals; every clock of the domain changes together. No domain may exceed its maximum frequency from the electrical characteristics. A forbidden CPUDIV value is stored but not used, and the PAC reports a violation.

A new CPUDIV takes a short while to apply; until then INTFLAG.CKRDY reads 0, and with INTENSET.CKRDY = 1 an interrupt fires once the new setting is in force. Writing CPUDIV again while CKRDY is 0 can make the system unstable or hang, and the PAC reports a violation. CKRDY is a synchronous wake-up source.

Writing a module's bit in AHBMASK or APBxMASK to 0 or 1 stops or starts its bus clock. A module whose APB clock is stopped cannot be read or written until its bit is set again; a module on several buses has a bit for each. Stopping NVMCTRL's clock breaks Flash reads by the CPU; stopping MCLK's own clock or the APB bridge it sits on leaves the mask registers unreachable until a system reset.
In Idle MCLK keeps running on the main clock. In Standby it stops unless a synchronous clock is needed.

The reset controller collects every reset source, puts the device in its start state for that source and records the cause in RCAUSE. Sources: power-supply resets (POR, BOD12, BOD33); user resets (RESETN pin, watchdog, system reset request); and Backup-mode exits (RTC and the battery backup power switch, BBPS).

RSTC is always on and always enabled, in every sleep mode, and keeps running in debug halt. Its bus clock CLK_RSTC_APB is gated in MCLK. After a power-on reset RCAUSE names POR. Software reads RCAUSE early in boot to decide what to do. Writable registers can be PAC write-protected, not against an external debugger.

Pulling RESETN low gives the external reset. POR, BOD12 and BOD33 come from SUPC, the watchdog reset from the WDT, the system reset request from the CPU setting SYSRESETREQ in its reset control register, and the NVM reset from NVMCTRL (for instance a BKSWRST command). Backup mode ends on the BBPS signalling that the 3.3 V VDDIO supply is back, or on an RTC interrupt; either sets RCAUSE.BACKUP and updates BKUPEXIT.

Optional ECC on the SRAM corrects single-bit errors and detects double-bit errors, with an error interrupt. With it on, the top half of SRAM holds the check codes and is not available to software. Whether it is used is set by ECCDIS (RAM) in the NVM User Row. Its bus clock comes through the APB B bridge (MCLK.APBBMASK.RAMECC). It runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs and its interrupt can wake the device. All writable registers except INTFLAG and STATUS can be PAC write-protected, not against an external debugger.

The ECC logic gives single error correction and double error detection per 8-bit byte. A single error sets INTFLAG.SINGLEE, a double error INTFLAG.DUALE. The first error freezes its address in ERRADDR until both flags are cleared; a double error arriving while SINGLEE is set overwrites ERRADDR and sets DUALE too. Reading ERRADDR clears both flags, and an enabled flag keeps requesting until ERRADDR is read, the module is reset or the interrupt is turned off. Both sources share one NVIC line. With ECC turned off by its fuse, writes leave the ECC field unchanged and reads are neither corrected nor flagged.

The power manager handles five sleep modes (Off, Backup, Hibernate, Standby, Idle, deepest first) plus the gating of the switchable power domains, which software chooses for Standby, Hibernate and Backup. Software picks the mode and when to enter it; interrupts from enabled peripherals and any enabled reset bring the device back. SleepWalking works in Standby. In Hibernate and Backup the I/O pin states can be held so pins do not toggle while waking.

CLK_PM_APB is gated in MCLK and, once stopped, comes back only with a system reset. The PM interrupt goes to the NVIC. All writable registers except INTFLAG can be PAC write-protected, not against an external debugger.

The PM keeps running in debug halt. Standby requested under debug leaves the power domains on, so current measured then means nothing. Hibernate or Backup requested under debug keeps the core domains and debug modules on; leaving the mode by reset resets the core domains but not the debug logic, so the session continues. Off under debug resets the core domains. Hot plugging works in Standby but not in Hibernate, Backup or Off, where the DSU has no power. Cold plugging works in those modes if the external reset lasts longer than the mode's wake-up time. Waking from Backup takes under 200 µs typically, more if SUPC voltage scaling is on.

Apart from the supply domains (VDDANA, VDDIO and so on) the device has four power domains. PDCORESW holds the CPU and every peripheral outside the backup domain. PDBACKUP holds OSC32KCTRL, SUPC, RSTC, RTC and the PM. PDSYSRAM holds the system RAM, which can be partly or wholly off in Standby or Hibernate. PDBKUPRAM holds the backup RAM, which can be partly or wholly off in Backup. PDCORESW, PDSYSRAM and PDBKUPRAM can be switched off in Standby, Hibernate or Backup to save leakage.

Idle: CPU stopped, synchronous clocks stopped unless requested, logic kept. Standby: CPU and peripherals stopped, logic kept, PDSYSRAM fully or partly off if chosen. Hibernate: PDCORESW off, backup domain on so the RTC, 32 kHz sources and wake from RTC tamper pins still work; PDSYSRAM kept if chosen. Backup: only the backup domain on, for the same features; PDBKUPRAM kept if chosen. Off: the whole device unpowered. After a POR the PM is enabled and the device is in Active mode; the PM is always enabled and cannot be reset.

SLEEPCFG.SLEEPMODE selects the mode and the WFI instruction enters it. Because the write passes through bus bridges, read SLEEPCFG back and check it holds the wanted value before WFI. After power-up the low-power mode of MAINVREG needs time to settle; INTFLAG.SLEEPRDY sets when it has, and must be set before entering Standby, Hibernate or Backup. SLEEPRDY is also an interrupt source and a synchronous wake-up source.

The fastest wake-up: the CPU stops while peripherals keep working and AHB/APB clocks are still given on request, and the main clock keeps running. Enter with SLEEPMODE = IDLE and WFI, or automatically on return from the lowest-priority ISR when SLEEPONEXIT is set in the Cortex SCR. Any unmasked interrupt with enough priority to be taken returns the device to Active. GCLK clocks, regulators and RAM work as normal in Idle.

The lowest-power mode that keeps logic state and RAM contents. All clocks stop except those serving SleepWalking or kept on by ONDEMAND and RUNSTDBY settings (a SERCOM with RUNSTDBY = 1, for instance). Enter with SLEEPMODE = STANDBY and WFI; SLEEPONEXIT works as in Idle. Any peripheral that can raise an asynchronous interrupt wakes the device, which then runs the ISR or carries on after WFI according to PRIMASK. The regulator runs in low-power mode, moving to normal mode by itself while a SleepWalking task needs more power and back afterwards.

The lowest power short of Off: everything is off except the backup domain, whose peripherals keep running (the RTC on a 32.768 kHz oscillator, for instance). PM registers are kept except INTENCLR, INTENSET, INTFLAG and SLEEPCFG. Enter with SLEEPMODE = HIBERNATE or BACKUP and WFI; the device leaves on a Hibernate or Backup reset seen by the RSTC. Hibernate powers PDRAM from MAINVREG in low-power mode. Backup uses the backup regulator LPVREG, or the main regulator if VREG.RUNBKUP = 1, and PDBKUPRAM can be kept whole.
The device is entirely unpowered. Enter with SLEEPMODE = OFF and WFI; leave by pulling RESET low or by a power reset.

In Hibernate and Backup PORT loses power but the pin configuration is held. On exit, CTRLA.IORET = 0 releases the pins to PORT's reset values; IORET = 1 holds them until software writes IORET = 0, giving time to set PORT up.

In Standby, STDBYCFG.RAMCFG keeps PDSYSRAM fully, partly or not at all; during SleepWalking it is on whatever RAMCFG says. In Hibernate PDCORESW is off, HIBCFG.RAMCFG chooses PDSYSRAM's state and HIBCFG.BRAMCFG PDBKUPRAM's; the partial option keeps only the lowest 4 KB of backup RAM. In Backup PDCORESW and PDSYSRAM are off, PDBACKUP stays on and BKUPCFG.BRAMCFG chooses PDBKUPRAM's state. In Off every domain is off.

operation.topic: Regulators, RAM and NVM in sleep
operation.text: By default Standby and Backup put RAM, NVM and regulators into low-power mode. RAM goes low-power in Standby. The NVM goes low-power in Standby or Idle when not being accessed; NVMCTRL CTRLB.SLEEPPRM changes that. In Standby the PM picks the main or the low-power regulator for VDDCORE from what the device is doing. Idle leaves GCLK clocks, regulators and RAM working normally.

A peripheral can have its clocks woken briefly to do a task in Standby without waking the CPU; at the end it either wakes the device with an interrupt or the device goes back to Standby. On this device only GCLK clocks can do this, through on-demand sources. While a SleepWalking task runs every power domain is on, PDRAM included, and MAINVREG runs as the regulator chosen for Active (LDO or buck), not in its low-power mode. In Standby the system RAM can be kept as 0, 32 KB or all of it; in Backup the backup RAM as 0, 4 or 8 KB.

Waking from Standby adds up: turning gated power domains back on (zero if they stayed active; the time is in the electrical characteristics); MAINVREG climbing from its lower low-power-mode voltage to the Active level; the CPU clock source starting; and the first Flash access. STDBYCFG.FASTWKUP shortens the NVM and MAINVREG parts.

The supply controller runs the core (VDDCORE) and backup (VDDBU) regulators according to the sleep mode or user settings; in Active the core supply can be switched on the fly between an LDO and a buck converter. It manages a backup battery on VBAT with automatic switching of the backup domain between main and battery power. It has two brown-out detectors: BOD33 on the device supply (VDD or VBAT), continuous or sampled, normal or low-power, and BOD12 on VDDCORE. It provides the selectable reference for the ADC and DAC, a temperature sensor, and drives two output pins.

Main regulator MAINVREG (LDO or buck) in Active, Standby and Hibernate; low-power regulator LPVREG in Backup; controlled VDDCORE slope on voltage changes. Battery backup switch: to battery with automatic entry to Backup, back to main power with automatic exit or staying in Backup. Reference for ADC and DAC, temperature sensor. BOD33 with programmable threshold and action (reset, interrupt or battery switch) loaded from the NVM User Row at start-up, continuous or low-power sampled mode with programmable sample rate, hysteresis from Flash user calibration, monitoring VDD or VBAT. BOD12. Two output pins that can toggle on an RTC event.

SUPC sets up its OUT pins itself when an output is enabled. It works in every sleep mode except Backup, where BOD33 and the battery backup switch still work. CLK_SUPC_APB is gated in MCLK. BOD33 and its sampled mode need a 32 kHz clock asynchronous to the bus clock, so some writes are synchronized. Its interrupts go to the NVIC. In debug halt it keeps running. When a cold plug is detected BOD33 and BOD12 use the factory calibration instead of the user calibration; with hot plugging the BOD resets keep running. All writable registers except INTFLAG can be PAC write-protected.

After a power reset the LDO supplies VDDCORE, and its output level follows the sleep mode chosen in PM.SLEEPCFG.SLEEPMODE. In Active, writing VREG.SEL switches between LDO and buck: STATUS.VREGRDY drops to 0 when the switch starts and returns to 1 when it is done, and the VREGRDY interrupt flags the 0-to-1 change. In Standby and Hibernate MAINVREG runs in low-power mode; in Backup LPVREG supplies VDDCORE.

VDDCORE changes on entering or leaving Standby, Hibernate or Backup, and when SleepWalking starts in Standby. With VREG.VSEN set it moves in steps of typically 5 mV, one step every 2^VSPER × T (VREG.VSPER), to limit peak current drawn from the supply. STATUS.VCORERDY reads 0 during the change and 1 once the target is reached; the VCORERDY interrupt flags the 0-to-1 change. The controlled slope applies only on leaving sleep modes and when SleepWalking starts in Standby, not on entering sleep with no SleepWalking task.

SUPC makes a fixed 1.1 V bandgap and a variable reference, VREF. Both the reference output and the temperature sensor are off after any reset. VREF.VREFOE enables the reference output, VREF.TSEN the temperature sensor; with VREF.ONDEMAND = 0, enabling both at once is not recommended, since only the reference then reaches both ADC inputs. VREF.SEL chooses the voltage applied to analog modules such as the ADC.

Off at power-up, with the backup domain on main power. With BOD33.ACTION = BKUP the backup domain moves to VBAT when BOD33 sees VDD fall below BOD33.LEVEL, and back to VDD when VDD rises above it. The switch runs in every sleep mode. Battery backup mode is entered by WFI when BBPS.CONF = 0x1 forces it, or by BOD33 detecting loss of main power (ACTION = BKUP), which puts the device into Backup. It is left by a Backup-exit condition in the RSTC: when BOD33 sees main power return, BBPS.WAKEEN = 1 wakes the device and WAKEEN = 0 moves the backup domain to main power but stays in Backup; on an RTC exit the device stays on battery in Backup until main power returns.
BKOUT.EN hands an OUTx pin to SUPC. BKOUT.SETx drives it high, BKOUT.CLRx low, and BKOUT.RTCTGLx makes it toggle on each RTC event.

Configure before enabling: threshold (BOD33.LEVEL); behaviour in Active, Standby, Hibernate and Backup (ACTION, STDBYCFG, BKUP, RUNHIB, RUNBKUP); prescaler for sampled mode (PSEL); action and hysteresis (ACTION, HYST). The BOD33 register is enable-protected: writable only with ENABLE = 0 and STATUS.B33SRDY = 0, otherwise the write is dropped with an APB error; the enable bit itself is not protected. Its values load from the NVM User Row after power-on or user reset. BOD33.ENABLE turns it on and off.

Outside battery backup mode BOD33 compares VDD with BOD33.LEVEL and, on VDD falling below, raises an interrupt, a reset or the battery backup switch as BOD33.ACTION selects. In battery backup mode it watches VBAT and VDD in turn: VBAT below BOD33.VBATLEVEL gives a power-supply reset, and VDD above BOD33.LEVEL ends battery backup mode, waking the device if BBPS.WAKEEN is set. STATUS.BOD33DET shows the detection state.

In sampled mode BOD33 switches on at each tick of a sampling clock, checks the supply briefly and switches off until the next tick. It is chosen for Backup or Hibernate with BOD33.BKUPCFG = 1 or BOD33.HIBCFG = 1, at a rate set by BOD33.PSEL from the 32.768 kHz OSCULP32K; PSEL = 0 turns sampling off. Low-power mode is automatic in Backup and Hibernate and is chosen for Standby with BOD33.STDBYCFG = 1. A non-zero BOD33.HYST splits the threshold into a lower trip level VBOD- and an upper release level VBOD+ to ignore ripple; it also works in sampled mode.

BOD33 runs in Standby if enabled with BOD33.RUNSTDBY = 1, in low-power mode if BOD33.STDBYCFG = 1. For Backup or Hibernate set BOD33.RUNBKUP or BOD33.RUNHIB; it then runs in ultra-low-power mode, sampled if PSEL is non-zero, and always watches the backup domain supply (VDD or VBAT).

BOD12 is calibrated in production with its setting stored in the NVM User Row, which must be left unchanged. It resets the device when the 1.2 V core supply falls below its level, and is always off in Standby, Hibernate and Backup.

Interrupt sources: VCORERDY (asynchronous), VREGRDY (asynchronous), BOD33RDY (synchronous), BOD33DET (asynchronous), B33SRDY (synchronous), on one request line. BOD33.ENABLE is write-synchronized because the BOD prescaler counters run apart from the bus: writing it clears STATUS.B33SRDY, which sets again when done; writing the register meanwhile gives a PAC error without stalling the APB.

The watchdog resets the system if software does not clear it within a set time-out, with an early warning interrupt before that. Window mode adds a closed period at the start in which a clear also causes a reset, catching code that clears too often. It runs from OSCULP32K, independent of the CPU clock, in Active and every sleep mode except Hibernate, Backup and Off, and still resets or interrupts if the main clocks fail. Time-outs run from 8 to 16384 cycles in normal mode and 16 to 32768 cycles in window mode. It has an always-on option.

CLK_WDT_APB is gated in MCLK. The counter runs on CLK_WDT_OSC, 1.024 kHz from OSCULP32K, which is not accurate, so the actual time-out differs from device to device and software must allow for that. The counter clock is asynchronous to the bus, so some writes are synchronized. The WDT stops in debug halt. Its interrupt can wake the device. All writable registers except INTFLAG can be PAC write-protected, not against an external debugger.

CTRLA (apart from ENABLE), CONFIG and EWCTRL are enable-protected: writable only with CTRLA.ENABLE = 0. Protected CTRLA bits may be written in the same write that sets ENABLE, not the one that clears it. CONFIG.PER sets the time-out; window mode needs CTRLA.WEN = 1 and CONFIG.WINDOW. After a power-on reset CTRLA.ENABLE, CTRLA.ALWAYSON, CTRLA.WEN, CONFIG.WINDOW, CONFIG.PER and EWCTRL.EWOFFSET load from the NVM User Row. Writing ENABLE = 0 stops the WDT only if ALWAYSON is 0.

Once enabled, the WDT resets the system at the end of the CONFIG.PER period unless cleared. Writing 0xA5 to CLEAR restarts the period; writing anything else to CLEAR resets the system at once. There are 12 time-out settings, 8 ms to 16 s. INTENSET.EW enables the early warning interrupt (INTENCLR.EW disables it); in normal mode it comes EWCTRL.EWOFFSET after the start of the period.

Two periods follow each other: the closed window TOWDTW (CONFIG.WINDOW) and the open window TOWDT (CONFIG.PER), each 8 ms to 16 s, so the full time-out is their sum. Writing 0xA5 to CLEAR is accepted only in the open window; a clear during the closed window resets the system. The early warning interrupt, if enabled, comes when the open window starts.

Its one interrupt, Early Warning (EW), is an asynchronous wake-up source. The WDT keeps working in any sleep mode whose clock is running except Backup; on wake-up the CPU takes the interrupt if the NVIC is set up for it, or otherwise just continues after the sleep instruction. CTRLA.ENABLE, CTRLA.WEN, CTRLA.ALWAYSON and CLEAR are write-synchronized.

CTRLA.ALWAYSON = 1 keeps the WDT running whatever CTRLA.ENABLE says, and only a power-on reset clears it. CONFIG and EWCTRL then become read-only, so PER, WINDOW and EWOFFSET are fixed, though WEN can still switch window mode and INTENSET/INTENCLR still switch the early warning interrupt.

In normal mode EWCTRL.EWOFFSET gives the number of CLK_WDT_OSC cycles from the start of the period to the interrupt; an offset longer than the time-out means the reset comes first and the interrupt never does. In window mode the interrupt marks the opening of the window, so a sleeping system can wake on it, clear the WDT and sleep again. Example: normal mode, CONFIG.PER = 0x2 and EWCTRL.EWOFFSET = 0x1 give the interrupt at 16 CLK_WDT_OSC cycles and the reset at 32.

A 32-bit counter behind a 10-bit prescaler that usually runs all the time. It can wake the device by alarm or compare match, periodic tick, overflow, or its wake inputs, and make periodic events from prescaler taps, events and interrupts on compare or alarm, and overflow; a match can also clear the counter. On a 32.768 kHz clock the shortest tick is 30.5 µs and time-outs reach 36 hours; with a 1 s tick the longest time-out exceeds 136 years.

Counter modes of 32 bits (two compare registers) or 16 bits (four compare registers); a calendar mode with seconds, minutes, hours (12 or 24 h), day, month, year and leap-year correction; digital frequency correction; overflow, alarm/compare and prescaler interrupts and events, with optional clear on match; 8 backup registers kept in Backup; tamper detection with timestamp on an event or up to 5 debounced inputs, and active layer protection.

The RTC runs in any sleep mode whose clock is running and its interrupts can wake the device; its events can act without waking it. Only a POR or CTRLA.SWRST resets it. CLK_RTC_APB is gated in MCLK. It needs a 32.768 kHz or 1.024 kHz CLK_RTC_OSC, set up in OSC32KCTRL.RTCCTRL first, which is asynchronous to the bus clock. It has DMA requests, an interrupt and events. It halts in debug unless DBGCTRL says to keep running. All writable registers except INTFLAG can be PAC write-protected. A 32.768 kHz crystal with its load capacitors can go on XIN32 and XOUT32.

Mode 0 (COUNT32): 32-bit counter. Mode 1 (COUNT16): 16-bit counter. Mode 2 (CLOCK): clock/calendar with alarms. CTRLA.MODE, PRESCALER, MATCHCLR and CLKREP, and the CTRLB, EVCTRL and TAMPCTRL registers, are enable-protected: to change them on a running RTC write ENABLE = 0, wait for synchronization, then write; protected CTRLA bits can go with the write that sets ENABLE but not the one that clears it. CTRLA.SWRST resets everything except DEBUG and disables the RTC, which must be disabled before the reset.

With CTRLA.MODE = 0x0 the counter counts up on each rising edge of CLK_RTC_CNT to 0xFFFFFFFF, wraps to 0 and sets INTFLAG.OVF. COUNT is read and written as 32 bits. A match with COMP0 or COMP1 sets INTFLAG.CMPn on the next CLK_RTC_CNT edge; with CTRLA.MATCHCLR = 1 the counter also clears on the next cycle, giving periods longer than the prescaler events, and CMPn and OVF then set together.

With CTRLA.MODE = 0x1 the counter counts to the value in the 16-bit PER register, wraps to 0 and sets INTFLAG.OVF. COUNT is 16 bits. A match with a 16-bit COMPn sets INTFLAG.CMPn on the next CLK_RTC_CNT edge.

With CTRLA.MODE = 0x2 the CLOCK register holds seconds, minutes, hours (12 or 24 h by CTRLA.CLKREP, changeable only while disabled), day of month from 1, month from 1 (January) and a year value 0x00 to 0x3F added to a reference year of the user's choice, which must be a leap year (2016, 2020 and so on): 0x2D on a 2016 base is 2061. The source and prescaler must give the counter a 1 Hz clock. After 23:59:59 on 31 December of year 0x3F it wraps to 00:00:00 on 1 January of year 0x00 and sets OVF. A match with ALARM0 or ALARM1, on the fields MASKn.SEL selects, sets INTFLAG.ALARMn on the next counter clock edge (1 s later at 1 Hz). CTRLA.MATCHCLR clears the clock on an alarm match, setting ALARM0 and OVF together.

DMA request TAMPER sets when a timestamp is captured and clears when TIMESTAMP is read; CPU access to those registers can lose the request or corrupt the transfer. Interrupts: OVF, TAMPER, CMPn, ALARMn and PERn (a prescaler bit toggling), on one combined NVIC line. Output events: OVF, TAMPER, CMPn, ALARM, PERn and PERD (periodic daily), each enabled by its EVCTRL.xxxEO bit. Input event TAMPEVT captures the counter into the timestamp register (EVCTRL.TAMPEVTEI). In sleep the RTC runs while its clock does; on wake the CPU takes the interrupt or carries on after the sleep instruction, and periodic events can wake it through an event channel with its interrupt enabled.

Write-synchronized bits: CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, CTRLA.COUNTSYNC and CTRLA.CLOCKSYNC. Write-synchronized registers: COUNT, CLOCK, PER, COMPn, ALARMn, FREQCORR, MASKn and GPn. Read-synchronized: COUNT when CTRLA.COUNTSYNC = 1, CLOCK when CTRLA.CLOCKSYNC = 1, and TIMESTAMP.

Each of prescaler bits 2 to 9 can raise an event (EVCTRL.PEREOn, n = 0 to 7) or interrupt on its rising edge: PER0 every 8 CLK_RTC_OSC cycles, PER1 every 16, and so on. These do not depend on the counter's prescaler setting, except that CTRLA.PRESCALER = 0 stops them. For interrupts n runs 0 to 7 in modes 0 and 2 and 2 to 7 in mode 1.

Corrects a slow or fast oscillator in steps of about 1 ppm by adding or skipping one prescaler count once every 8192 CLK_RTC_OSC cycles; FREQCORR.VALUE sets how many times this happens per 128 such periods, for a resolution of 0.95367 ppm. It needs CTRLA.PRESCALER greater than 1. FREQCORR.SIGN gives the direction: positive adds counts and lengthens the period (slower), negative removes counts (faster). Corrections also shift the timing of periodic events at the end of each correction cycle.

Eight backup registers (BKUPn) keep their contents in Backup. Four general purpose registers (GPn) stay powered while the RTC is, and are reset only by an RTC reset or by tamper detection with CTRLA.GPTRST = 1. CTRLB.GPnEN enables GP 2n and 2n+1. The GP registers reuse the compare/alarm buffers: the even one the read buffer, usable only with that compare/alarm disabled, the odd one the write buffer once a compare/alarm write has finished (SYNCBUSY.COMPn = 0). Writing an even GP borrows the write buffer until SYNCBUSY.GPn clears, so write the even one before the odd one and save the odd value before changing the even. To restore the compare/alarm, write GPnEN = 0 and rewrite COMPn/ALARMn. Writing GP0 and GP1: wait for SYNCBUSY.COMP0 = 0 (and COMP1 in mode 1), set CTRLB.GP0EN, write GP0, wait for SYNCBUSY.GP0 = 0 (GP1 reads busy with it), then write GP1.

Five tamper channels, each set by TAMPCTRL.INnACT: off; wake (an INn edge of the TAMPCTRL.TAMPLVLn polarity sets INTFLAG.TAMPER without capturing the counter); capture (the same, plus the counter goes into TIMESTAMP); or active layer protection (a mismatch on an RTC signal looped from OUT to INn sets TAMPER and captures). TAMPID records which channels fired until software clears it. All channels share one TAMPER interrupt, and input event TAMPEVT can also raise a tamper condition (EVCTRL.TAMPEVTEI).

Each input has its own debouncer, enabled by TAMPCTRL.DEBNCn, with one shared set-up in CTRLB and one period for all set by CTRLB.DEBF. Without debouncing INn is detected asynchronously. Synchronous debouncing (CTRLB.DEBASYNC = 0) synchronizes INn over two CLK_RTC periods, then needs it stable for four CLK_RTC_DEB periods. Asynchronous debouncing (DEBASYNC = 1) takes the first edge at once and ignores further edges until INn has been stable for four CLK_RTC_DEB periods. Majority debouncing (CTRLB.DEBMAJ) needs INn valid in two of three CLK_RTC_DEB periods.

Detecting a tamper and capturing COUNT or CLOCK into TIMESTAMP takes three CLK_RTC periods; read TIMESTAMP once INTFLAG.TAMPER is set. With CTRLB.DMAEN = 1 the capture raises a DMA request, so DMA can read TIMESTAMP and TAMPID one after the other. No new capture happens until TAMPER is cleared, by reading TIMESTAMP or writing 1 to it; of several tamper events close together only the first may be timestamped, but TAMPID records each. TAMPEVT always captures; an INn input captures only with its INnACT set to capture, a wake input updates TAMPER and TAMPID only. Read TIMESTAMP once, clear TAMPER, and read again only after TAMPER sets again.

Detects a broken trace: an RTC-generated signal leaves on the OUT pin, runs over the parts to be protected, and returns on an INn pin; a mismatch is a tamper. Steps: set CTRLB.RTCOUT to output the prescaler signal and route the pins in PORT; pick its frequency with CTRLB.ACTF; set TAMPCTRL.INnACT = 3 for the input; then enable with CTRLB.RTCOUT. The RTC compares INn with the expected OUT level at each CLK_RTC falling edge, so the trace may delay the signal by up to half a CLK_RTC period.

The DMAC moves data between memories and peripherals without the CPU, and has a CRC engine. Channels take software, event or peripheral triggers and request the arbiter, which picks one active channel at a time; the fetch engine loads that channel's transfer descriptor from SRAM and the transfer runs. A higher-priority channel can interrupt it, the descriptor being written back to SRAM first. Four bus interfaces: data transfer, descriptor fetch and write-back (AHB hosts) and the register interface (APB client). Bursts, a pre-fetch channel and quality of service keep latency low.

Transfers between any mix of memory and peripherals (each direction, and memory to memory). Triggers from software, the event system or peripheral requests. Descriptors in SRAM, single or linked into multi-buffer or circular lists. Up to 32 channels, each with automatic descriptor fetch and suspend/resume. Four priority levels per channel with fixed or round-robin order within a level. 1 to 256 KB per block. Static or incrementing addresses. Interrupts on block complete, error and suspend. 8 event inputs (channels 0 to 7) for normal, periodic or conditional transfers or suspend/resume; 4 event outputs (channels 0 to 3) on AHB, block or transaction transfer complete. Per-channel write-back of the running descriptor. CRC-16 (CRC-CCITT) or CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3).

The DMAC runs in any sleep mode whose clock is running; its interrupts can wake the device and its events act without waking it. Hardware or software reset returns all registers to reset values. It needs CLK_DMAC_AHB (MCLK.AHBMASK). Its interrupt goes to the NVIC and its events to the event system. It halts in debug unless DBGCTRL keeps it running. All writable registers except INTPEND and CHINTFLAG can be PAC write-protected, not against an external debugger.

A beat is one bus access, sized by BTCTRL.BEATSIZE. A burst is beats back to back without CPU interference. A block is what one descriptor moves, 1 to 64k beats, and can be interrupted. A transaction is every block of a linked descriptor list. Descriptors must stay in SRAM. For each beat an output event is optional; for each block, interrupts and an output event. At the end of a transaction the channel is suspended or disabled, as configured.

Before enabling the DMAC write BASEADDR (descriptor section) and WRBADDR (write-back section) and enable the priority levels in use (CTRL.LVLENx). Before enabling a channel write its number to CHCTRLA, then its trigger action (CHCTRLA.TRIGACT) and source (CHCTRLA.TRIGSRC), and set up its first descriptor: BTCTRL.BEATSIZE, BTCTRL.VALID = 1, BTCNT, SRCADDR and DSTADDR. For CRC set CRCCTRL.CRCSRC, CRCCTRL.CRCPOLY and, for I/O input, CRCCTRL.CRCBEATSIZE first.

BASEADDR and WRBADDR are writable only with CTRL.DMAENABLE = 0; CTRL.SWRST only with DMAENABLE = 0 and CRCCTRL.CRCSRC = 0; CHCTRLA.SWRST only with that channel disabled; CRCCTRL and CRCCHKSUM only with CRCSRC = 0. CTRL.DMAENABLE turns the DMAC on and off, CHCTRLA.ENABLE a channel (after its number is set), and a non-zero CRCCTRL.CRCSRC the CRC. CTRL.SWRST resets every register except DBGCTRL; CHCTRLA.SWRST resets one disabled channel.

A channel's first descriptor must be valid before it is enabled and triggered. BASEADDR points at channel 0's first descriptor; all first descriptors sit together in channel order. WRBADDR points at channel 0's running descriptor in the write-back section, likewise in channel order. Using the lowest channels saves memory. The two sections may be separate or shared (BASEADDR = WRBADDR); separate sections let a transaction repeat without rewriting its first descriptor and shorten the time from first fetch to first burst.

An enabled, unsuspended channel that gets a trigger joins the pending queue and sets PENDCH.PENDCHx. The arbiter chooses the next channel, whose descriptor goes into the pre-fetch channel and moves to the active channel when the current burst ends, clearing PENDCHx; BUSYCH.BUSYCHx sets or stays set. After its burst(s) a channel rejoins the queue, waits for a trigger, suspends or disables; in the last three cases BUSYCHx clears. A channel suspended while pending leaves the queue but keeps PENDCHx (CHINTFLAGn.SUSP shows it) and rejoins on resume; a channel disabled while pending leaves the queue and clears PENDCHx.

ACTIVE.LVLEXx shows a level with a pending or transferring channel. CHPRILVL.PRILVL gives each channel one of up to four levels, and with all levels enabled (CTRL.LVLENx) a higher level number wins. Within a level, PRICTRL0.RRLVLENx = 0 gives static order, lowest channel number first, which can starve high-numbered channels; RRLVLENx = 1 gives round-robin, the last channel served going to the back, with its number kept in PRICTRL0.LVLPRIx.

Once granted, the channel's descriptor is fetched over the fetch bus, from BASEADDR for a new block or from WRBADDR for one in progress, and data moves over the data bus from source to destination address. Arbitration happens after every burst: if the same channel wins, BTCNT drops by the beats of a burst, the optional beat event is given and the next burst runs; if another wins, BTCNT is written back first. When BTCNT reaches zero BTCTRL.VALID clears, the descriptor is written back, and the transfer-complete and suspend interrupts and block event are given if enabled. After the last block DESCADDR is 0 and the channel suspends or disables (BTCTRL.BLOCKACT); otherwise the next descriptor is loaded, and copied into the channel's write-back slot, ahead of the next arbitration.

A transfer starts on a request from software, a peripheral or an event, chosen per channel in CHCTRLAn.TRIGSRC. CHCTRLAn.TRIGACT sets what one trigger moves: a block (0x0, default), a burst (0x2) or a whole transaction (0x3). With one descriptor the channel disables after its block; with a list, after the last descriptor, waiting for a trigger before each block until then. A trigger arriving during a transfer is held pending (CHSTATUSn.PEND, also in PENDCH); only one is held per channel and further ones are lost. CHSTATUSn.BUSY (also in BUSYCH) is set while the trigger action runs.

Source and destination addresses (SRCADDR, DSTADDR) can each be fixed or incrementing. BTCTRL.SRCINC = 1 increments the source, BTCTRL.DSTINC = 1 the destination. BTCTRL.STEPSIZE sets a larger step for one of them: for the source when BTCTRL.STEPSEL = 1, for the destination when STEPSEL = 0; the other steps by one beat.

With single-beat bursts (CHCTRLAx.BURSTLEN = SINGLE) a channel asks for the bus to write as soon as the FIFO can pass one beat; otherwise it waits for the FIFO to reach the threshold in CHCTRLAx.THRESHOLD. If reading finishes below the threshold, the write starts anyway; if the FIFO empties while reading continues, it waits for the threshold again.

An AHB bus error during a transfer disables the active channel and sets CHINTFLAG.TERR (with an interrupt if enabled); BTCNT is not decremented and is written back before the channel stops. Fetching an invalid descriptor (BTCTRL.VALID = 0), or resuming onto a next-descriptor address of 0, suspends the channel and sets CHINTFLAG.SUSP and CHSTATUS.FERR, with an interrupt if enabled.

Each descriptor's DESCADDR points at the next; the transaction ends after the block whose DESCADDR is 0x00000000. To add one at the end, build it in SRAM with DESCADDR = 0 and point the old last descriptor at it. To insert C between A and B: impossible while B is running; if A has not started, clear A's VALID, point A at C and C at B, set A's VALID; if A is running, suspend the channel by software, do the same, and resume. Changing a descriptor in a list: enable the suspend interrupt and the channel, build the new descriptor (DESCADDR, DSTADDR, SRCADDR, BTCTRL with VALID and optionally suspend), clear VALID on the list and on the descriptor to change, and read DESCADDR back from write-back memory. When the DMA has not yet fetched the one to change, update its DESCADDR, optionally clear suspend, set VALID and optionally resume. If it is running that one, suspend, wait for the interrupt, update DESCADDR in write-back memory, clear the interrupt and resume, then update the list entry the same way. Repeat as needed.
Each priority level has its own QoS setting (PRICTRL0.QOSn). A channel carries its value into the pre-fetch or active slot, and the higher of the two values applies to all DMAC buses.

Writing the Suspend command to CHCTRLB.CMD suspends a channel after its current burst; the command clears itself, CHINTFLAG.SUSP sets and the suspend interrupt fires if enabled. BTCTRL.BLOCKACT = 0x2 or 0x3 suspends the channel after a block; it stays enabled and keeps taking triggers but leaves arbitration. Fetching an invalid descriptor also suspends it, with CHSTATUS.FERR set. A disabled channel ignores Suspend. The Resume command restarts a suspended channel where it stopped, or, if given before a suspend, makes it skip the next one.

Only the lowest channels take event inputs. Set up the event system and CHEVCTRL.EVIE = 1 first. Normal transfer: an event triggers a beat or burst, is acknowledged at once and sets CHSTATUS.PEND and PENDCH.PENDCHn; an event arriving while pending is lost. Conditional transfer on strobe: a peripheral trigger is registered only when it coincides with an event, for timed or periodic transfers. Conditional transfer: each peripheral trigger is stored when an event arrives (one peripheral the event source, another the trigger). Conditional block transfer: an event must arrive before a block starts and is acknowledged when the block ends. Suspend: acknowledged when the current AHB access ends. Resume: acknowledged at once, clearing CHINTFLAG.SUSP. Skip next block suspend: resumes a suspended channel, or is held until the next block suspend, which it cancels. Increase priority: raises the channel to the top priority and maximum QoS until its trigger action completes.

Only channels with event outputs offer them; CHEVCTRL.EVOE enables one and CHEVCTRL.EVOMODE picks its kind. Transfer events (EVOMODE = DEFAULT) are one-CLK_DMAC_AHB-cycle strobes chosen per descriptor in BTCTRL.EVOSEL: a block event at the end of each block (set it in the last descriptor only for a transaction-complete event) or a burst event at the end of each burst. The trigger action event (EVOMODE = TRIGACT) is a level, high from the trigger until its action completes.

Disabling a channel stops it cleanly; disabling the DMAC stops every channel. The active channel stops after its current beat and the write-back update; the others stop on the next clock. CHCTRLA.ENABLE clears when a channel has stopped and CTRL.DMAENABLE when the whole DMAC has.

Checks data for corruption with CRC-16 (CRC-CCITT) or CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3), giving a 16- or 32-bit checksum; a CRC-n catches any single error burst of n bits or fewer and all but 2^-n of longer bursts. The input is one DMA channel or the APB interface (CRCCTRL.CRCSRC); the result is in CRCCHKSUM, bit-reversed and complemented for CRC-32. CRCCTRL.CRCPOLY chooses the polynomial, CRC-16 by default. The engine works byte by byte: on a DMA channel it uses the channel's beat size; from the APB, CRCCTRL.CRCBEATSIZE selects 8, 16 or 32 bits and each byte written to CRCDATAIN is processed in turn, so a 32-bit write takes four cycles. Write new data only while CRCSTATUS.CRCBUSY is clear. On a DMA channel the checksum is ready when the transaction completes or aborts; SRAM, Flash or I/O data can be checked by sending it through a channel, with CRCDATAIN as the destination.

Computes the checksum of a memory block automatically. When the channel is enabled and its descriptor fetched, CRCCHKSUM loads the initial value CHKINIT from the descriptor's DSTADDR; the DMA reads the source data, and at the end the result is in CRCCHKSUM and CHINTFLAGn.TCMPL sets. Linked descriptors continue the calculation, and the channel disables after the last. Set-up: CRCCTRL.CRCSRC to a DMA channel; reserve descriptor memory; in each descriptor set DESCADDR, DSTADDR = CHKINIT in the first, SRCADDR, BTCNT, CRCCTRL.CRCMODE = CRCGEN and the interrupts; enable the channel.

Checks a memory block repeatedly against the expected CRC stored in its last location. After loading CHKINIT as above and reading the whole block, the result is compared with zero (CRC-16) or the CRC-32 magic number.
