A mismatch disables the channel and sets CHSTATUSn.CRCERR and CHINTFLAGn.TERR; a match sets CHINTFLAGn.TCMPL and the DMA re-fetches the single descriptor, or goes back to the first of a list, and runs again on the next trigger. Set-up as for generation, with CRCCTRL.CRCMODE = CRCMON.

Per-channel interrupts: TCMPL (block complete), TERR (bus error or invalid descriptor) and SUSP (channel suspended), all on one NVIC line. INTSTATUS shows which channels have pending interrupts and CHINTFLAG which condition; INTPEND gives the lowest channel with one pending and its flags. Output event CH comes at block or beat completion as BTCTRL.EVOSEL selects, enabled by CHEVCTRLx.EVOE. Input event actions TRIG, CTRIG, CBLOCK, SUSPEND, RESUME, SSKIP and INCPRI are enabled by CHEVCTRLx.EVIE; with several events on one channel, every enabled action responds to any of them. Not every channel has event inputs and outputs.

Turns up to 16 pins (EXTINT0 to 15) into interrupt lines, each maskable on its own, sensing rising, falling or both edges or a high or low level, with a spike filter, optional debouncing, and synchronous or asynchronous edge detection; asynchronous lines can wake the device from sleep modes with every clock stopped. Each pin can also make an event. A separate NMI pin works the same way but drives the CPU's non-maskable interrupt.

The pins must be set up in PORT. Every interrupt works down to Standby, and the EIC can mask some to stop them waking the device. CLK_EIC_APB is gated in MCLK. Filtering, synchronous edge detection and debouncing need a clock, either GCLK_EIC (wider frequency choice) or CLK_ULP32K from OSCULP32K (lowest power), both asynchronous to the bus clock. Each EXTINT line and the NMI have their own interrupt request lines; the NMI needs no interrupt set-up. It keeps running in debug halt. All writable registers except INTFLAG and NMIFLAG can be PAC write-protected.

Enable CLK_EIC_APB; set up the NMI in NMICTRL if used; enable GCLK_EIC or CLK_ULP32K if the NMI uses edge detection or filtering, or any EXTINT uses filtering, synchronous edge detection or debouncing (GCLK_EIC for filtering above 32.768 kHz; CLK_ULP32K, chosen with CTRLA.CKSEL = 1, for lowest power); write sense and filter settings in CONFIG0 or CONFIG1; optionally enable asynchronous mode and debouncing; then set CTRLA.ENABLE. CTRLA.CKSEL, EVCTRL, CONFIGn, ASYNCH, DEBOUNCEN and DPRESCALER are enable-protected; protected CTRLA bits can go in the write that sets ENABLE but not the one that clears it. CTRLA.SWRST resets and disables the EIC.

CONFIGn.SENSEx chooses the condition for each pin; meeting it sets INTFLAG.EXTINT[x]. In edge mode the flag sets again only on a new edge after clearing; in level mode it sets again at once if the pin still matches. CONFIGn.FILTENx = 1 adds a majority filter that samples the pin three times on the EIC clock and passes the value two or more samples agree on. Level detection without filter, and asynchronous edge detection, need no EIC clock and give asynchronous interrupts and events. Filtering, synchronous edge detection and debouncing request the EIC clock themselves (GCLK_EIC must be enabled in GCLK if chosen); the pin is then sampled at that rate, so pulses shorter than two EIC clock periods may be missed.

The NMI pin senses edges or levels as set in NMICTRL.NMISENSE, with filtering by NMICTRL.NMIFILTEN; edge detection or filtering needs GCLK_EIC or CLK_ULP32K. NMISENSE alone turns it on, without enabling the EIC. A detection sets NMIFLAG.NMI, which always raises an interrupt request.

ASYNCH.ASYNCH[x] = 0 (default) samples EXTINT or NMI on the EIC clock (CTRLA.CKSEL) and flags a change between two samples; the EIC clock is needed. ASYNCH[x] = 1 lets the pin set its flag directly with no EIC clock requested. Both modes work in Idle and Standby.

Edge detection can add a debouncer, synchronous or asynchronous as ASYNCH[x] selects, clocked by the EIC clock and ticked by a low-frequency clock from DPRESCALER.DPRESCALERn. It needs CONFIGy.SENSEx set to RISE, FALL or BOTH and excludes the filter on that pin. A sample differing from the valid pin state on a low-frequency tick counts up a transition counter; a sample equal to it (on each EIC clock with DPRESCALER.TICKON = 0, or each tick with TICKON = 1) resets the counter. The threshold is 4 (DPRESCALER.STATESn = 0) or 8 (STATESn = 1) in synchronous mode and 4 in asynchronous mode. PINSTATE gives the debounced pin states.

The pin is sampled on the EIC clock, and an edge counts once the sample has differed from the valid state for 4 or 8 low-frequency ticks in a row; then PINSTATE[x] changes and INTFLAG.EXTINT[x] sets. Needs the EIC clock; works in Idle and Standby.

The pin feeds an edge detector directly: an edge away from the valid state changes PINSTATE[x] and INTFLAG.EXTINT[x] at once, after which the detector ignores the pin until four low-frequency ticks pass with no edge, any edge restarting the count. The EIC clock is requested; works in Idle and Standby.

Sources are the EXTINT pins and the NMI, each with its own request line; EXTINT interrupts are enabled in INTENSET and disabled in INTENCLR, while the NMI is always on. When one EXTINT is mapped to two or more pins, only the first one set up works. Output event EXTINTx, enabled in EVCTRL.EXTINTEO, comes when the pin matches its CONFIGn condition. In sleep a pin wakes the device when it matches its condition and its INTENSET bit is set. CTRLA.SWRST and CTRLA.ENABLE are write-synchronized.

An IEEE 802.3 Ethernet MAC for 10 and 100 Mbit/s, half or full duplex at either speed; it keeps the GMAC name in its registers but has no gigabit mode. It connects to a PHY over MII or RMII, manages it over MDIO, and moves frames to and from memory with its own AHB DMA. Features: RMON/MIB statistics counters, programmable DMA burst length and endianness, automatic pad and CRC on transmit, automatic discard of received frames with errors, IP/TCP/UDP checksum offload on receive and transmit for IPv4 and IPv6, address filtering on four specific 48-bit addresses and four type IDs, unicast and multicast hash matching, promiscuous mode, Wake-on-LAN, jumbo frames to 10240 bytes, full-duplex pause-frame flow control and half-duplex flow control by forced collisions, 802.1Q VLAN tag recognition, programmable inter-packet gap stretch, an IEEE 1588 time stamp unit with PTP frame recognition and 802.1AS support, 802.1Qav credit-based shaping on the two highest-priority queues, and 802.3az Energy Efficient Ethernet.

Signal interfaces: MII or RMII to an external PHY, MDIO for PHY management, an APB client port for its registers, an AHB host port for memory access, and the internal GTSUCOMP signal that flags a TSU timer compare match.

Its pins are set up in PORT. It keeps working in Idle and Standby while REF_CLK or GRXCK runs. Any GMAC interrupt wakes the device from Idle; from Standby only the Wake-on-LAN interrupt wakes the CPU, and its ISR flags are not set. Register access and the GMAC MCK come from MCLK; in MII mode GTXCK and GRXCK are external clocks, and in RMII mode the reference clock REF_CLK is external. One interrupt line goes to the NVIC. The timestamp-comparison event goes to EVSYS.

The transmit side takes data from the FIFO and adds preamble, padding and the frame check sequence. In half duplex it follows CSMA/CD: transmission waits while CRS is active, and a collision (COL) during transmission sends a jam sequence and retries after a random back-off; CRS and COL do nothing in full duplex. The receive side checks preamble, FCS, alignment and length, can strip the CRC, and accepts jumbo frames up to 10240 bytes when enabled. The address checker matches four specific 48-bit addresses and four type IDs, has a 64-bit hash register for unicast and multicast matching, recognises the all-ones broadcast address, can copy every frame or drop all untagged frames, and detects Wake-on-LAN events. Receive checksum offload (IPv4 and IPv6) can discard frames with bad checksums.

The IEEE 1588 TSU is a 94-bit timer: bits [93:46] count seconds (registers TSH and TSL), bits [45:16] count nanoseconds (TN), and bits [15:0] hold fractions of a nanosecond. Bits [45:0] wrap at one second, when an interrupt is raised. Each MCK period adds a programmable increment with a resolution of about 15.2 fs, and the value can be read, written and stepped up or down in 1 ns units over the APB. Eight further 80-bit registers capture the time PTP event frames are sent and received, each update raising an interrupt. A comparator checks the 48 seconds bits and the upper 22 nanoseconds bits against NSC, SCL and SCH; on a match it drives GTSUCOMP and can raise the interrupt at bit 29 of the interrupt status register.

The DMA feeds the MAC FIFO with scatter-gather access to memory and buffers whole frames in dual-port SRAM packet buffers on both paths, so it tolerates long AHB latencies. Full store and forward holds each complete frame: a collided frame is replayed from the buffer rather than fetched again, frames received with errors are dropped before reaching the AHB, and transmit checksum offload works. Partial store and forward (full duplex only, enabled with the watermarks in TPSF and RPSF) starts forwarding once a programmed amount is buffered, to cut latency; the transmit watermark must be at least 20, the receive watermark has no limit. Received packets can be flushed manually, or automatically when no AHB buffer is free. Transmit and receive each have their own descriptor list, every descriptor pointing at a memory buffer, so a frame may be scattered.

Received frames, optionally with FCS, go into AHB buffers of 64 bytes to 16 Kbytes (DCFGR, default 128 bytes). A list of two-word descriptors, starting at the address in RBQB, holds each buffer's address and its status. A frame longer than one buffer fills buffers in turn; all but the last get a status of zeros apart from start-of-frame on the first, and the last carries the full frame status. The GMAC sets bit 0 of word 0 when it has used a buffer, and software clears it to give the buffer back. The first buffer of a frame may start up to three bytes past the word boundary (NCFGR bits 14 and 15), shortening it by that much. Write RBQB before enabling reception; afterwards writes are ignored and reads return the current pointer, valid only with reception off. The internal queue pointer steps two words per buffer and returns to RBQB after a descriptor with its wrap bit set.

An error during reception recovers only the buffer being written; earlier buffers of that frame stay used, so a fragment shows up as a start-of-frame buffer following one without end-of-frame. A sound 10/100 network has no over-length frames and no CRC-errored frames over 128 bytes, and collision fragments are under 128 bytes, so with the default 128-byte buffers fragments are rare. In full store and forward only good frames leave the DMA, though a DMA error (a used bit read on a later buffer) can still leave one. If the descriptor read is already marked used, the buffer-not-available status bit sets, an interrupt fires and the receive resource error count goes up; the descriptor is then re-read for every new frame. Without full store and forward that frame is discarded; with it, frames wait in the packet buffer unless DCFGR.DDRP is set to discard them (off by default), which can overflow the buffer. Overrun happens when the packet buffer is full or HRESP is not OK (full store and forward), or otherwise when the AHB is not granted in time, HRESP is not OK, or a new frame starts before the last one's write-back ends; the overrun interrupt fires and the buffer is reused by the next recognised frame. NCR.FNP = 1 flushes one packet from the receive packet buffer, but only while the RX DMA is idle.

A transmit frame is 1 to 16384 bytes, spread over one or more buffers (zero-length buffers allowed, at most 128 per frame). Descriptors are two words, starting at the address in TBQB: a byte address (the low bits offset the data from the word boundary) and a control/status word. With automatic CRC the MAC also pads frames to 64 bytes; with CRC disabled in the descriptor the frame must already be at least 64 bytes and no pad is added. After transmission the status and used bit are written to word 1 of the frame's first buffer. TBQB can be written only while transmission is disabled or halted; halting keeps the queue pointer so transmission resumes after the last good frame, and clearing NCR.TXEN resets the pointer to TBQB (disabling receive does not reset the receive pointer).

Word 1 is set up with the length, whether the MAC adds CRC and whether the buffer is the frame's last. NCR.TSTART starts transmission; it halts on reading a descriptor with its used bit set, on a transmit error, or on NCR.THALT (which waits for the current frame to finish). A received pause frame suspends transmission when NCR.TXPF is set. TSTART may be written again while transmitting; TSR.TXGO shows the running state and clears when transmit is disabled, a used descriptor is read, THALT is written, or a transmit error (too many retries, underrun) occurs. A collision during a multi-buffer frame restarts it from its first buffer, replayed from the packet buffer. A used bit read in the middle of a multi-buffer frame is a transmit error: transmission stops, GTXER asserts and the FCS is bad. After an error or used bit, writing TSTART restarts from the first descriptor of the interrupted frame.

Buffer management uses SINGLE or INCR accesses. Data transfers use the fixed burst length set in DCFGR.FBLDO (SINGLE, INCR4, INCR8 or INCR16) when there is room and data enough, and SINGLE accesses at the start or end of a buffer and at each 1 Kbyte boundary, which bursts never cross. A fixed burst ends early only on an AHB error or when receive or transmit is disabled in NCR.

The transmit packet buffer keeps fetching frame data from memory until full and then holds that level. Three words per packet (two with a 64-bit data path) at the end of each packet hold its status and statistics, so status, statistics and interrupts follow the order frames were fetched. An AHB error while fetching stops further fetches; frames already buffered are still sent, and then the error is reported in order. In full store and forward a frame too big for the packet buffer is flushed and the DMA halts with an error, so the buffer must hold the largest frame to be sent; the MAC starts only once the whole frame is buffered, so it cannot underflow, and the frame stays until sent or abandoned. In partial store and forward the MAC starts once enough data is in; if it then outruns the DMA, transmission ends early, the buffer is flushed, and only NCR.TSTART restarts it. In half duplex a frame stays buffered until sent or abandoned after too many retries; in full duplex it is removed as it goes. A collided frame is retried from the buffer and flushed after 16 failed attempts.

The receive packet buffer stores frames with their status and statistics (three words per packet, two on a 64-bit path). In full store and forward a frame with an error is flushed at once and only its status and statistics reach the registers; good frames are burst to memory once their status is known. When the buffer fills, later packets are dropped and the RX overflow interrupt fires. In partial store and forward the DMA starts moving data before the status is known and picks the status up as soon as it arrives.

Data arrives 32 bits at a time and is processed in bytes, then sent over MII. The MAC adds preamble and start-of-frame delimiter, pads to 60 bytes if needed, and appends the inverted 32-bit CRC to reach at least 64 bytes; the no-CRC bit in the last buffer's descriptor (or from the FIFO interface) suppresses both. In full duplex frames go at once, at least 96 bit times apart. In half duplex it waits for carrier sense to drop plus 96 bit times; on a collision it finishes any preamble or SFD, sends a 32-bit jam, and backs off by a time from the low 10 bits of transmit data XORed with a 10-bit pseudo-random number, using 1 bit after the first collision, 2 after the second and so on up to 10 (truncated binary exponential back-off, IEEE 802.3 clause 4.2.3.2.5). After 16 consecutive collided attempts it reports an error and stops. Collisions and late collisions are treated alike, the late collision reported in descriptor word 1 bit 26, TSR bit 7 and interrupt status bit 5. A transmit DMA underrun appends a bad CRC and asserts GTXER, which cannot happen with the packet buffers.

With NCFGR bit 28 set, in full duplex only, the gap after a frame grows with that frame's length: IPGS bits [7:0] multiply the previous frame length (with preamble) and bits [15:8] plus one divide it. The gap never falls below 96 bit times.

With the back-pressure bit set in NCR, or the HDFC bit in the UR register, in 10 or 100 Mbit/s half duplex, the transmitter sends 64 bits (16 nibbles of 1011, or 64 ones in bit-rate mode) whenever a frame comes in, forcing a collision.

Works on a 16-bit path, checks preamble, FCS, alignment and length, and keeps the destination address for the address checker. A frame found too long is marked bad and stops going to memory; the DMA recovers the buffer of a bad frame. NCFGR bit 17 stores frames without their FCS and reports the length four bytes shorter. Alignment, CRC, short, long, jabber and symbol errors each increment a statistics counter. NCFGR bit 26 keeps CRC-errored frames (the FCS error counter still counts) and, outside jumbo mode, marks FCS validity in descriptor word 1 bit 13, for protocols such as EtherCAT. NCFGR bit 16 discards frames of 64 to 1518 bytes whose measured length is shorter than their length field (bytes 13 and 14), counting them in a 10-bit statistics register; length fields of 0x0600 or more are not checked.

IP, TCP and UDP checksums can be checked on receive (NCFGR bit 24, RXCOEN) and generated on transmit (DCFGR bit 11). The IPv4 header checksum is the 16-bit ones' complement of the ones' complement sum of the header's 16-bit words; TCP and UDP checksums cover the header, the data and an IP pseudo header. The protocol stack must know the offload is there. On receive the IPv4 header checksum is checked (RFC 791) when any VLAN header is four octets with CFI clear, encapsulation is RFC 894 Ethernet type or RFC 1042 SNAP, the packet is IPv4 and the header length is valid; TCP (RFC 793) or UDP (RFC 768) checksums are checked for IPv4 or IPv6 packets with a good IPv4 header checksum and no fragmentation. The result and SNAP status replace the type ID bits in the receive descriptor, and a packet with a wrong checksum is discarded and counted. Transmit offload needs full store and forward, since the whole frame must be buffered before the checksums are written into its headers; the frame must be recognised and given without FCS (descriptor word 1 bit 16 clear). If a checksum cannot be generated, bits 22:20 of the write-back status say why and the frame is sent without substitution.

Which frames reach memory depends on the NCFGR settings, on what the specific-address, type ID and hash registers hold, and on each frame's destination address and type field. Unless NCFGR bit 25 is set, no frame is copied while the GMAC is transmitting in half duplex when its destination address arrives. Each byte is sent LSB first, and a frame opens with its 6-byte destination address, whose first bit is the group bit (1 multicast, 0 unicast; all ones is broadcast). Each of the four specific addresses uses a bottom register (first four bytes) and a top register (last two): writing the bottom deactivates it and writing the top activates it, and a match passes the frame. Four type ID registers, each enabled by bit 31 and zero (disabled) at reset, match the length/type field (bytes 13 and 14 in untagged, non-SNAP frames); any kind of match passes the frame, and the descriptor tells which type ID matched when receive checksum offload is off.

operation.topic: GMAC broadcast, hash and promiscuous modes
operation.text: Broadcast frames (0xFFFFFFFFFFFF) are stored only while the no-broadcast bit in NCFGR is 0. The 64-bit hash register is split into HRB (low) and HRT (high); the unicast and multicast hash enable bits in NCFGR turn hash matching on. A frame matches when the bit its 6-bit hash index points at is set, as multicast if da[0] is 1 and multicast hash is enabled, or as unicast if da[0] is 0 and unicast hash is enabled. All ones in the hash register with multicast hash enabled receives every multicast frame. Copy All Frames stores everything except frames too long, too short, with FCS errors (unless NCFGR bit 26 is set) or with GRXER asserted. NCFGR bit 23 stops pause frames being stored whatever else matches.

The four-byte VLAN tag sits at the 13th byte of the frame; NCFGR bit 8 raises the accepted frame length to 1536 bytes to allow for it. A VID of 0x000 marks a priority-tagged frame. The receive descriptor reports VLAN tagged (bit 21), priority tagged (bit 20, which implies bit 21), the priority (bits 19:17) and CFI (bit 16). The discard-non-VLAN bit in NCFGR rejects all untagged frames.

Four events, enabled by bits [19:16] of the WOL register, can wake the device: a magic packet, an ARP request to the device's IP address, a specific address 1 match, and a multicast hash match. Receive must be enabled in NCR, though no receive buffer is needed. ARP, specific-address and multicast events fire even on errored frames; a magic packet must be error free. Magic packet (bit 16): destination matches specific address 1, at least six 0xFF bytes, then 16 copies of the specific address 1 value. ARP request (bit 17): broadcasts allowed (NCFGR bit 5), broadcast destination, type ID 0x0806 in bytes 13 and 14, ARP operation 0x0001 in bytes 21 and 22, and the low 16 bits of the target protocol address (bytes 41 and 42) equal to WOL bits [15:0]; field positions shift for a VLAN tag, and a target value of 0x0000 never matches. Specific address 1 (bit 18): destination equals specific address 1. Multicast (bit 19): multicast hashing enabled (NCFGR bit 6), destination matches the hash and is not broadcast.

PTP frames over Ethernet, UDP/IPv4 or UDP/IPv6 are recognised, and output signals mark the time-stamp point (from start-of-frame delimiter to end of frame) for every frame and the passage of PTP event frames. Sync frames are recognised with both the 802.1AS multicast address 0180C200000E and the 1588 addresses, so both work at once. A time stamp is taken as the start-of-frame delimiter crosses the MII and can raise an interrupt (IER); the frame reaches memory only if the filters pass it. Sync and delay_req times go to TSSx, EFTx and EFRx; the version 2 peer delay messages Pdelay_Req and Pdelay_Resp go to PEFTx and PEFRx. Four encapsulations are recognised: version 1 over UDP/IPv4 multicast, and version 2 over UDP/IPv4 multicast, UDP/IPv6 multicast and Ethernet multicast. Version 1 sync and delay request frames need IP type, UDP, destination 224.0.1.129, 130, 131 or 132, UDP port 319 and control field 0x00 (sync) or 0x01 (delay request). Version 2 frames are typed by the message type in the first PTP byte (0x0 sync, 0x1 delay_req, 0x2 Pdelay_Req, 0x3 Pdelay_Resp), the version being in the second byte. With Ethernet multicast 011B19000000 sync and delay request are recognised (message type 00 and 01); with 0180C200000E sync, Pdelay_Req and Pdelay_Resp (00, 02, 03).

TI bits [7:0] set the nanoseconds added each clock cycle, and TISUBN adds 16 bits of sub-nanosecond increment (about 15 fs resolution). TI bits [15:8] are an alternative increment, used after the number of increments in bits [23:16]; zero there means it is never used. The 8-bit count field supports clocks up to 50 MHz in 200 kHz steps; with whole-nanosecond increments alone only 8, 10, 20, 25, 40, 50, 100, 125, 200 and 250 MHz would work. Examples: a 10.2 MHz clock increments 98 ns for 50 cycles then 100 ns (98 ns × 50 + 100 ns = 5000 ns), TI = 0x00326462; a 49.8 MHz clock increments 20 ns for 248 cycles then 40 ns (20 ns × 248 + 40 ns = 5000 ns), TI = 0x00F82814.

With NCFGR bit 13 set, a received pause frame with non-zero quantum pauses transmission (IEEE 802.3 clause 31, annexes 31A and 31B). A valid pause frame is addressed to specific address 1 or to 0x0180C2000001, has type 0x8808 and opcode 0x0001, and has no FCS or other error (errored ones are discarded); each valid one loads the Pause Time register and counts in the pause-frames-received statistic. Interrupt status bit 12 flags a non-zero-quantum pause frame and bit 13 a zero-quantum one, each if enabled in the mask register. After the current frame, nothing is sent until the pause time reaches zero; pausing happens only in full duplex, though the interrupt still fires in half duplex. The pause time counts down every 512 bit times once transmission stops, or every GTXCK cycle with the retry test bit (NCFGR bit 12) set; reaching zero also sets interrupt bit 13.

Writing 1 to NCR bit 11 or bit 12 sends a pause frame, provided full duplex is selected and transmit is enabled; it goes at once if transmit is idle, otherwise between frames. The frame carries destination 01-80-C2-00-00-01, source from specific address 1, type 88-08, opcode 00-01, a pause quantum, zero fill to minimum length and a valid FCS. Bit 11 takes the quantum from the Transmit Pause Quantum register (0xFFFF, the maximum, at reset); bit 12 sends quantum zero. Afterwards interrupt status bit 14 sets and only the pause-frames-transmitted statistic counts it. Pause frames may also be sent as ordinary frames.

IEEE 802.3az: a transmit path with nothing to send can go into low-power idle (LPI), and the PHY can follow its partner's transmit path into low power on its receive side; the link stays up, no frames are lost, and each direction is independent. Both ends must have advertised LPI in auto-negotiation. Low power is controlled at the MII reconciliation sublayer, entered only when there is nothing to transmit, and should not be requested until the link has been up at least one second. LPI is requested on the MII by holding tx_en low and tx_er high while txd = 0x01; the PHY then sends sleep, goes quiet and sends periodic refreshes (periods in 802.3az table 78-2). LPI ends with normal idle for the wake time, which has a default and can be tuned with LLDP (802.3az clause 79). Receive-side LPI is flagged when sleep and refresh signalling is seen.

802.1Qav credit-based shaping on the two highest-priority queues, enabled in the CBS control register, limits their traffic so other queues can send. Each queue has a credit counter in bytes and may transmit only with non-negative credit. While held off by another queue's transmission its credit rises at IdleSlope (CBSISQx), which must be below portTransmitRate (the MAC's rate in bit/s); while transmitting it falls at sendSlope = portTransmitRate - IdleSlope, and may go negative, which holds the queue off afterwards but never cuts a transfer short. The highest-priority queue always goes first whatever the credits. Both slopes are limited to portTransmitRate divided by the number of bits moved per MII clock; at 100 Mbit/s that is 100 Mbit/s / 4 = 0x17D7840.

MII (txd[3:0], rxd[3:0]) and RMII (txd[1:0], rxd[1:0]) both run at 10 or 100 Mbit/s, chosen by the speed bit in NCFGR. The jumbo frames bit in NCFGR accepts frames up to 10240 bytes, beyond IEEE 802.3 and off by default; larger frames are then discarded.

Configuration such as loopback and frequency ratios is changed only with transmit and receive disabled. Changing loopback takes three separate NCR writes: disable transmit and receive, change loopback, re-enable. Receive list: allocate N buffers of the DCFGR buffer length and 8N bytes of descriptors, all with bit 0 of word 0 clear (owned by the GMAC) and the wrap bit (word 0 bit 1) on the last; write the list address to the receive queue pointer; then set the address registers and enable reception in NCR. Transmit list: allocate N buffers of 1 to 2047 bytes (up to 128 per frame) and 8N bytes of descriptors with word 1 bit 31 clear and the wrap bit (word 1 bit 30) on the last; write the list address to the transmit queue pointer; then enable transmission in NCR. The hash pair and the four specific address pairs are written bottom first: writing the bottom disables matching on that pair and writing the top re-enables it, at any time. For example, to match 21:43:65:87:A9:CB, specific address 1 bottom (0x98) = 0x8765_4321 and top (0x9C) = 0x0000_CBA9.

The PHY Maintenance register is a shift register: writing it sends a management frame on MDIO (IEEE 802.3 section 22.2.4.5), the MSB going out and the LSB coming in on each MDC cycle. Network Status bit 2 sets when the shift is done, about 2000 MCK cycles later with NCFGR bits 18:16 = 010, and raises an interrupt; on a read the data bits then hold the PHY's reply. MDC must not exceed 2.5 MHz (400 ns minimum period) and is MCK divided by a ratio set by three NCFGR bits.

Eighteen interrupt conditions are ORed into one interrupt line; the Interrupt Status register tells them apart and clears on read by default (it can be set to write-one-to-clear). All are disabled at reset; IER enables, IDR disables, and IMR reads 1 for a disabled interrupt.

To send: enable transmit in NCR; put the data in memory (buffers need not be contiguous, any byte lengths); write buffer addresses to word 0 and control and length to word 1 of the descriptors; write the first descriptor's address to the transmit queue pointer; enable interrupts; set NCR.TSTART. A received frame is stored when it matches a specific address, a type ID or the hash, is a permitted broadcast, or copy-all is on. It is written at the receive queue pointer's buffer; when complete the descriptor gets the match reason and is handed to software and the receive-complete interrupt sets, and software copies the data and clears the ownership bit. Too slow a write sets the receive overrun interrupt, no free buffer sets receive-buffer-not-available, and a failed frame is counted and dropped silently.

Statistics registers occupy 0x100 to 0x1B0: octets, frames, broadcast, multicast and pause frames sent; sent frames by size (64, 65 to 127, 128 to 255, 256 to 511, 512 to 1023, 1024 to 1518, over 1518 bytes); transmit underruns; single, multiple, excessive and late collisions; deferred frames; carrier sense errors; octets, frames, broadcast, multicast and pause frames received; received frames by size (64 to 1518 in the same bands and 1519 to maximum); undersize, oversize and jabber frames; FCS, length field, symbol and alignment errors; receive resource errors and overruns; IP header, TCP and UDP checksum errors. Each clears when read and sticks at all ones, so read them often enough. Receive counters count only while NCR.RXEN is set. Read bits 31:0 of the octets-sent and octets-received counters before bits 47:32.

Controls the Flash, which has two banks: reads from one bank continue during a write or erase in the opposite bank (read-while-write). Two 32-bit AHB ports read and write the main address space, a third AHB port serves the SmartEEPROM (EEPROM emulation), and a 32-bit APB port takes commands and configuration. Every NVM section, calibration and system configuration included, is memory mapped. Features: programmable read wait states, per-region write and erase protection, extra protection for a bootloader, a security bit that locks the device, power-down of the Flash in sleep with wake on sleep exit or on first access, a one-line cache per AHB port, dual-bank firmware update, and error correction (ECC).

No pins. It runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs, and its interrupt (one line to the NVIC) can wake the device. The Flash enters low power automatically when the PM enters Standby, or on the SPRM command, and wakes on leaving sleep, on an AHB access or when a command needs it, as CTRLA.PRM sets; PM STDBYCFG.FASTWKUP trades wake-up time against static power. Two synchronous clocks, CLK_NVMCTRL_AHB and CLK_NVMCTRL_APB. When the AHB clock changes, the wait states must suit it (the electrical characteristics give the number per frequency range): CTRLA.AUTOWS sets them automatically, or CTRLA.RWS sets a fixed number. AHB bursts can fill the NVM page buffer without re-arbitration so concurrent writers keep their data whole. All writable registers except INTFLAG can be PAC write-protected. With the security bit set the NVM cannot be accessed. Reading a buffered-mode SmartEEPROM from a debugger is intrusive, since the NVM page buffer must be flushed if that page being read is being modified.

AHB0 and AHB1 give access to the main array, the auxiliary pages and the NVM page buffer; AHB2 reaches the SmartEEPROM, which reads and writes a reserved area of the NVM indirectly. After power-up the controller runs a power-up sequence, stalling AHB access, and then works with no configuration. The SWRST command resets the NVM, repeats the power-up sequence (reloading calibration) and resets all APB registers; STATUS.READY is low while it runs and every AHB access stalls until it ends.

The main address space holds the two banks, BANKA and BANKB, which can be swapped. The auxiliary space holds three kinds of page: USER (user configuration), CB (calibration) and FS (factory and signature). Each bank is made of blocks of sixteen 512-byte pages. Low blocks of the main space can be reserved for a bootloader with the BOOTPROT fuses and high blocks for the SmartEEPROM. CB (factory calibration and system configuration): 0x00800000, 1 page, read-only. FS (factory signature): 0x00806000, 4 pages, read-only. USER (start-up configuration; its first word is reserved and configures the device at NVMCTRL start-up): 0x00804000, 1 page, read-write. Main space: 0x00000000, PARAM.NVMP pages, read-write, in 32 equal regions each lockable against write and erase; RUNLOCK shows their state, loaded at power-up from the region lock fuses in the NVM LOCKS field, and the LR and UR commands change it. Bootloader: from 0x00000000, (15 - STATUS.BOOTPROT) × 8192 bytes, read-only unless STATUS.BPDIS is set; a write or erase inside it sets STATUS.PROGE and STATUS.LOCKE; the SBPDIS and CBPDIS commands set and clear BPDIS, so a new bootloader can be written without rewriting the user page and restarting; chip erase never erases it, even with BPDIS set. SmartEEPROM raw data: at PARAM.NVMP × 512 - 2 × SEESTAT.SBLK × 8192, size 2 × SEESTAT.SBLK × 8192, neither readable nor writable: an AHB0/1 access causes a HardFault, and a command addressed there is discarded with INTFLAG.DONE and INTFLAG.ADDRE set.

With STATUS.AFIRST = 1 BANKA sits at the base of the main address space, otherwise BANKB; the banks' start addresses depend on AFIRST and the Flash size. The AHBMUX arbitrates AHB0, AHB1 and SmartEEPROM accesses by fixed priority: AHB0 first, then AHB1, then SmartEEPROM, then AHB2. An accepted transfer must finish its data phase, so a lower-priority access already granted can stall a higher one when wait states are above zero. Bursts are not re-arbitrated, so several hosts can write the NVM page buffer without software semaphores when used with the automatic write modes (ADW, AQW, APW) and burst sizes that are a multiple of the write size; CTRLA.AHBNS0 and CTRLA.AHBNS1 force re-arbitration of bursts on AHB0 and AHB1.

The main space is split into 32 equal regions whatever BOOTPROT and SmartEEPROM are set to, each with a lock bit against write and erase; all are unlocked when shipped. The Lock Region and Unlock Region commands act on the region holding ADDR (written by software or taken from the last AHB write) until the next reset; RUNLOCK shows the state. The power-up default is changed by writing the user page and takes effect after the next reset. LR and UR change only RUNLOCK, not the user page.

Reads and automatic page writes address the main space directly over the AHB; manual page writes, erases and other operations are commands written to CTRLB.CMD with CTRLB.CMDEX = 0xA5. STATUS.READY clears while a command runs; a command written then is ignored and sets INTFLAG.PROGE, and an invalid command sets PROGE and DONE. CTRLA sets the power reduction mode, read wait states and write mode. ADDR, the address argument, updates on APB writes to it and on AHB writes to the NVM page buffer; APB writes to it are dropped with INTFLAG.ADDRE when a command is reading it, while the NVM page buffer is being written (until the NVM page buffer write, or in automatic modes the write command, is done), or when a command runs at an illegal address. While ADDRE is set every command needing an address is discarded with PROGE set, so clear ADDRE first.

Reads address the main or auxiliary space over the AHB and return after CTRLA.RWS wait states. The two banks cannot be read at once; simultaneous reads are arbitrated AHB0 first, then AHB1, then AHB2, lower priorities stalling. Reading a bank stalls while that bank is programmed or erased, unless suspend is used; reading the other bank does not stall.

A debugger Chip Erase erases the whole main space except the BOOTPROT section; otherwise EP erases a page and EB a block, and WP writes a page and WQW a quad-word, as the address space allows. A region can be locked after programming against stray writes and erases. Data goes through the AHB into the NVM page buffer, one NVM page in size and shared by both banks; while a write command runs (STATUS.READY = 0) an AHB write stalls until it ends, but the NVM page buffer can be written during a block erase. Page buffer writes must be 32-bit; 8- and 16-bit writes cause a PAC error. Internally the buffer is written 64 bits at a time through PBLDATA[1] and PBLDATA[0], which hold one 64-bit section: words within a section may come in any order, and moving to another section resets PBLDATA to all ones, so a lone 32-bit write fills the other word of its section with ones. Each AHB write stores its address in ADDR; once loaded, a page is written by CMD = WP with the key, after its block has been erased. STATUS.LOAD shows the buffer holds data.

CTRLA.WMODE: MAN (default) writes only on command, ADDR holding the last AHB write address; issue a write before moving to another page. ADW runs WQW on the quad-word at ADDR when the last word of a double-word is written, the other double-word of the buffer being all ones. AQW runs WQW when the last word of a quad-word is written. AP runs WP when the last word of a page is written. In each automatic mode STATUS.READY goes low during the write and INTFLAG.DONE sets at the end. The modes apply to the main space and the USER page; the USER page has no page write, so AP writes it as AQW. Manual procedure: erase the block; fill the NVM page buffer through the main address space; do one read on AHB0 as a read memory barrier; issue WP (whole buffer to that page (at ADDR)) or WQW (the quad-word at ADDR); READY stays low and same-bank AHB access stalls until done. Automatic procedure: erase the block before the last buffer write; the write starts at the second word (ADW), fourth word (AQW) or last word of a page (APW); a partly filled page needs a manual write. A busy command interface stalls the AHB until it takes the automatic write, so writes can be chained without polling, but code that must not stall the bus checks STATUS.READY after each unit. The region must be unlocked. Manual example: set WMODE to manual; wait for READY; clear the NVM page buffer (CTRLB); wait for READY; clear INTFLAG.DONE; write the data in 32-bit words; issue a page write; wait for READY; clear DONE.

Reading from one bank goes on without AHB stalls while the opposite bank is being written or erased. Both banks cannot be read at once (reads go in series), both cannot be programmed or erased at once (a command arriving before the previous one ends is ignored with INTFLAG.PROGE set), and there is no read-while-write on the auxiliary pages: a read there stalls and no command is accepted until the previous one ends.

CTRLA.SUSPEN = 1 lets a read interrupt an EB or WP, including ones started by the SmartEEPROM: the controller suspends the operation, waits for the NVM, serves the read (and any reads that follow), then resumes. Suspending sets INTFLAG.SUSP (write 1 to clear) and STATUS.SUSP shows the state. A read in that page being programmed, or in a 128 KB sector holding a block under erase, cannot suspend, and power reduction cannot be entered while a command is suspended.

operation.topic: NVM page buffer clear, erase and lock
operation.text: The NVM page buffer returns to all ones after every WP or WQW; the PBC command clears a partly written buffer, PBLDATA0 and PBLDATA1 included. STATUS.LOAD is set from the first load until WP, WQW or PBC. Writing the buffer while a write command runs stalls the AHB, so poll STATUS.READY first. A page must be erased before writing; erase sets all bits to 1, by block in the main space (EB) or by page on the USER page (EP). Erasing in a locked region does nothing and sets INTFLAG.LOCKE and INTFLAG.PROGE. To erase, write any address in the block or page to ADDR and issue the command; the NVM page buffer may be written meanwhile.

Cuts the Flash's static power; a command or AHB access wakes it and is served after the wake-up time, which PM STDBYCFG fast wake-up shortens. CTRLA.PRM: MANUAL enters on SPRM and leaves on an AHB access, CPRM or any other command. SEMIAUTO also enters when the system enters Standby, or when an AHB access or command completes in Standby, and leaves as MANUAL. FULLAUTO enters as SEMIAUTO and also leaves when the system leaves Standby. STATUS.READY is high in power reduction (commands are accepted) and STATUS.PRM is high. Power reduction cannot start while a command is suspended: automatic entry waits until it resumes and ends, and SPRM is discarded with INTFLAG.PROGE set while STATUS.SUSP is high.

operation.topic: NVM safe update with dual banks
operation.text: Firmware running from Flash can write a new version of itself into the other bank (BANKB when STATUS.AFIRST = 1, else BANKA), then issue BKSWRST. That command, atomic with no NVM fetch possible during it, stalls the AHB ports; if PARAM.SEE = 1 and 0 < SEESTAT.SBLK < 11 it moves the SmartEEPROM data to the first bank, keeping the same active sector; programs the AFIRST fuse to 0 if it was 1, or erases it to 1; and resets the device, RSTC.RCAUSE showing an NVMCTRL reset. The new firmware then runs from the bank last programmed. With SmartEEPROM configured, its reserved space (2 × SEESTAT.SBLK × 8192 bytes) must be smaller than half the NVM, and when each bank holds its own application (or one a bootloader) both banks must reserve the SmartEEPROM area, so each bank's code space is the bank size less that area.

Through AHB2, part of the NVM looks like RAM with 8-, 16- and 32-bit access. Since a programmed NVM word can always take more zeros but a 1 can only come back by erasing a block, virtual pages are mapped to physical pages (SEEP) that are kept until a bit must go from 0 to 1; then the virtual page moves to a new physical page in the reserved area. Writing virtual pages uses up the SmartEEPROM's cycling endurance. Region lock bits do not apply to it even where a region overlaps it. It lives in the bank not mapped at address 0 (BANKB when STATUS.AFIRST = 1), so the CPU is not halted when it is accessed. Address spaces: DATA from offset 0x0, 512 B to 64 KB depending on SEESTAT.PSZ and SBLK, write-protected by the non-volatile SEESTAT.LOCK (commands LSEE and USEE); REGISTER from offset 0x10000, 20 B, write-protected by SEESTAT.LOCK or the volatile SEESTAT.RLOCK (commands LSEER and USEER).

Two virtual sectors (SEES) occupy the last blocks of BANKB (STATUS.AFIRST = 1) or BANKA (AFIRST = 0); one is active and the other stays erased for reallocation. SEESTAT.ASEES (0: SEES0, 1: SEES1) loads at reset from a fuse set by ASEES1 and cleared by ASEES0, and follows those commands at once. At most 128 virtual pages. Allocation assigns a SEEP to a virtual page the first time and reallocation assigns a new one, each writing the virtual page index and next free page. SEEP size (PSZ) and blocks per SEES (SBLK) are configurable. The virtual size is the most data the SmartEEPROM holds; an access beyond it causes a HardFault. The raw data sits in the top blocks of the main space and cannot be reached over AHB0 or AHB1.

The wear leveling factor is the least ratio by which accesses to one physical Flash cell are divided once a SEES holds its maximum number of SEEP, which PSZ and SBLK set; with two SEES it is twice that maximum.

Writes need SEESTAT.LOCK = 0, or they are dropped with a HardFault; LSEE and USEE lock and unlock writing. Set the SBLK and PSZ fuses for total size and page size; point an 8-, 16- or 32-bit pointer at the SmartEEPROM address; wait while SEESTAT.BUSY is set; write as to RAM; with automatic reallocation disabled (SEECFG.APRDIS) check the SEESFULL flag that the active sector is not full; read back through the pointer after BUSY clears. SEECFG.WMODE picks page buffer handling: UNBUFFERED (default) writes a page after every buffer update; BUFFERED writes only when a different NVM page is reached, improving wear but more exposed to power loss, SEESTAT.LOAD showing unwritten data and SEEFLUSH writing it out. INTFLAG.SEEWRC marks a completed AHB write: unbuffered, the NVM holds the data unless INTFLAG.SEESOVF was raised; buffered, likewise when SEESTAT.LOAD = 0, otherwise the data is still in the NVM page buffer.

By default hardware reallocates when the next free page reaches the maximum SEEP number; SEECFG.APRDIS = 1 stops that and the SEERALOC command starts it by hand. Reallocation erases the inactive sector, copies the valid data into it (dropping stale data) and swaps the active sector with ASEES1 or ASEES0; SEESTAT.BUSY shows it running. In buffered mode flush the NVM page buffer first or its contents are lost. BKSWRST starts the same process, copying within the active sector into the first bank, atomically. The CPU may stall for a few milliseconds at the end of a reallocation; critical code can run from TCM, RAM or the CMCC. Because the SEEP outnumber the virtual size, free SEEP always remain.

The auxiliary space holds the user configuration: the bootloader size (the section from offset 0, protected against write, erase and chip erase), the SmartEEPROM blocks per sector (SBLK, loaded into SEESTAT.SBLK at reset), the SmartEEPROM virtual page size (PSZ, loaded into SEESTAT.PSZ), the region lock bits (shown in RUNLOCK) and the SmartEEPROM lock bit (shown in SEESTAT.LOCK).

The security bit locks the whole chip against external access. To set it: issue SSB (a connected debugger keeps access, DSU STATUSB.PROT = 0); check INTFLAG.PROGE and INTFLAG.DONE; reset the NVMCTRL (SWRST) or the device so the start-up sequence reads the bit again; DSU STATUSB.PROT then reads 1. Only a debugger Chip Erase clears it, after all volatile memory and NVM are cleared; protection status updates at the end of the command with no reset needed.

The NVM is read 128 bits at a time, and AHB0 and AHB1 each have a 128-bit cache line, saving power on sequential reads and time when wait states are needed. Both are on by default; CTRLA.CACHEDIS[0] and CACHEDIS[1] turn them off per port. Commands that change NVM contents invalidate the lines.

ECC is always on. Each 128-bit fetch is checked as two 64-bit double-words by two decoders in parallel, correcting single errors and detecting double errors on the fly; correction does not apply to SmartEEPROM accesses. An error anywhere in the quad-word is reported on its first access, not only in the word addressed. On detection INTFLAG.ECCSE (single) or ECCDE (dual) sets, ECCERR.ADDR takes the quad-word-aligned byte address (a fetch at 0x100C reports 0x1000), and ECCERR.TYPEL and TYPEH give NONE, SINGLE or DUAL for the low and high double-words. Reading ECCERR clears both flags and resets the types to NONE; an error during that read reports the old information and then loads the new one. While a single error is pending (ECCSE or ECCDE set), new single errors are ignored and the first dual error overwrites ECCERR; while a dual error is pending (ECCDE set), all new errors are ignored.

A reset during a write or erase leaves the block or page contents unpredictable, so such operations must not be interrupted. To lower the risk of a brown-out reset on power loss, check the supply before programming, or prefer WQW to WP since a short command is likelier to finish on a given decoupling capacitor. After a reset during a write or erase, erase the affected block before reading or programming it.

Chip erase, started from the DSU, covers the whole system. Volatile memories are cleared and the NVM array erased together (not the BOOTPROT section); then STATUS.AFIRST is set to 1 if no BOOTPROT section is defined (else left), SEESTAT.ASEES = 1, SEESTAT.LOCK = 0 and DSU STATUSB.CELCK = 0. If every internal NVM verify passed, the security bit is cleared and DSU STATUSB.PROT clears; otherwise DSU STATUSA.DONE and STATUSA.FAIL are set and the operation ends. The CB, FS and USER pages and the BOOTPROT section are untouched.

The Integrity Check Monitor is a DMA engine with a SHA hash unit (SHA1, SHA224, SHA256, FIPS 180-2) that works from descriptors in memory (the ICM descriptor area). It either hashes a list of memory regions and stores the digests (in the ICM hash area), or monitors memory by recomputing each region's hash and comparing it with a stored digest, raising an interrupt on a mismatch. It has an AHB host DMA port, monitors up to four non-contiguous regions, gathers blocks through linked lists, and limits its bus load with a programmable burden. Processing period: 85 or 209 clock cycles for SHA1, 72 or 194 for SHA224 and SHA256.

No pins, DMA or events. It runs only while its clocks run, so only with the CPU in Active mode. MCLK gates its bus clocks: CLK_ICM_AHB through AHBMASK.ICM and CLK_ICM_APB through APBCMASK.ICM. One interrupt line to the NVIC, which must be set up before the ICM.

Built from a DMA interface, a monitoring state machine, an integrity scheduler, context registers, the SHA engine and configuration and status registers. Used purely as a SHA unit it needs the message padded as FIPS 180-4 specifies; for memory checking padding is optional. Each processing period produces an N-bit digest: 160 for SHA1, 224 for SHA224, 256 for SHA256. Once enabled, it fetches region descriptors in turn from a circular main list (up to four regions), each of four words giving the region's layout and its own hash settings. With a descriptor loaded, TRSIZE (in RCTRL) blocks go to the SHA engine, and the digest is then written to memory (write back) or compared with a reference digest in memory (compare), a mismatch raising an interrupt if enabled. The list ends at a descriptor with WRAP or EOM set in RCFG; for continuous monitoring set WRAP and clear EOM in the last one. A region may gather data through a secondary list, which cannot change the region's settings, the ICM returning to the main list at its end. The BBC field of CFG limits the ICM's memory bandwidth, monitoring being a background task.

A contiguous memory area both the ICM and the CPU can reach, starting at the address in the HASH register, a multiple of 128 bytes. With CDWBN = 0 (write back) the digest of region RID is written at HASH + (RID << 5); with CDWBN = 1 (compare) the reference digest is fetched from that same address.

The descriptor area is contiguous memory reachable by the ICM and the CPU. On activation the ICM fetches from DSCR, and with several regions from DSCR + (RID << 4). Each main-list descriptor is four words: RADDR (first byte address of the region), RCFG, RCTRL (TRSIZE[15:0], the transfer size of this chunk) and RNEXT (address of a secondary list, 0 for none); in a secondary-list descriptor the RCFG word is unused. Example: three blocks monitored as two regions, region 0 made of two separate blocks (its main descriptor's RNEXT pointing at a secondary descriptor for the second block) and region 1 one contiguous block, each with its own SHA algorithm, the wrap bit making monitoring continuous.

The ICM can simply compute a SHA1, SHA224 or SHA256 digest. Put the data's start address in a descriptor (a multiple of four 32-bit words) whose own address goes in DSCR, aligned to 64 bytes (six LSBs zero). Data already padded needs one descriptor with RCFGn.EOM = 1; otherwise RNEXT can point at a separately stored padding area, and the ICM joins the two and leaves the result at HASH. Clear CDWBN and WRAP in RCFGn and WBDIS, EOMDIS and SLBDIS in CFG. With RHIEN and ECIEN at 0, RHC[i] and REC[i] set when the result for region i is at HASH, and setting RHC[i] or REC[i] in IER raises an interrupt. The short processing period gives the SHA unit more bandwidth and the long one leaves more of the bus to others: SHA1 takes 85 or 209 clock cycles, SHA256 and SHA224 72 or 194, each plus 2 cycles to synchronise the start command.

With CFG.ASCD set the ICM first goes through the main list once in write-back mode (CDWBN = 0, EOM = 0), and on reaching RCFGn.WRAP = 1 switches to active monitoring with CDWBN set and EOM cleared in its context; writes to CDWBN and EOM in RCFGn then have no effect.

An undefined register access sets ISR.URAD (if unmasked) and UASR.URAT records the first one's source: a reserved descriptor field found set to one when loaded, CFG, DSCR or HASH changed during active monitoring, or a read of a write-only register. Only writing 1 to CTRL.SWRST clears URAD and URAT.

The Peripheral Access Controller locks and unlocks the write access to peripheral registers and reports access violations: writes to protected registers, illegal accesses, enable-protected accesses, and accesses during clock synchronization or software reset, one interrupt flag per peripheral. It also reports client-bus errors when a non-existent address is accessed.

No pins or DMA. It runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs, its interrupt can wake the device, and its event can act on the system without waking it. CLK_PAC_APB is gated in MCLK. One interrupt line (NVIC line ERR). The event goes to EVSYS. With the CPU halted by the debugger, write protection of every peripheral is off and the PAC works normally. Every writable register can be PAC-protected except the PAC's own WRCTRL, INTFLAGAHB and INTFLAGA/B/C...; protection never applies to an external debugger.

The PAC is enabled after reset and only a hardware reset resets it. It sets, clears or locks write protection for every peripheral on every peripheral bridge. A violation updates INTFLAGn for bridge n (A, B, C ...), and STATUSn shows which peripherals on that bridge are protected. Peripheral access errors come from a write to a protected peripheral (only registers marked as PAC write-protected can be; the data is not written, the peripheral returns an error and its INTFLAGn bit sets), an access to an unimplemented register, or a write to a write-synchronized register while synchronization runs. Any INTFLAGn bit requests an interrupt if enabled. An access to an address with no bridge or peripheral sets the matching INTFLAGAHB bit.

WRCTRL takes a peripheral identifier (PERID) and a KEY choosing clear protection (writes allowed), set protection (writes to protected registers refused) or set and lock (protected until a hardware reset). STATUSn shows the result. Only 32-bit writes to WRCTRL count; other accesses do nothing and cause a PAC write error. Setting protection on an already protected peripheral, clearing it twice, set-and-lock on a protected peripheral, or any write to a locked peripheral is an error, which helps check that every protect is followed by an unprotect; where a protected peripheral is used from several contexts such as interrupts, keep an interrupt from arriving while another level changes the protection, or have the handler read STATUS before unprotecting. Errors on PAC registers (key error, double protect and so on) set INTFLAGx.PAC.

One interrupt, ERR: a peripheral access violation in a peripheral the PAC controls, or a bridge error; it is a synchronous wake-up source. Its flags are in INTFLAGAHB and INTFLAGn, it is enabled with INTENSET and disabled with INTENCLR, and it stays active until the flag clears, the interrupt is disabled or the PAC resets; all its sources are ORed into one NVIC request, so read INTFLAGAHB and INTFLAGn to find the cause. Interrupts must be enabled globally. EVCTRL.ERREO = 1 makes the ERR output event whenever an interrupt flag bit sets. In sleep the PAC stays enabled while a bus host (CPU, DMA) runs, still catching errors and making interrupts and events.

OSCCTRL enables, disables, calibrates and monitors the two crystal oscillators XOSC0 and XOSC1, the DFLL48M and the two FDPLL200M PLLs (the 32.768 kHz oscillators are under OSC32KCTRL). Their status is gathered in STATUS, and status changes can raise interrupts through INTENSET, INTENCLR and INTFLAG. DFLL48M: internal 48 MHz oscillator with no external parts, usable open loop as a programmable oscillator or closed loop as a precise multiplier of a known frequency. XOSCn: 8 to 48 MHz, tunable gain, programmable start-up time, crystal or external clock on XIN, clock failure detection with safe clock switch and a failure event. FDPLL200Mn: 96 to 200 MHz output from a 32 kHz to 3.2 MHz reference, four selectable references each, adjustable digital loop filter and DCO filter for the four-stage differential ring oscillator, a fractional part giving 1/32 of a reference-clock step, and a built-in test mode controller.

It keeps working in every sleep mode in which its clock source runs; its interrupts can wake the device and its events can act without waking it. It supplies XOSCn, DFLL48M and FDPLL200Mn to GCLK. The DFLL48M takes its reference GCLK_DFLL48M_REF from GCLK; its logic runs on its own output, asynchronous to CLK_OSCCTRL_APB, so some register writes need synchronization. The FDPLL200Mn need a reference GCLK_DPLL, plus a 32 kHz clock GCLK_DPLL_32K when the lock timer is used; both may come from GCLK and/or external oscillators. One interrupt line to the NVIC; events go to EVSYS. It keeps running when the CPU is halted by the debugger. All writable registers except INTFLAG can be PAC write-protected, never against a debugger. The 8 to 48 MHz crystal goes between XIN and XOUT with any load capacitors it needs (values in the electrical characteristics).

Each XOSCn works with an external clock on XIN or with an 8 to 48 MHz crystal between XIN and XOUT, and can feed the GCLK generators. At reset it is off and its pins are free for GPIO or other peripherals; in crystal mode OSCCTRL takes both pins, in external-clock mode only XIN, leaving XOUT for GPIO. XOSCCTRLn.ENABLE turns it on; XTALEN = 1 selects crystal mode, XTALEN = 0 the external clock input. In crystal mode set the current controls XOSCCTRLn.IPTAT and IMULT to suit the crystal frequency. XOSCCTRLn.ENALC = 1 lets an amplitude loop adjust the swing automatically, usually lowering power; there LOWBUFGAIN = 0 (default) allows a low amplitude, and LOWBUFGAIN = 1 roughly doubles the amplitude to cure stability problems. After a hard reset, or waking from a sleep mode in which it was off, the output is masked for the start-up time set in XOSCCTRLn.STARTUP; STATUS.XOSCRDYn then sets, raising an interrupt if INTENSET.XOSCRDYn is set.

The clock failure detector (CFD) watches the XOSCn clock and can switch to a safe clock, made from the DFLL48M through a prescaler, when it fails, and back again when it recovers. It is off at reset, does not watch a disabled oscillator, and pauses while the XOSCn is not requested in on-demand mode or is halted in Standby. Start the DFLL48M first, then set XOSCCTRLn.CFDEN; failures are not detected until the XOSCn start-up time has passed. The CFD then needs at least one rising and one falling XOSCn edge in every 4 safe-clock periods; otherwise STATUS.XOSCFAILn and INTFLAG.XOSCFAILn set, with an interrupt if INTENSET.XOSCFAILn is set and an event if EVCTRL.CFDEOn is set. Monitoring continues, STATUS.XOSCFAILn following the clock's activity. On failure the safe clock takes over from the XOSCn clock and STATUS.XOSCCKSWn sets; the oscillator itself is left running, and software must turn it off and reconfigure the system clocks. If the XOSCn recovers, writing XOSCCTRLn.SWBEN = 1 switches back, and hardware clears SWBEN. The prescaler XOSCCTRLn.CFDPRESC divides the DFLL48M by 2^CFDPRESC (CFDPRESC 0 to 15) so the safe clock is no faster than the monitored clock: for an 8 MHz crystal and a 48 MHz DFLL the division must exceed 6 (48/8), for example 8, so CFDPRESC = 3. No failure event is output once switched to the safe clock. In sleep the CFD runs as the XOSC sleep behaviour allows, and its interrupt can wake the device.

Works open loop or closed loop; closed loop needs an accurate low-frequency reference to give an accurate CLK_DFLL48M. Its output can feed the GCLK generators (GCLK.GENCTRLn.SRC = DFLL). It is factory-calibrated to 48 MHz open loop, the calibration loaded into DFLLVAL.COARSE and DFLLVAL.FINE at reset. Open loop is selected after any reset; the frequency follows DFLLVAL.COARSE and FINE, which may be changed while the DFLL is running, and CLK_DFLL48M is usable once STATUS.DFLLRDY sets.

Closed loop regulates the output continuously against a reference, fine-tuning itself once the multiplier is set. After enabling the DFLL48M: route the reference through peripheral channel 0 (GCLK_DFLL48M_REF) by setting GCLK.PCHCTRL0.GEN to a generator and choosing that generator's source in GCLK.GENCTRLn.SRC; set the largest coarse and fine steps in DFLLMUL.CSTEP and FSTEP (small steps give little overshoot but slower locking, large steps the reverse; keep each at or below half the maximum of DFLLVAL.COARSE and FINE); set DFLLMUL.MUL, keeping the output within the device's maximum frequency; then set DFLLCTRLB.MODE. In closed loop COARSE and FINE are read-only and driven by the tuner, which starts from the COARSE value already there, so presetting COARSE near the final value shortens coarse locking. Locking runs in two stages: coarse sets COARSE quickly and then STATUS.DFLLLCKC; fine tunes FINE and then sets STATUS.DFLLLCKF. DFLLCTRLB.BPLCKC skips the coarse stage, keeping COARSE and setting DFLLLCKC at once. Both lock bits can raise interrupts (INTENSET.DFLLCKC, DFLLCKF). The clock is usable at STATUS.DFLLRDY, its accuracy depending on which locks are set; lock times are in the electrical characteristics.

In closed loop the ratio of CLK_DFLL48M to its reference is measured continuously and its difference from DFLLMUL.MUL is kept in DFLLVAL.DIFF. With DFLLCTRLB.STABLE = 0 the tuner follows drift without losing lock, so FINE may change after every measurement; if FINE overflows or underflows through large temperature or voltage drift, STATUS.DFLLOOB sets (interrupt if INTENSET.DFLLOOB) and DFLLMUL.MUL must be written again; DFLLOOB also sets when coarse lock cannot be found. With STABLE = 1 COARSE and FINE stay fixed after lock, and DIFF shows any drift. If the reference stops or runs below CLK_DFLL48M/(2 × MULMAX), STATUS.DFLLRCS sets (interrupt if INTENSET.DFLLRCS); detection can take on the order of 2^17 CLK_DFLL48M cycles. The DFLL then runs as if open loop and returns to closed loop when the reference restarts.

A new frequency can take several microseconds to appear, which with a small DFLLMUL.MUL can keep the loop from locking. Chill cycles, which skip measuring the output for a cycle, are on by default (DFLLCTRLB.CCDIS = 1 turns them off) and may double the lock time. Quick Lock, also on by default (DFLLCTRLB.QLDIS = 1 turns it off), relaxes the lock criteria, spreading the frequency more than chill cycles with the same average. For up to 30 reference-clock periods between a lock flag and a settled frequency the accuracy is limited; small FSTEP and CSTEP and Quick Lock off minimise cycle-to-cycle jitter during lock search. DFLLCTRLB.LLAW = 1 makes the DFLL lose its locks when disabled, so it must lock again from scratch; with LLAW = 0 it restarts with its old settings and locks even without a reference, so check both locks are reached before sleeping, and fine tracking then corrects drift quickly once the reference returns (with STABLE = 0). DFLLCTRLB.WAITLOCK = 0 releases the clock when STATUS.DFLLRDY rises, WAITLOCK = 1 only at fine lock, which is more accurate but slower to start. Accuracy at fine lock depends on the fine step size and on the accuracy of the reference.

Makes the 48 MHz USB clock from USB start-of-frame packets: set DFLLCTRLB.USBCRM and DFLLCTRLB.MODE; never set USBCRM with USB disabled. To change the reference: disable USB, put the DFLL open loop, change DFLLCTRLB.USBCRM, return to closed loop, enable USB. GCLK_DFLL48M_REF must be disabled in this mode; the SOF replaces the generic clock reference, and the DFLL status bits in OSCCTRL.STATUS follow USB activity and mean nothing. A connected device gets a SOF every 1 ms, so the multiplication factor is set to 0xBB80 for 48 MHz. BPLCKC is ignored and the COARSE value in DFLLVAL is used as the final coarse value; the calibrated 48 MHz COARSE value loaded from NVM at reset may not suit other modes, so software may save and restore it. Locking goes straight to the fine search. Clear DFLLCTRLB.QLDIS and set CCDIS to lock faster; STABLE is ignored and an automatic jitter reduction is used instead.

Each DPLLn keeps its output CLK_DPLLn coherent with its reference by phase comparison. Four references: XOSC32K, XOSC0, XOSC1, or a generic clock (GCLK_DPLL), chosen in DPLLnCTRLB.REFCLK. The output is low while the controller is disabled. With DPLLnRATIO.LDRFRAC = 0 it runs in integer mode, otherwise in fractional mode, which adds jitter. Integer example: fCKR = 32 kHz and fCLK_DPLLn = 112 MHz give a ratio of 3500, so LDR = 3499. Fractional example: fCKR = 32 kHz and 112.003000 MHz give 3500.9375 (3500 + 3/32), so LDR = 3499 and LDRFRAC = 3.

DPLLnCTRLA.ENABLE turns the PLL on and off; DPLLnSYNCBUSY.ENABLE is set when the bit changes and clears when CLK_DPLLn has sampled it high, or when the output has stopped on disable. The output is stable once enabled and locked. With DPLLnCTRLB.LTIME non-zero a fixed user lock time validates lock; with LTIME = 0 lock follows DPLLnSTATUS.LOCK and the lock time depends on the filter and target frequency. DPLLnCTRLB.WUF (wake-up fast) opens the output clock gate at the end of the start-up time, before the frequency has settled, which saves some hundreds of µs. Once the first acquisition is over, DPLLnCTRLB.LBYPASS decides whether lock still gates the output.

To change reference, disable the DPLLn, change DPLLnCTRLB.REFCLK and enable it again; the output is ready when DPLLnSTATUS.CLKRDY sets. DPLLnCTRLB.DIV[10:0] divides an XOSC reference. DPLLnRATIO (LDR[12:0] integer, LDRFRAC[4:0] fractional) may be changed while running, provided LBYPASS = 0, LTIME is not 0x0 (its default) and GCLK_DPLLn_32K is set up in GCLK as the lock timer clock. A written value reads back at once and DPLLnSYNCBUSY.DPLLRATIO stays set until it takes effect; STATUS.DPLLnLDRTO sets when the analog cell has taken the new value, at which point DPLLnSTATUS.LOCK clears and sets again when the frequency settles (a change of LDRFRAC alone does not clear LOCK). DPLLnCTRLB.FILTER selects the digital loop filter, its coefficients adjusted automatically to balance stability and jitter, and DPLLnCTRLB.DCOFILTER[2:0] sets the sigma-delta DAC low-pass filter of the DCO.

Interrupt sources, each on a 0-to-1 transition of its STATUS bit: XOSCRDYn (crystal oscillator n ready), XOSCFAILn (clock failure), DFLLRDY, DFLLOOB (out of bounds), DFLLCKF (fine lock), DFLLCKC (coarse lock), DPLLnLCKR (lock rise), DPLLnLCKF (lock fall), DPLLnLTTO (lock timer time-out) and DPLLnLDRTO (loop divider ratio update complete). Flags are in INTFLAG, enabled with INTENSET and disabled with INTENCLR; a request lasts until the flag clears, the interrupt is disabled or OSCCTRL resets. All share one interrupt line, so read INTFLAG to find the cause; interrupts must be enabled globally. The CFD gives the XOSCFAILn event when STATUS.XOSCFAILn sets, not while STATUS.XOSCCKSWn is set; EVCTRL.CFDEOn enables it.

DFLL48M registers needing synchronization, flagged in DFLLSYNC from the access until done: DFLLCTRLA.ENABLE (write), DFLLCTRLB (read), DFLLVAL (read and write), DFLLMUL (write). DPLL registers needing write synchronization, flagged in DPLLnSYNCBUSY: DPLLnCTRLA.ENABLE and DPLLnRATIO.

OSC32KCTRL controls XOSC32K, the 32.768 kHz crystal oscillator (start-up time selectable; takes a crystal or an external clock on XIN32; has clock failure detection, switching to a safe clock, with a failure event) and the always-on ultra-low-power internal RC oscillator OSCULP32K, whose calibration loads from the Flash factory calibration at reset. Both offer 1.024 kHz outputs.

It runs in any sleep mode where a 32 kHz oscillator runs, and its interrupts can wake the device. It supplies XOSC32K and OSCULP32K to GCLK, the RTC and the WDT. CLK_OSC32KCTRL_APB is gated in MCLK. Interrupt lines go to the NVIC and events to EVSYS. It keeps running when the debugger halts the CPU. All writable registers except INTFLAG can be PAC write-protected, never against a debugger. The 32.768 kHz crystal goes between XIN32 and XOUT32 with any load capacitors it needs.

Works with an external clock on XIN32 or a 32.768 kHz crystal between XIN32 and XOUT32. At reset it is off and the pins are free; in crystal mode it takes both pins, in external-clock mode only XIN32. XOSC32K.ENABLE turns it on and off; XTALEN = 1 selects crystal mode, 0 the external clock input. XOSC32K.CGM sets the crystal gain, trading low power against speed. XOSC32K.EN32K enables the 32.768 kHz output and EN1K the 1.024 kHz output. XOSC32K.WRTLOCK = 1 locks the configuration until a power-on reset. With ENABLE = 0 it is always stopped. With ONDEMAND = 0 it keeps running through every reset except power-on, since crystal start-up is slow. After a reset or wake-up from a mode where it was off, its output is masked for the start-up time in XOSC32K.STARTUP; then STATUS.XOSC32KRDY sets, raising an interrupt if INTENSET.XOSC32KRDY is set. It can clock the GCLK generators or the RTC: enable the matching output (EN32K or EN1K) before enabling GCLK or the RTC, and disable them before changing their clock selection.

The CFD watches the XOSC32K clock with short latency and can switch to a safe clock from OSCULP32K through a prescaler, and back on recovery. In sleep it stops whenever the oscillator is not requested by a peripheral. It is reset only at power-on and does not watch a disabled oscillator. With OSCULP32K running, set CFDCTRL.CFDEN; failures are not detected until the XOSC32K start-up time has passed. The CFD then needs at least one rising and one falling edge in every 4 safe-clock periods (the monitor period); otherwise STATUS.XOSC32KFAIL and INTFLAG.XOSC32KFAIL set, with an interrupt if INTENSET.XOSC32KFAIL is set and an event if EVCTRL.CFDEO is set. Monitoring continues and STATUS.XOSC32KFAIL follows the clock's activity. On failure both the 32 kHz and 1 kHz outputs are replaced by OSCULP32K's and STATUS.XOSC32KSW sets; the XOSC32K is left running, and software must turn it off if wanted and reconfigure the system clocks. Writing CFDCTRL.SWBACK = 1 returns to the recovered XOSC32K, and hardware clears SWBACK. The prescaler (division up to 2) applies to both safe-clock outputs, keeping the safe clock no faster than the monitored one: with a 32 kHz crystal and a 32 kHz OSCULP32K, XOSC32K.CFDPRESC = 0 gives a safe clock of the same frequency. No failure event is output once switched to the safe clock. The CFD interrupt can wake the device.

A tunable, low-speed, ultra-low-power oscillator, factory-calibrated at typical voltage and temperature. It is enabled after power-on reset and always runs except during POR. OSCULP32K.WRTLOCK = 1 locks its configuration until POR. It can clock the GCLK generators or the RTC; disable them before changing their clock selection. The WDT uses its 1.024 kHz output, always running and enabled internally when the WDT asks for it. The RTC clock, any of the oscillator outputs, is chosen in RTCCTRL before the RTC is enabled, and the RTC should be disabled before changing it.

Interrupts XOSC32KRDY (crystal ready) and XOSC32KFAIL (clock failure), each on a 0-to-1 transition of its STATUS bit and each a synchronous wake-up source, share one interrupt line; flags are in INTFLAG, enabled with INTENSET and disabled with INTENCLR, and a request lasts until the flag clears, the interrupt is disabled or the module resets. Interrupts must be enabled globally. The CFD event XOSC32KFAIL comes when STATUS.XOSC32KFAIL sets, not while the clock-switch bit is set; EVCTRL.CFDEO enables it.

The Frequency Meter measures a clock (GCLK_FREQM_MSR) against a known reference (GCLK_FREQM_REF), giving the ratio to 24-bit accuracy. Either clock can be any of their GCLK sources, including the GCLK_IO[7:0] pins once set up in PORT.

It runs in Idle sleep while its clocks run and its interrupt can wake the device from Idle; disable it before sleeping for the lowest power. CLK_FREQM_APB is gated in MCLK. GCLK_FREQM_REF clocks the reference timer and GCLK_FREQM_MSR a ripple counter; both must be set up and enabled in GCLK first. One interrupt line to the NVIC; no DMA or events. It keeps running, and cannot be halted, when the debugger halts the CPU. All writable registers except CTRLB, INTFLAG and STATUS can be PAC write-protected.

FREQM counts measured-clock periods during REFNUM reference periods (CFGA.REFNUM, a duration of REFNUM/fCLK_REF) and stores the count in VALUE.VALUE. GCLK_FREQM_REF has to run slower than GCLK_FREQM_MSR. Before enabling, configure and enable both generic clocks and write a non-zero CFGA.REFNUM (CFGA is enable-protected). CTRLA.ENABLE enables and CTRLA.SWRST resets and disables it; both are write-synchronized. CTRLB.START begins a measurement, STATUS.BUSY is set until it ends, and INTFLAG.DONE then sets with an interrupt if INTENSET.DONE is set (DONE is the only interrupt, a synchronous wake-up source). Check STATUS.OVF before trusting VALUE[23:0]; after an overflow reduce REFNUM or use a faster reference, clear OVF by writing 1, and start again.

The Event System passes signals (events) straight from peripherals that make them (generators) to peripherals that act on them (users), with no CPU and no bus or RAM bandwidth used; what makes an event and what an event does is set in each peripheral, and one peripheral can have several generators and users. 32 channels, each able to take any generator; all offer an asynchronous path, and channels 0 to 11 also a synchronous or resynchronized path clocked by their own GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNEL_n. 119 event generators and 67 event users. Configurable edge detection, SleepWalking and interrupts for sleep modes, software events, each user picking its channel, and static or round-robin interrupt priority.

No pins or DMA. EVSYS can wake the CPU from every sleep mode except Backup and Off, even with its channel and bus clocks stopped; some generators make events with their clocks stopped, and a channel on a synchronous or resynchronized path restarts its generic clock without waking the system. CLK_EVSYS_APB is gated in MCLK; the GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNEL_n clocks of channels 0 to 11 (the only ones that can be synchronous or resynchronized) handle detection and propagation and must be set up in GCLK first. One interrupt line to the NVIC. It keeps running when the debugger halts the CPU and can be made to halt instead. All writable registers except INTPEND and CHINTFLAGn can be PAC write-protected, never against a debugger.

Channels carry events from generators to peripherals or I/O pins. A generator may feed several channels, but a channel takes one generator. Set-up: enable the event output in the generator (an EO bit in its EVCTRL, such as AC.EVCTRL.WINEO0 or RTC.EVCTRL.OVFEO); set the user multiplexer (USERm) and then the channel (CHANNELn); set the user's event action (EVACT in its EVCTRL, such as TC.EVCTRL.EVACT, where it has one); enable the user's event input (an EI bit, such as AC.EVCTRL.IVEI0 or ADC.EVCTRL.STARTEI). EVSYS is always enabled; CTRLA.SWRST resets every register and cancels events in progress. Each user has a multiplexer that picks one channel (USERm.CHANNEL), always set before the channel; the USERm register description lists the users. A channel picks one generator in CHANNELn.EVGEN (0, no generator, by default) and can also make events by software command.

CHANNELn.PATH chooses the path. Asynchronous: the event goes straight from generator to user with no channel clock needed and no clock latency; the channel makes no interrupts, CHSTATUS reads zero, edge detection must be off, and each user chooses which edge acts. Synchronous: for a generator clocked from the same generic clock generator as the channel; otherwise a change may be missed and the event lost. Resynchronized: for a generator on a different generic clock generator, the channel resynchronizing the event. Synchronous and resynchronized paths can make interrupts and update CHSTATUS, and need edge detection set in CHANNELn.EDGSEL: rising, falling or both edges.

Maximum routing latency: asynchronous, device dependent (set by internal routing); synchronous, one GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNEL_n cycle; resynchronized, three GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNEL_n cycles. Propagation of an event into a user's peripheral clock domain takes up to three peripheral clock cycles. Generator, channel and user clocks must be chosen to respect these latencies, or events and actions may be lost. With CHANNELn.ONDEMAND = 1 a resynchronized channel's latency grows by two GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNEL_n cycles, up to five.

On synchronous and resynchronized paths only (they read zero on asynchronous ones): CHINTFLAGn.OVR sets when a new event arrives while a user on the channel is not ready, or before every user has handled the previous event; CHINTFLAGn.EVD sets when the channel's generator event is detected; CHSTATUSn.BUSYCH is set while an event awaits handling by all its users, and CHSTATUSn.RDYUSR when all users are ready. Writing SWEVT.CHANNELn = 1 makes a software event on that channel. INTSTATUS lists channels with pending interrupts. The arbiter re-evaluates whenever an interrupt becomes pending or is cleared, and INTPEND gives the highest-priority channel with its flags and status; writing a flag bit to INTPEND clears that flag on the channel in INTPEND.ID. Static priority (PRICTRL.RRENx = 0, default) favours low channel numbers and can starve high ones; round-robin (PRICTRL.RREN = 1) gives the last-granted channel, kept in PRICTRL.PRI, the lowest priority next time. OVR and EVD interrupts per channel are asynchronous wake-up sources, enabled with CHINTENSET and disabled with CHINTENCLR, lasting until the flag clears, the interrupt is disabled or EVSYS resets; all are ORed into one NVIC request. Interrupts must be enabled globally.

EVSYS interrupts can wake the device from Idle or Standby. To run in Standby a channel needs CHANNELn.RUNSTDBY = 1. With CHANNELn.ONDEMAND = 1 the channel requests GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNEL_n when its generator's event is detected.

PORT controls the I/O pins, arranged in groups of up to 32 pins (how many groups depends on the package). Each pin is general-purpose I/O under software control or is handed to a peripheral. As I/O, each pin is an input or a push-pull output with selectable drive strength and pull-up or pull-down; the input buffer can be turned off to save power and its sampling chosen.
