Direction and output value of any set of pins in a group can be set, cleared or toggled in one atomic 8-, 16- or 32-bit write (DIRSET, DIRCLR, DIRTGL, OUTSET, OUTCLR, OUTTGL) without touching the others. Up to four event inputs per group can set, clear, toggle or drive a pin's output. PORT sits on the high-speed bus matrix through an AHB/APB bridge.

Pins are named Pxy: a group letter (A, B, C and so on) followed by a pin number 00 to 31, for example PA24 or PC03; some lines are not bonded out on some devices. A pin can be given to one of several peripheral functions, which then drives its output and reads its pad. During reset every line is an input with input buffer, output buffer and pull all disabled. In Backup sleep the PORT registers and input synchronizers lose their contents (not restored at power-up), but the pad latches keep their output value and pull settings. PORT runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs. CLK_PORT_APB is gated in MCLK and may be divided from the CPU clock; concurrent PORT accesses can add one cycle of APB latency. No DMA or interrupts. Events go to EVSYS; PORT always drives an event onto a pin asynchronously, so the EVSYS channel must use the asynchronous path. It keeps running in debug halt. All writable registers can be PAC write-protected, never against a debugger. Selecting an analog function on a pin, connected directly by analog buses, turns off the pad's digital functions.

Each group's registers repeat at offsets of 0x80 (group A index 0, B index 1 ...: base PORT + 0x80 × group). DIR bit y = 1 makes pin y an output and 0 an input; OUT bit y then drives it high (1) or low (0). PINCFGy holds each pin's extra settings. IN gives the pin value, readable in either direction, resynchronized to the PORT clock, sampled only while PINCFGy.INEN = 1. PINCFGy.PMUXEN = 1 hands the pin to the peripheral chosen in PMUXn instead of PORT. Out of reset, ordinary pads belong to PORT, output drivers off (high impedance) and input buffers off, whether or not a clock runs; special pins such as the debugger's may differ. Output: set DIR bit y, or DIRSET bit y to leave other pins alone, and write OUT; OUTSET, OUTCLR and OUTTGL set, clear and toggle OUT bits. Input: clear DIR bit y (or DIRCLR), set PINCFGy.INEN, read IN. By default the synchronizer runs only on a read request, delaying it two PORT clocks; CTRL.SAMPLINGn makes the synchronizers of a group of eight pins run continuously, removing the delay at higher power. Peripheral function: set PMUXEN in PINCFGy (byte offset PINCFG0 + y) and choose the function in PMUXO or PMUXE of PMUXn (byte offset PMUX0 + y/2); the peripheral must also be set up and enabled.

PINCFGy sets a pin push-pull or pulled; doing pulls there avoids intermediate states while direction and value change. With the pull enabled, OUT chooses pull-up (1) or pull-down (0). A push-pull output drives low or high from OUT with no current limit beyond the pin's own capability; an input with no external pull floats. Enabling the output driver turns the pull off. With DIR, INEN and PULLEN all 0 (reset or analog I/O), digital input, output and pull are all off.

Input events EVU0 to EVU3 come from EVSYS, possibly from another clock domain, and act on pins: OUT drives the pin to the event's level, SET sets it on an event, CLR clears it, TGL toggles it. OUT acts with no internal latency; SET, CLR and TGL take effect within three clock cycles of the event's rising edge. In Standby only OUT is available. EVCTRL.EVACTn chooses each event's action, EVCTRL.PORTEIn enables it, and EVCTRL.PIDn chooses its one pin; several actions may be enabled, and with several events connected any enabled action follows any of them. A pin can be targeted by up to four events; when SET, CLR and TGL events coincide on one pin, one action is executed as the table shows. Asynchronous OUT events can leave a pin at unpredictable levels depending on timing; with several OUT events on one pin the lowest event line wins and the rest are ignored. The CPU's APB access has priority over EVSYS events, except that a pin with EVACTn = OUT follows its event directly whatever OUT holds.

Up to eight SERCOM instances, each a serial engine that is set to one mode at a time: I2C (also SMBus compatible), SPI, or USART, chosen by CTRLA.MODE[2:0]; once a mode is chosen and the instance enabled, all of its resources serve that mode. The engine holds a transmitter with a single transmit buffer, a receiver with a double receive buffer, a baud-rate generator and address match/mask logic. It runs from its internal generic clock or from an external clock; with an external clock it works in every sleep mode. It can be served by DMA and has a 32-bit data extension for fewer bus accesses.

Each SERCOM has four internal pads, PAD[3:0]; the I2C, SPI and USART signals reach them through a multiplexer whose setting belongs to each mode, and the pads reach pins through PORT. A SERCOM keeps working through every sleep mode that leaves its chosen clock on, and its interrupts can wake the device.

The bus clock CLK_SERCOMx_APB is gated in the Main Clock Controller (MCLK). Two generic clocks come from GCLK: GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE, needed when the SERCOM acts as host, and GCLK_SERCOMx_SLOW, needed only by some functions. Both must be set up and enabled in GCLK before use. They are asynchronous to the APB clock, so some register writes and reads are synchronized across the clock domains (marked Write-Synchronized and Read-Synchronized per register).

DMA requests go to DMAC and the interrupt line to the NVIC, each to be configured before use. No events and no analog connections. The SERCOM keeps running while the CPU is halted in debug unless DBGCTRL tells it to halt. Every writable register can be PAC write-protected except INTFLAG, STATUS, DATA and ADDR; PAC protection does not apply to an external debugger.

On the transmit side: one write buffer feeding a shift register. On the receive side: a shift register and a receive buffer of one level in I2C or two levels in USART and SPI. The baud-rate generator runs on GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE or an external clock. Address matching serves SPI and I2C. Registers named in capitals are synchronous to the system clock and visible to the CPU; the lower-case blocks can run on GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE or an external clock.
CTRLA.ENABLE = 1 enables the SERCOM and 0 disables it. CTRLA.SWRST = 1 returns every register except DBGCTRL to its reset state and leaves the SERCOM disabled.

The baud-rate generator makes the internal clocks for asynchronous and synchronous transfers from the baud reference fref, which is the serial engine clock (internal or external), and the BAUD register. Asynchronous transfers transmit on the divide-by-16 output and receive on the divide-by-1 output; synchronous transfers use the divide-by-2 output; the choice follows the operating mode automatically. Asynchronous arithmetic mode uses a 16-bit BAUD value (0 to 65,535). Asynchronous fractional mode uses a 13-bit BAUD value and a 3-bit fractional part FP, with BAUD at least 1; it is the mode used for auto-baud detection. Synchronous mode uses an 8-bit BAUD value (0 to 255). S, the number of samples per bit, is 16, 8 or 3.

The address logic compares 7 or 8 bits (by mode) and can accept a single address, either of two addresses, or a span of addresses. Masked address: ADDR.ADDR is the address and ADDR.ADDRMASK masks bits out of the comparison; a mask of all zeros matches one address and all ones accepts every address. Two unique addresses: a match on either ADDR.ADDR or ADDR.ADDRMASK. Range: any address from ADDR.ADDRMASK (lower limit) to ADDR.ADDR (upper limit) inclusive matches.

Interrupt sources depend on the mode; each has its own flag in INTFLAG, set when its condition occurs, enabled by writing 1 to its bit in INTENSET and disabled by writing 1 in INTENCLR. A request stays active until the flag is cleared, the interrupt disabled or the SERCOM reset; interrupts must also be enabled globally. No events. The SERCOM works in any sleep mode where its serial clock, external or from the baud-rate generator, runs, and its interrupts can wake the device.

The USART is a SERCOM mode. Its transmitter has a single write buffer, so frames can follow one another with no gap, a shift register and frame-format logic; its receiver has a shift register feeding a two-level receive buffer, with status bits for error checking, and data and clock recovery that synchronize to and filter noise from asynchronous input. Features: full duplex; asynchronous with clock recovery or synchronous; internal or external clock in either; 5 to 9 data bits with 1 or 2 stop bits; even or odd parity, generated and checked; LSB- or MSB-first; detection of frame errors and buffer overflow; noise filtering with false start-bit detection and a digital low-pass filter; collision detection; works in all sleep modes; up to half the system clock with an internal clock and up to the system clock with an external clock; RTS/CTS flow control; IrDA modulation and demodulation to 115.2 kbps; LIN host; LIN client with auto-baud and break detection; ISO 7816 T=0 and T=1 smart-card protocols; RS485; start-of-frame detection; DMA; 32-bit data extension.

The USART keeps working through any sleep mode that leaves its source clock on, and its interrupts can wake the device. CLK_SERCOMx_APB is gated in MCLK; GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE must be set up in GCLK and is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some writes are synchronized. DMA requests go to DMAC, the interrupt to the NVIC. No events, no analog connections. It keeps running in debug halt unless DBGCTRL halts it. Writable registers can be PAC write-protected except INTFLAG, STATUS and DATA; not against an external debugger.

Lines: RxD receives, TxD transmits, XCK carries the clock in synchronous operation. A frame is one start bit (always low), 5 to 9 data bits sent MSB or LSB first, an optional even or odd parity bit after the data, and one or two stop bits (always high). After the stop bits the next frame may start at once or the line goes idle, which is high.

CTRLA (except ENABLE and SWRST), CTRLB (except RXEN and TXEN) and BAUD are enable-protected: writes are ignored while the USART is enabled or being enabled, and writes made while it is being disabled take effect once disabling ends. Set-up order before enabling: CTRLA.MODE external (0x0) or internal (0x1) clock; CTRLA.CMODE asynchronous (0) or synchronous (1); CTRLA.RXPO for the receive pad; CTRLA.TXPO for the transmit and clock pads; CTRLB.CHSIZE character size; CTRLA.DORD bit order; for parity, CTRLA.FORM = 0x1 and CTRLB.PMODE even or odd; CTRLB.SBMODE stop bits; with an internal clock, BAUD for the baud rate; then CTRLB.RXEN and CTRLB.TXEN. CTRLA.ENABLE turns the USART on and off; CTRLA.SWRST resets every register but DBGCTRL and disables it.

In both synchronous and asynchronous modes the shift and sample clock comes from the baud-rate generator or from the XCK pin. CTRLA.CMODE = 1 selects synchronous and 0 asynchronous; CTRLA.MODE = 0x1 selects the internal clock and 0x0 the external one. Asynchronous mode uses the 16-bit BAUD value, synchronous mode the eight low bits of BAUD.

In synchronous mode CTRLA.MODE decides whether XCK is an input or an output; edges behave the same with internal and external clocks, and RxD is sampled on the XCK edge opposite the one on which TxD changes. CTRLA.CPOL = 0: data changes on the rising XCK edge and is sampled on the falling edge. CTRLA.CPOL = 1: data changes on the falling edge and is sampled on the rising edge. With the clock supplied on XCK (CTRLA.MODE = 0x0) the shift registers run directly from XCK, which is not synchronized to the system clock and may run at up to the system frequency.

TxDATA and RxDATA share the DATA address: a write goes to TxDATA and a read returns RxDATA. Writing DATA starts a transmission; the data moves to the shift register when it is empty and the frame is sent. INTFLAG.DRE says DATA is empty and may be written; INTFLAG.TXC sets when the whole frame including stop bits is out, transmit buffer and shift register are empty and nothing new was written. CTRLB.TXEN = 0 disables the transmitter only after ongoing and pending transmissions are done. The receiver starts on a valid start bit, samples each bit at the baud rate or XCK clock into the shift register up to the first stop bit (a second stop bit is ignored), then moves the frame into the two-level receive buffer and sets INTFLAG.RXC; DATA may then be read. CTRLB.RXEN = 0 disables the receiver, flushes the receive buffer and loses any frame in progress.

STATUS holds three receive error bits: FERR (frame), BUFOVF (overflow) and PERR (parity). Each stays set until 1 is written to it, and all clear when the receiver is disabled. CTRLA.IBON = 1 raises STATUS.BUFOVF at the moment of overflow, and software empties the receive FIFO by reading RxDATA until INTFLAG.RXC clears. CTRLA.IBON = 0 carries the overflow through the receive FIFO with the data: reading that data then sets INTFLAG.RXC together with STATUS.BUFOVF and INTFLAG.ERROR.

Clock recovery locks incoming asynchronous frames on RxD to the internal baud clock, and data recovery samples each bit and low-pass filters it for noise immunity. The range of baud mismatch the receiver accepts depends on the internal baud clock's accuracy, the incoming bit rate and the frame length; a transmitter too fast or too slow cannot be synchronized to the start bit. Mismatch comes from reference clock instability and from the generator's inability to divide exactly, so BAUD is chosen for the smallest error. The recommended maximum receiver error assumes the receiver and transmitter share the total error equally, and it allows for clock source and baud generator errors.

Worked example at 2 Mbps: x16 sampling, 10 data bits, no parity, one start and one stop bit, fBAUD = 32 MHz × 1 (BAUD = 0) / 16, so the baud generator adds no offset error. The receiver accepts +3.3 % to −4.35 %; with a transmitter error of up to +3.0 % / −4.05 % accepted, a recommended maximum Rx error of ±1.5 % leaves a security margin. The transmitter's error depends on the external transmitter; it should lie within the recommended maximum Rx error, and a larger one is acceptable only within the accepted receiver error.

CTRLA.FORM = 0x1 enables parity. Even parity (CTRLB.PMODE = 0) sets the parity bit so the count of ones including it is even; odd parity (CTRLB.PMODE = 1) makes it odd. On reception the checker compares computed and received parity and sets STATUS.PERR on a mismatch.

RTS/CTS out-of-band flow control: TXD to the remote RXD, RXD from the remote TXD, CTS from the remote RTS, RTS to the remote CTS. Available only with the internal clock (CTRLA.MODE = 1), asynchronous mode (CTRLA.CMODE = 0) and the flow-control pinout (CTRLA.TXPO = 2). The receiver drives RTS high while it is disabled or its receive FIFO is full, telling the remote to stop after the frame in progress; writing CTRLB.RXEN sets or clears RTS after a synchronization delay; when the FIFO fills, RTS rises at once and the frame being received waits in the shift register until there is room. STATUS.CTS gives the CTS level; a character starts only while CTS = 0, and when CTS rises the transmitter finishes the frame in progress and stops.

IrDA-compliant encoding up to 115.2 kb/s, with CTRLB.ENC = 1, asynchronous mode (CTRLA.CMODE = 0) and 16x sampling (CTRLA.SAMPR[0] = 0). Each low bit is sent as a high pulse 3/16 of a bit period wide. The decoder resynchronizes its baud counter at the start of each zero pulse and accepts a pulse at least as long as RXPL.RXPL sets, passing it to the receiver when the counter reaches mid-bit. Transmit and receive polarity are opposite: a 0 bit is sent as a high pulse, while a low pulse that passes the width test reads as a 0 bit. Example: RXPL.RXPL = 19 requires a pulse of at least 20 serial-engine clocks; with BAUD = 0xE666, 160 SE cycles per bit, that is 2/16 of a bit, and shorter low pulses are rejected.

operation.topic: USART break detection, auto-baud and LIN client
operation.text: Needs CTRLA.FORM = 0x04 or 0x05 (auto-baud frame), CTRLA.CMODE = 0 (asynchronous) and 16x sampling with fractional baud generation (CTRLA.SAMPR = 1). More than 11 consecutive dominant bit times at the configured rate is a break field: INTFLAG.RXBRK sets and the USART expects a sync character of 0x55. A different sync character sets STATUS.ISF and INTFLAG.ERROR and leaves the baud rate alone. Every LIN frame starts with break then sync. After the break, the sync field's start bit starts a counter that runs for 8 bit times; its 13 upper bits (count / 8) become BAUD.BAUD and its 3 lower bits BAUD.FP, loaded after a synchronization delay. Data characters may follow.

Needs CTRLA.FORM = 0x02 (LIN host frame), CTRLA.CMODE = 0 (asynchronous) and 16x sampling with fractional baud generation (CTRLA.SAMPR = 1). The host sends a header of break, sync and identifier; the addressed client answers with 1 to 8 data bytes and a checksum. CTRLB.LINCMD = 0x1: software sends the header by writing DATA three times, any value (for example 0x00) to send the break, 0x55 for the sync, then the identifier, best paced by INTFLAG.DRE so no gap is added; software sets the break-to-sync delay. CTRLB.LINCMD = 0x2: writing the identifier to DATA sends break, sync and identifier in hardware, with the break-to-sync and sync-to-ID delays set by CTRLC.HDRDLY. CTRLC.BRKLEN sets the break length in host mode.

Available with the USART frame format (CTRLA.FORM = 0x00 or 0x01) and the RS485 pinout (CTRLA.TXPO = 0x3). A transmit-enable pin TE drives an external line driver: it is high while the transmitter is active, through the whole frame and stop bits, and stays high for CTRLC.GTIME further bit times of guard time. INTFLAG.TXC sets when the guard time ends and TE falls.

ISO/IEC 7816 mode talks to smart cards and security access modules, T=0 and T=1. Set-up: CTRLA.FORM = 0x07; inverted transmit and receive (CTRLA.RXINV = 1, CTRLA.TXINV = 1), so data bits appear on the line negated; CTRLA.TXPO and CTRLA.RXPO on the same data pin for one bidirectional line; even parity (CTRLB.PMODE = 0); 8-bit characters (CTRLB.CHSIZE = 0); T=0 with CTRLA.CMODE = 1 or T=1 with CTRLA.CMODE = 0. The USART is the host and supplies the clock: SCK to the card's CLK and TXD/RXD to its I/O. The line is half duplex and driven only while transmitting, so only one of receiver and transmitter may be enabled at a time; enabling both gives unpredictable results.

A T=0 character is a start bit, eight data bits, a parity bit and a guard time of two bit times; CTRLC.GTIME adds more guard time. The transmitter does not drive the line during the guard time. With no parity error the next character follows the guard time. A receiver that finds a parity error pulls the line low during the guard time (NACK), lengthening the character by one bit time, sets STATUS.PERR and keeps the character out of the receive FIFO. RXERRCNT counts, to a ceiling of 255, the parity errors it received plus NACKs the remote transmitter returned, and clears when read. CTRLC.INACK = 1 sends no NACK on a parity error, stores the character in the FIFO and sets STATUS.PERR; INACK overrides DSNACK. A non-zero CTRLC.MAXITER makes the transmitter repeat a NACKed character up to MAXITER times; reaching the limit sets STATUS.ITER and resets the iteration counter, and an acknowledged repeat stops repetition and clears the counter. CTRLC.DSNACK = 1 limits successive NACKs sent to MAXITER; at the limit the character is taken as correct, an ACK is sent, STATUS.ITER sets and the counter resets.

T=1 uses CTRLA.CMODE = 0 with one or two stop bits; the transmitter leaves the line undriven after the stop bits. Parity is generated on transmit and checked on receive; a parity error sets STATUS.PERR and the character still goes into the receive FIFO. The receiver signals no errors on the line and the transmitter does not retransmit.

With receiver and transmitter joined, by pin configuration or externally, CTRLB.COLDEN = 1 compares each received bit with the bit sent; both CTRLB.RXEN and CTRLB.TXEN must be 1. Characters received while the transmitter is idle cause no collision. On a collision the USART aborts the transfer, flushes the transmit buffer, clears CTRLB.TXEN after a synchronization delay (SYNCBUSY.CTRLB is set until then; TxD is then tri-stated), sets STATUS.COLL and INTFLAG.ERROR, and sets INTFLAG.TXC since the transmit buffer is empty. Software re-enables the transmitter once SYNCBUSY.CTRLB is clear.

operation.topic: USART loop-back, start-of-frame detection and sample adjustment
operation.text: Loop-back: CTRLA.RXPO and CTRLA.TXPO on the same data pins; the loop closes at the pad, so the signal can be seen on the pin too. Start-of-frame detection (CTRLB.SFDE = 1, asynchronous or synchronous): a 1-to-0 transition on RxD powers up the 8 MHz internal oscillator and enables the USART clock, and the rest of the frame is received if the baud rate is slow enough against the oscillator's start-up time, which varies with supply and temperature. In Standby the fast start-up internal oscillator must be the GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE source, or the first frame, and any frames until the oscillator is stable, may be corrupted by baud mismatch. With INTENSET.RXS set the Receive Start interrupt fires at the start bit; without it, the oscillator and USART clock stay on for the frame and the CPU wakes on receive complete. Sample adjustment: in asynchronous mode the bit value is a majority vote of three middle samples, chosen by CTRLA.SAMPA; with SAMPA = 0 these are samples 7-8-9 at 16x and 3-4-5 at 8x oversampling.

CTRLC.DATA32B makes DATA reads and writes 32 bits wide, for receive and transmit separately. Bytes go out and come in in order 0 to 3, byte 0 in bits 7:0. Only character sizes of 8 bits or less; a smaller character still occupies an 8-bit lane, with unused bits zero on receive and ignored on transmit. INTFLAG.RXC rises every four received bytes, INTFLAG.DRE every four for transmit. For frames that are not a multiple of 4 bytes, LENGTH.LEN and LENGTH.LENEN are written before the frame starts, and only while DATA32B is enabled: LENEN = 0x1 (transmit) or 0x2 (receive) sets LEN characters, 1 to 255, and the last RXC or DRE comes with the last byte. One length counter serves either transmit or receive, not both at once (using both gives unpredictable results); it resets when LEN is reached or LENEN is written 0. Writing LENGTH during a frame gives unpredictable results, and without LENEN a remainder that is not a multiple of 4 bytes may be lost.

DMA requests: RX, set while the two-level receive buffer holds data and cleared by reading DATA; TX, set while the transmit buffer is empty and cleared by writing DATA. Interrupt sources DRE, RXC, TXC, RXS, CTSIC, RXBRK and ERROR are asynchronous and can wake the device from any sleep mode; each has its own INTFLAG bit, enabled in INTENSET and disabled in INTENCLR, and a request lasts until its flag is cleared, it is disabled, or the USART resets. No events.

In sleep, with CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 1: on the internal clock GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE can run in every sleep mode and any interrupt can wake the device; on an external clock the receive complete interrupt can wake it. With RUNSTDBY = 0: the internal clock stops once any transfer in progress ends and receive complete can wake the device; an external clock is disconnected once the transfer ends and all reception is dropped. Writes to CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, CTRLB.RXEN and CTRLB.TXEN are synchronized; CTRLB.RXEN is synchronized in its own way.

SPI is a SERCOM mode. On both host and client side there is a shift register, one transmit buffer and a receive buffer two levels deep; the host uses the baud-rate generator, the client may use the address match logic. Features: full duplex over four wires (MISO, MOSI, SCK, SS); one-level transmit and two-level receive buffer; all four SPI modes; single-direction operation frees MISO or MOSI for another function; LSB- or MSB-first; DMA; 32-bit extension. Host: fSCK = 1/tSCK from an 8-bit clock generator, SS driven by hardware if wanted, and inter-character spacing if wanted. Client: fSCK = 1/tSSCK, optional 8-bit address match, works in all sleep modes, wakes on an SS transition.

In SPI mode the SERCOM sets the direction and value of its pins. PINCFGn.DRVSTR still sets the drive strength of SERCOM outputs; PINCFGn.PULLEN still works on SERCOM inputs but can only enable or disable a pull-down, never a pull-up. With the receiver disabled the data input pin is free for other use. In host mode SS is driven by hardware when CTRLB.MSSEN = 1.

The SPI keeps working through any sleep mode that leaves its source clock on, and its interrupts can wake the device. CLK_SERCOMx_APB is gated in MCLK; GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE must be set up in GCLK and is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some writes are synchronized. DMA requests go to DMAC, the interrupt to the NVIC. No events, no analog connections. It keeps running in debug halt unless DBGCTRL halts it. Writable registers can be PAC write-protected except INTFLAG, STATUS and DATA; not against an external debugger.

A synchronous high-speed interface that runs as host, which starts and controls every transfer, or client. Transmit is single buffered, so the next character can be written during the current one; receive is double buffered. A transaction is one or more characters of 8 or 9 bits. The host pulls the chosen client's SS low to start, both load their shift registers, and the host clocks SCK; data moves host to client on MOSI and client to host on MISO, one character each way at a time. The host raises SS to end the transaction.

CTRLA (except ENABLE and SWRST), CTRLB (except RXEN), BAUD and ADDR are enable-protected: writes are ignored while the SPI is enabled or being enabled, and writes made while it is being disabled take effect afterwards. Set-up order: CTRLA.MODE = 0x2 (client) or 0x3 (host); CTRLA.CPOL and CTRLA.CPHA for the transfer mode; CTRLA.FORM frame format; CTRLA.DIPO for the receive pad and CTRLA.DOPO for the transmit pads; CTRLB.CHSIZE character size; CTRLA.DORD bit order; as host, BAUD for the rate and CTRLB.MSSEN = 1 for hardware SS; then CTRLB.RXEN = 1. CTRLA.ENABLE turns it on and off; CTRLA.SWRST resets every register except DBGCTRL and disables it.

As host (CTRLA.MODE = 0x3) SCK comes from the baud-rate generator in synchronous mode, using the 8-bit BAUD value to make SCK and clock the shift register. As client (CTRLA.MODE = 0x2) the external host's SCK clocks the shift register. TxDATA and RxDATA share the DATA address: writes go to transmit and reads return received data.

CTRLA.CPHA sets SCK phase and CTRLA.CPOL its polarity, giving four modes; data is shifted out and latched on opposite SCK edges so it has time to settle. CTRLA.DORD = 0 sends MSB first and 1 LSB first.

With CTRLB.MSSEN = 1 hardware drives SS. With MSSEN = 0, SS is any general-purpose I/O set as output, and software pulls it low before and high after the transaction. A character written to DATA moves to the shift register, then INTFLAG.DRE sets and the next may be written. As each character goes out one comes in; with the receiver enabled it moves to the two-level receive buffer in the clock cycle of its last bit and INTFLAG.RXC sets, and DATA returns it. INTFLAG.TXC sets when the last character is out and DATA holds nothing new.

While SS is high the client is idle with MISO tri-stated; software may write DATA whenever INTFLAG.DRE is set. With SS low and SCK running it samples and shifts by the selected mode; DRE sets when TxDATA loads into the shift register. Each received character moves into the two-level receive buffer in the cycle of its last bit, with INTFLAG.RXC set. INTFLAG.TXC sets when the host raises SS. A write to DATA needs as many as three SCK cycles before it is ready for the shift register at the next character boundary, so the first character of a transaction is not DATA's content unless preloading is used; for several characters per transaction DATA must be written with at least three SCK cycles left in the current character, or the previously received character is sent. After DATA empties, INTFLAG.DRE takes three CLK_SERCOM_APB cycles to set.

STATUS.BUFOVF, the only receive error, stays set until 1 is written to it and clears when the receiver is disabled. CTRLA.IBON = 1 raises it at once on overflow, and software reads RxDATA until INTFLAG.RXC falls. CTRLA.IBON = 0 carries the overflow through the receive FIFO: reading that data then sets INTFLAG.RXC together with STATUS.BUFOVF and INTFLAG.ERROR, and RxDATA reads zero.

As client (CTRLA.MODE = 0x2) with CTRLA.FORM = 0x2 the address logic checks the first character of each transaction. On a match INTFLAG.RXC sets, MISO is enabled and the transaction proceeds; an address match can wake the device from sleep. With no match the whole transaction is ignored. With 9-bit frames only the lower 8 bits are compared with ADDR. Preload must be off (CTRLB.PLOADEN = 0).

At the start of a transaction a client first sends what is in its shift register: the reset value after a reset, or the last character of the previous transaction. CTRLB.PLOADEN = 1 loads one character from DATA into the shift register while the synchronized SS is high, so no dummy character is sent; a second character written before SS falls waits in DATA. Enough time must pass between SS falling and the first SCK sampling edge, covering SS synchronization to the system domain and the MISO-to-SCK setup time.

In parallel: with CTRLB.MSSEN = 0 the host drives a separate general-purpose SS line to each client, and only the selected client drives the shared tri-state MISO. In series (daisy chain): one common SS enables all n clients, the host shifts n characters per transaction, and SS may be driven by hardware or by software through GPIO depending on CTRLB.MSSEN.

Loop-back: CTRLA.DIPO and CTRLA.DOPO on the same data pins; the loop closes at the pad, so the signal can be seen on the pin too. Hardware SS (host, CTRLB.MSSEN = 1): SS goes low at least one baud cycle before transmission and stays low at least one baud cycle after; between back-to-back frames SS goes high for at least one baud cycle. Each of these intervals T is one to two baud cycles depending on the transfer mode. With MSSEN = 0 the SS pins are software-driven GPIO.

operation.topic: SPI select-low detection and inter-character spacing
operation.text: Client: with CTRLB.SSDE = 1 a high-to-low SS transition sets INTFLAG.SSL and can wake the CPU. Host: a non-zero CTRLC.ICSPACE holds SCK still and stalls the next character for at least that many baud cycles between characters (for example 4 baud cycles for ICSPACE = 4).

CTRLC.DATA32B = 1 makes DATA reads and writes 32 bits wide; bytes are sent and received in order 0 to 3, byte 0 in bits 7:0; only 8-bit characters. For frames not a multiple of 4 bytes, LENGTH.LEN and LENGTH.LENEN are written before the frame begins and only with DATA32B enabled. Client: with address recognition (CTRLA.FORM = 0x2) and a match, the address enters the FIFO as byte 0 and data starts at byte 1; INTFLAG.RXC rises every 4 bytes; a 32-bit holding register on the core clock side raises INTFLAG.DRE once DATA is taken, for the next word. If the bytes clocked while SS is low are not a multiple of LENGTH.LEN, STATUS.LENERR sets and the remaining bytes go out at the start of the next frame unless the SERCOM is disabled and re-enabled to flush its pipelines; if LEN is not a multiple of 4 the last RXC comes with the last byte. The length counts received bytes, or clocks when the receiver is off. Without preload, DATA written before SCK starts is sent one byte late, while the counter still counts the first empty byte. Reaching LEN resets the length, Rx-byte and Tx-byte counters; for several lengths in a row INTFLAG.TXC must rise before DATA is written for the next. Writing LENGTH during a frame gives unpredictable results; without LENEN a remainder short of 4 bytes goes out in the next frame. Host: with LENGTH.LENEN = 1, LENGTH.LEN sets 1 to 255 data bytes per transaction; RXC rises every 4 bytes and on the last; the transmit holding buffer works as for the client; TXC must rise before DATA is written for the next length.

DMA requests: RX, set while the receive FIFO holds data and cleared by reading DATA; TX, set while the transmit buffer is empty and cleared by writing DATA. Interrupt sources DRE, RXC, TXC, SSL and ERROR are asynchronous and can wake the device from any sleep mode; each has its own INTFLAG bit, enabled in INTENSET and disabled in INTENCLR, and a request lasts until its flag is cleared, it is disabled, or the SPI resets. No events.

Host with CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 1: GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE keeps running in Idle and Standby and any interrupt can wake the device. Host with RUNSTDBY = 0: the clock stops after the transaction in progress and any interrupt can wake the device. Client with RUNSTDBY = 1: receive complete can wake the device. Client with RUNSTDBY = 0: all reception, including the transaction in progress, is dropped. Writes to CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE and CTRLB.RXEN are synchronized; CTRLB.RXEN in its own way.

I2C is a SERCOM mode; an instance is either host or client. Each side has its own shift register plus one transmit and one receive buffer; the host uses the baud-rate generator and the client the address match logic. Features: host or client; DMA; compatible with Philips I2C, SMBus and PMBus; 100 kHz, 400 kHz, 1 MHz and 3.4 MHz modes; 32-bit data extension; 4-wire operation; slew-rate limited outputs and filtered inputs. Client: works in all sleep modes, wakes on address match, and matches 7-bit and 10-bit addresses in hardware as a unique address with or without the 7-bit general call address, an address range, or two unique addresses (usable with DMA).

In I2C mode the SERCOM sets direction and value of its pins and the internal pull-ups are disabled, so external pull-up resistors are needed. The I2C keeps working through any sleep mode that leaves its source clock on, and its interrupts can wake the device. CLK_SERCOMx_APB is gated in MCLK. GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE can clock the I2C as host; GCLK_SERCOM_SLOW is needed only for some functions such as SMBus timing; both are set up in GCLK, and being asynchronous to the bus clock some writes are synchronized. DMA requests go to DMAC, the interrupt to the NVIC. No events, no analog connections. It keeps running in debug halt unless DBGCTRL halts it. Writable registers can be PAC write-protected except INTFLAG, STATUS, DATA and ADDR; not against an external debugger.

Two lines: SDA for data and SCL for the clock. The host opens with a start condition followed by the 7-bit client address and one bit saying read or write; the addressed client acknowledges, and data packets follow, each 8 data bits and one acknowledge bit. After a NACK from either side the host either sends a stop condition to end the transaction or a repeated start to carry on. Conditions: S start, Sr repeated start, P stop; R (1) host read, W (0) host write; A (0) ACK, A-bar (1) NACK.

CTRLA (except ENABLE and SWRST), CTRLB (except ACKACT and CMD), BAUD, and ADDR in client operation are enable-protected: writes are ignored while the I2C is enabled or being enabled and take effect after disabling completes. Set-up: CTRLA.MODE = 0x4 (client) or 0x5 (host); optionally CTRLA.SDAHOLD for SDA hold time; as client, CTRLC.SDASETUP for minimum SDA setup time; optionally CTRLB.SMEN for smart mode; optionally CTRLA.LOWTOUTEN for SCL low time-out. Host: CTRLA.INACTOUT for the inactive-bus time-out and BAUD for the rate. Client: CTRLB.AMODE for the address match configuration and ADDR.ADDR and ADDR.ADDRMASK to suit. CTRLA.ENABLE turns it on and off; CTRLA.SWRST resets every register except DBGCTRL and disables it.

Bus state logic (start and stop detectors and a bit counter) watches the bus in all sleep modes while the GCLK_SERCOM clocks run, and is active while the host is enabled. STATUS.BUSSTATE reads UNKNOWN (0b00) after the host is enabled; it goes to IDLE (0b01) when software writes 0b01 to it, when a stop condition is seen, or on an inactive-bus time-out set for SMBus (CTRLA.INACTOUT); once known it never returns to UNKNOWN. From IDLE, a start by another host makes it BUSY (0b11), which returns to IDLE on a stop or a time-out (if configured). Writing ADDR.ADDR while IDLE makes a start and enters OWNER (0b10); a stop at the end of a transaction without lost arbitration returns to IDLE. A packet collision while OWNER loses arbitration and the state is BUSY until a stop. A repeated start changes the state only if arbitration is lost during it. A protocol violation can hang the I2C; CTRLA.SWRST = 1 recovers it.

The host is byte-oriented and interrupt driven; most events are handled automatically, operations auto-trigger, and a smart mode (SMEN) further reduces software. Two interrupt strategies: with CTRLA.SCLSM = 0 the host holds SCL low either ahead of or after the ACK bit; with CTRLA.SCLSM = 1, interrupts come only after the ACK bit, for use when DATA need not be checked before acknowledging. High-speed (Hs) mode requires CTRLA.SCLSM = 1.

Modes: Standard (Sm) to 100 kHz, Fast (Fm) to 400 kHz, Fast-mode Plus (Fm+) to 1 MHz and High-speed (Hs) to 3.4 MHz. In Sm, Fm and Fm+, BAUD sets SCL low (TLOW) and high (THIGH) times while rise (TRISE) and fall (TFALL) times come from the bus; with the wired-AND bus TFALL counts within TLOW, and TRISE lasts until a high level is detected. TLOW, TSU;STO (stop setup), TBUF (idle bus time from a stop to the next start), THD;STA (repeated start hold) and TSU;STA (repeated start setup) are timed from BAUD.BAUDLOW, or from BAUD.BAUD when BAUDLOW = 0. THIGH is timed from BAUD.BAUD. TRISE depends on bus impedance; TFALL follows from bus impedance and the current limit of the open-drain driver and can usually be taken as zero. Fm+ calls for a nominal SCL high:low ratio of 1:2; at least one of BAUD.BAUD and BAUD.BAUDLOW must be non-zero. In smart mode the shortest time from an SDA transition to the SCL rising edge after a DATA write is 6 APB cycles; if long rise times need more, software must control the time between writing DATA and clearing the interrupt flag, and smart mode cannot then be used. In Hs mode there is no SCL synchronization: GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE and BAUD.HSBAUD (and HSBAUDLOW) set the rate; Hs calls for a nominal 1:2 high:low ratio and at least one of HSBAUD and HSBAUDLOW must be non-zero.

Writing the client address and direction bit to ADDR.ADDR starts a transaction; if the bus is busy the host waits for idle, then sends a start and the address packet. Then one of four cases. Arbitration lost or bus error: INTFLAG.MB and STATUS.ARBLOST set (with STATUS.BUSERR on a bus error), SDA output is disabled and SCL released, and the host may not act until the bus is idle; software clears the flag, and the rest clear on the next ADDR.ADDR write. STATUS.RXNACK always holds the last acknowledge received. No ACK: INTFLAG.MB and STATUS.RXNACK set and the clock is held; the client may be busy or asleep; the next step is a stop (preferred) or a repeated start to resend; under SMBus a client must ACK its address, so no answer means it is absent. Write, ACK received: INTFLAG.MB sets, RXNACK clears, clock held; software writes DATA.DATA to send, writes ADDR.ADDR for a repeated start and new address, or issues a stop. Read, ACK received: the host reads the first byte, then INTFLAG.SB sets, RXNACK clears and the clock is held; software acknowledges to keep reading (or smart mode does, sending ACK or NACK per CTRLB.ACKACT), sends a new address, or stops.

Host write: after the address INTFLAG.MB sets and writing DATA.DATA sends each byte while the host watches for collisions; a collision loses arbitration and sets STATUS.ARBLOST, a success brings an ACK and clears RXNACK, and MB sets either way, so ARBLOST is best checked first in the MB handler, address and data alike. RXNACK must be checked after every data byte, and the host may not keep sending after a NACK. Host read with SCLSM = 0: when SB sets one byte is in and the host must answer ACK or NACK; if arbitration is lost while sending a NACK, SB does not set and MB reports it. With SCLSM = 1: when SB sets the byte is in and the ACK or NACK set by CTRLB.ACKACT has been sent; ACKACT is then set for the next byte, and software reads DATA and issues a command unless in smart mode.

An Hs transfer begins in full speed with a host code 0b00001nnn (nnn unique to the host), written to ADDR.ADDR with ADDR.HS = 0, which no client acknowledges; arbitration happens only in this phase. After the code and NACK the host write interrupt fires, and the client address is written to ADDR.ADDR with ADDR.HS = 1; the host then sends a repeated start and the address with direction in Hs mode, and stays in Hs until a stop. Each further repeated start needs ADDR.HS = 1 written again with the new address. Hs transmission needs CTRLA.SPEED = 0x2 and CTRLA.SCLSM = 1.

With ADDR.TENBITEN = 1, writing ADDR.ADDR sends two address bytes, which the client acknowledges. Read or write, the host first sends the 10-bit address with direction bit ADDR.ADDR[0] = 0. A NACK after the first byte raises the write interrupt and sets STATUS.RXNACK; if the first byte is acknowledged the host sends the second and sees the write interrupt after it. For a read: write the 10-bit address to ADDR.ADDR[10:1] with TENBITEN = 1 and ADDR.ADDR[0] = 0; on the host-on-bus interrupt write ADDR[7:0] = 11110 address[9:8] 1 with TENBITEN cleared, giving a repeated start and the first byte with read direction; then transfer data.

The client is byte-oriented and interrupt driven, with automatic handling of most events and a smart mode (CTRLB.SMEN). After a start the address match logic checks the address; a mismatch is ignored until the next start, a match sets INTFLAG.AMATCH and SCL is held low until AMATCH is cleared, giving software unlimited time. STATUS.DIR, updated only on a valid address, gives the direction. STATUS.COLL set means the last packet addressed to the client collided; a collision releases SDA and SCL without telling software, so the next AMATCH is the first sign; collisions are meant to follow the SMBus Address Resolution Protocol. Read (DIR = 1): SCL is held; after an ACK hardware sets INTFLAG.DRDY to ask for data, after a NACK the client waits for a new start and match. Write (DIR = 0): SCL is held; after an ACK the client waits for data, a repeated start or a stop. CTRLB.CMD = 0x3 acknowledges in either direction, since its action follows STATUS.DIR, and writing 1 to INTFLAG.AMATCH also sends the ACK or NACK set by CTRLB.ACKACT. Data: the client waits for or starts sending a byte by writing DATA.DATA; INTFLAG.DRDY sets for each byte received or sent; received bytes are acknowledged per CTRLB.ACKACT and SCL is held until software acts. After a sent byte a NACK (STATUS.RXNACK = 1) means a stop or repeated start comes next, and the client must release SDA; a stop sets INTFLAG.PREC and the client returns to idle. With CTRLA.SCLSM = 1 the client stretches SCL only after an ACK: on a match the ACKACT response is sent at once and AMATCH sets, and software writes 1 to AMATCH to clear it.

With CTRLA.SPEED = 0x2 and CTRLA.SCLSM = 1 the client switches between full speed and Hs by itself: a start followed by a host code and NACK switches it to Hs and sets STATUS.HS until a stop. With ADDR.TENBITEN = 1 the two address bytes after a start are checked; the first is always acknowledged and the second raises the address interrupt. A write continues with N data bytes; a read continues with a repeated start and 11110 ADDR[9:8] 1, giving a second address interrupt with DIR set, matched because the client was addressed by the preceding 10-bit address.

With CTRLB.GCMD = 1 and 7-bit addressing, INTFLAG.PREC sets on a stop only if the client was addressed since the last stop; with GCMD = 0 a stop without an address match does not set PREC. In a group command the host sends commands to several devices in one transmission ended by a single stop, at which every addressed client starts executing its command; this client may be addressed after a repeated start among others, and gets its stop interrupt at the final stop.

Three hardware SCL-low time-outs, timed by GCLK_SERCOM_SLOW, which must run from a 32.768 kHz oscillator: TTIMEOUT, an SCL low of 25 to 35 ms in a single low period, enabled by CTRLA.LOWTOUTEN; TLOW:SEXT, a cumulative client clock-low extension of 25 ms from start to stop of one message, enabled by CTRLA.SEXTTOEN; TLOW:MEXT, a cumulative host clock-low extension of 10 ms within one byte, measured from start, or from an ACK, to the next ACK or stop, enabled by CTRLA.MEXTTOEN. An SMBus-compatible SDA hold time is also available.

operation.topic: I2C smart mode, 4-wire mode and quick command
operation.text: In smart mode, reading DATA.DATA by itself sends the acknowledge (ACK or NACK) that CTRLB.ACKACT selects. CTRLA.PINOUT = 1 selects 4-wire mode, which skips the chip's own I2C output stage (outputs SDA_OUT and SCL_OUT on PAD[2] and PAD[3]); joining an I2C bus then takes an outside tri-state buffer that meets the I2C specification. CTRLB.QCEN = 1 enables quick command: INTFLAG.SB or INTFLAG.MB sets right after the client acknowledges the address, and software then issues a stop or repeated start through CTRLB.CMD or ADDR.ADDR.

CTRLC.DATA32B = 1 makes DATA reads and writes 32 bits wide, bytes in order 0 to 3 with byte 0 in bits 7:0. For frames not a multiple of 4 bytes, LENGTH.LEN and LENGTH.LENEN are set before the transfer, and only with DATA32B enabled. Client: AMATCH sets once the address is in DATA, then DRDY every 4 bytes. LENGTH may be written before the frame or while AMATCH is set; a frame of other than LEN bytes sets STATUS.LENERR; if LEN is not a multiple of 4 the last DRDY comes with the last byte of a host read, and the last byte of a host write is NACKed automatically; address recognition resets the length counter. After a full-speed host code no data is received and a repeated start is expected, so the length is not counted and no LENERR arises whatever LENEN says. With SCLSM = 1 on a host write, CTRLB.ACKACT applies only to every 4th byte and the rest are ACKed, so ACKACT = 1 written in the final interrupt NACKs the last byte of a word. Writing LENGTH during a frame gives unpredictable results; without LENEN a remainder short of 4 bytes is lost. Host: ADDR.ADDR is written, optionally with ADDR.LEN and ADDR.LENEN; with LENEN = 1, LEN sets 0 to 255 data bytes, after which a NACK (host reads) and a stop are generated automatically. SB or MB rises every 4 bytes, and on a host read whose LEN is not a multiple of 4 the last SB comes with the last byte. With SCLSM = 1 on a host read, ACKACT applies only to every 4th byte. A client NACK before LEN bytes of a host write generates a stop automatically and sets STATUS.LENERR and INTFLAG.ERROR.

DMA needs smart mode (CTRLB.SMEN = 1). Client: an address match raises the address interrupt, and after it is serviced data moves by DMA; requests are RX, set when host write data arrives and cleared by reading DATA, and TX, raised when a host read wants a byte and cleared by writing DATA. Host: ADDR is written with ADDR.ADDR, ADDR.LEN and ADDR.LENEN; with LENEN = 1, LEN sets 0 to 255 data bytes, which DMA moves, followed by an automatic NACK (host reads) and stop. A client NACK before LEN bytes of a host write generates a stop and sets STATUS.LENERR and INTFLAG.ERROR. Host requests are RX, set when host read data arrives and cleared by reading DATA, and TX, raised when a host write wants a byte and cleared by writing DATA.

Client interrupt sources ERROR, DRDY, AMATCH and PREC, and host sources ERROR, SB (client on bus) and MB (host on bus), are asynchronous and can wake the device from any sleep mode. Each has its own INTFLAG bit, enabled through INTENSET and disabled through INTENCLR; a request lasts until its flag is cleared, it is disabled, or the I2C resets, and interrupts must be enabled globally. No events.

Host: GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE keeps running in Idle; with CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 1 it also runs in Standby; with RUNSTDBY = 0 it stops once any transaction in progress ends; any interrupt can wake the device. Client: RUNSTDBY = 1 lets the address match interrupt wake the device; with RUNSTDBY = 0 all receptions are dropped. Write-synchronized: CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, CTRLB.CMD, writes to STATUS.BUSSTATE, ADDR.ADDR in host operation, DATA in host operation and LENGTH in client operation.

The QSPI is a synchronous serial host interface. In SPI mode it talks to ordinary serial devices (ADC, DAC, LCD controller, CAN controller, sensor) with 8-, 16- or 32-bit data. In serial memory mode it drives serial Flash in single-bit SPI, dual SPI or quad SPI, mapped into the system address space like the other memories, so code can execute in place (XIP) without being copied to SRAM. Host interface: programmable clock phase and polarity, and programmable delays from one transfer to the next, from CS to the clock, and for the time CS stays inactive. Serial memory mode: a flexible instruction register for any serial Flash, 24-bit addresses by default and a 32-bit address mode for Flash larger than 128 Mbit, continuous read mode, on-the-fly scrambling and unscrambling, and double data rate for reads. One DMA channel for receive and one for transmit; register write protection.

The QSPI pins are set up through PORT. The QSPI keeps working through any sleep mode that leaves its source clock on, and its interrupts can wake the device. Three clocks, each gated in MCLK: the bus clock CLK_QSPI_APB, the module clock CLK_QSPI_AHB, and the fast clock CLK_QSPI2X_AHB taken from the high-speed clock domain (fHS). In DDR mode CLK_QSPI2X_AHB must run at twice CLK_QSPI_AHB; in SDR it is unused. The three clocks are synchronous, can be divided by a prescaler, and can keep running with the module clock off. DMA requests go to DMAC; DMAC writes must be 32-bit aligned, and a single byte written within a 32-bit word needs the rest of the word filled with ones. The interrupt goes to the NVIC. No events. The QSPI keeps running in debug halt. All writable registers can be PAC write-protected except CTRLA, TXDATA and INTFLAG; not against an external debugger.

The QSPI is always the host and starts and controls every transfer. TXDATA can be loaded with the next character during the current one; received data goes to RXDATA. The QSPI is enabled after power-on reset. CTRLA.ENABLE = 1 enables it, 0 disables it, and CTRLA.SWRST = 1 resets it. It starts in single data rate (SDR), where CLK_QSPI2X_AHB is unused and may be off. Double data rate (DDR), for reads only, is set by INSTRFRAME.DDREN = 1 and needs CLK_QSPI2X_AHB running before DDREN is written.

SCK is CLK_QSPI_AHB divided by a value from 1 to 255, so the fastest rate is the host clock and the slowest CLK_QSPI_AHB / 256. BAUD.CPOL sets clock polarity and BAUD.CPHA clock phase, giving four modes; the client must use the same mode. All four are available in SPI mode (CTRLB.MODE = 0); serial memory mode (CTRLB.MODE = 1) and DDR transfers (INSTRFRAME.DDREN = 1) support mode 0 only. With CPHA = 0 the MISO bit before the first is undefined, normally the MSB of the previous character; with CPHA = 1 it is normally the LSB of the previous character.

Several transfers can run while CS is held active, and three delays shape them: CTRLB.DLYCS, the minimum time CS stays high between deactivation and activation; CTRLB.DLYBCT, a delay between consecutive transfers (not programmable in serial memory mode, where DLYBCT is ignored); and BAUD.DLYBS, the delay from CS assertion to the first SCK edge. They adapt the QSPI to a peripheral's speed and bus release time.

With CTRLB.MODE = 0 the QSPI is a plain SPI host running from its baud-rate generator and driving CS and SCK. It has one shift register and two holding registers, TXDATA and RXDATA. A write to TXDATA moves at once into the shift register and the transfer starts; MISO is shifted in as MOSI is shifted out, so nothing is received without transmitting. Data written to TXDATA during a transfer waits there; at the end the received word moves to RXDATA and the waiting word starts the next transfer. INTFLAG.DRE sets when TXDATA moves into the shift register, clears when TXDATA is written, and triggers the transmit DMA channel. INTFLAG.TXC marks the end of transfer, after the DLYBCT delay if that is non-zero; CLK_QSPI_AHB may then be switched off. INTFLAG.RXC sets when received data reaches RXDATA and clears when it is read; data arriving before RXDATA was read sets INTFLAG.ERROR (overrun), and while it is set data is still loaded into RXDATA. Sequence: on enable and DRE = 0, CS goes low, DLYBS, the serializer loads TXDATA (DRE = 1), the transfer runs, RXDATA takes the serializer (RXC = 1), DLYBCT, then if DRE = 0 the next transfer follows, otherwise CS goes high and DLYCS elapses. CTRLB.DATALEN sets the data length and CTRLB.CSMODE the chip-select behaviour.

operation.topic: QSPI chip-select with and without DMA
operation.text: With DMA, the DMA reloads TXDATA as soon as DRE sets, so CS normally stays low for the whole transfer and CTRLB.CSMODE = 0x1 is not required; but a higher-priority DMA transfer or buffers in slow memory such as Flash or SDRAM can delay the reload so CS toggles between words and some clients lose the transfer, which CSMODE = 0x1 prevents. With CSMODE = 0x0, CS does not always rise between two transfers to the same peripheral: if TXDATA is reloaded before the current transfer ends, CS stays asserted; for peripherals that need CS released after each transfer, CSMODE = 0x2 is the recommended setting. Without DMA, the processor may not reload TXDATA in time to keep CS low, especially with DLYBCT = 0; CSMODE = 0x1 holds CS low until CTRLA.LASTXFER marks the end, even if TXDATA is not reloaded, and LASTXFER must be set before the last data is written to TXDATA for CS to rise after it.

With CTRLB.MODE = 1 the QSPI is a serial Flash controller in single-bit, dual or quad SPI: it reads the Flash so the CPU can execute from it, and sends commands such as program, erase and lock. Data then moves not through TXDATA and RXDATA but by reading and writing the QSPI memory space, 0x0400 0000 to 0x0500 0000. That region may be cached for speed; for Flash devices whose command or status registers appear in the region, either the data cache is disabled or the cache line is invalidated before the status register is read.

A frame carries an 8-bit instruction code (optional in some cases); an address of 24 bits, or 32 bits for Flash larger than 128 Mbit (16 Mbyte), needed by instructions such as read, program, erase and lock; an optional option code of 1, 2, 4 or 8 bits, used to switch some Flash devices into XIP or continuous read mode for lower read latency; optional dummy cycles needed by some reads; and optional data bytes for transfers such as read or program. Instruction, address/option and data can each go in single-bit, dual or quad SPI.

For a frame with an address and no data, write the address to INSTRADDR.ADDR; with data, the address comes from the data access in the QSPI memory space instead. Write the instruction and option codes to INSTRCTRL.INSTR and INSTRCTRL.OPTCODE. Then write INSTRFRAME: without data this sends the frame; with data the first access to the QSPI memory space sends it (read INSTRFRAME first to synchronize the APB and AHB accesses). INSTRFRAME fields: WIDTH chooses the lanes; INSTREN, ADDREN, OPTCODEEN and DATAEN enable instruction, address, option code and data; OPTCODELEN sets the option length (0: 1 bit, 1: 2 bits, 2: 4 bits, 3: 8 bits), which must suit WIDTH (with WIDTH = 6 the option goes in quad SPI and is at least 4 bits); ADDRLEN sets 24 (0) or 32 (1) address bits; TFRTYPE sets the transfer type; DUMMYLEN sets the dummy cycles between address/option and data on reads.

With TFRTYPE other than 0x1 and CTRLB.SMEMREG = 0, the frame carries the address of the first system bus access and later addresses are unused; each bus access makes one SPI transfer of the same size (a half-word access gives 16 bits, a byte access 8 bits). With CTRLB.SMEMREG = 1 accesses go through the QSPI registers, the frame carries the INSTRADDR address, each write of INSTRFRAME or TXDATA makes a byte transfer, a byte is read with each RXDATA read, and CTRLA.LASTXFER ends the transfer. With TFRTYPE = 0x1 the first frame carries the address of the first read; whenever reads stop being sequential a new frame goes out with the latest address, so the Flash can be read at random, and SPI transfer sizes may differ from bus access sizes. Without data the INSTREND flag in INTFLAG marks the frame's end; with data, software sets CTRLA.LASTXFER when the data is done and INSTREND then marks the end. Depending on CSMODE, software may then wait for INTFLAG.CSRISE.

operation.topic: QSPI read memory transfer and continuous read
operation.text: An instruction with DATAEN = 1 and TFRTYPE = 0x1 reads the Flash at any address, which allows execute in place: once INSTRFRAME is written, any address in the QSPI space can be read, bus addresses matching Flash addresses. With fetch enabled, several frames can go out before LASTXFR is written, a new one at each non-sequential address. Continuous read mode (CRM), offered by some serial Flash, drops the instruction code from later frames: a specific option code makes the Flash keep the instruction, which it then reuses, shortening reads at the many non-sequential addresses. It must be enabled in both the Flash (by option code) and the QSPI (INSTRFRAME.CRMODE = 1 with TFRTYPE = 0x1). If the Flash does not support CRM or has it disabled, CRMODE must stay 0 or the data read is invalid.

Scrambling works only toward memories: data is scrambled on writes and unscrambled on reads, on the fly with no loss of throughput, so data held off chip is hard to recover by probing the pins of either device. SCRAMBCTRL.ENABLE = 1 turns it on. The method depends on the user key in SCRAMBKEY.KEY, which is write-only, plus by default a device-dependent random value that cannot be set or read; with that value included (SCRAMBCTRL.RANDOMDIS = 0) data scrambled by one device cannot be unscrambled by another. RANDOMDIS = 1 uses the key alone, so several devices sharing the same key can read the data. Data scrambled with a lost key cannot be recovered, so the key must be kept in reliable non-volatile memory.

DMA requests: RX, set when RXDATA holds data and cleared when it is read; TX, set when TXDATA is empty and cleared when it is written. With DMA in RX memory mode, a read of the QSPI memory space is needed to trigger the first request. CPU access to registers that set or clear a DMA request can lose the request or corrupt the transfer. One interrupt line, INTREQ, is active when any INTFLAG bit is set and enabled; each source has its own flag, enabled in INTENSET and disabled in INTENCLR, and a request lasts until its flag is cleared, it is disabled, or the QSPI resets. Every source is ORed onto one NVIC request, so INTFLAG must be read to find the cause; interrupts must be enabled globally.

A USB 2.1 compliant interface for device and embedded host modes, at full speed (12 Mbit/s) and low speed (1.5 Mbit/s), with Link Power Management (LPM-L1), transceivers, pull-up and pull-down resistors and series resistors all on chip, and a 1 kHz SOF clock on an external pin. Device mode has 8 endpoint addresses, each with an IN and an OUT endpoint (16 endpoints), each configurable as control, interrupt, bulk or isochronous, with no endpoint size limit, payloads selectable up to 1023 bytes, feedback endpoints and crystal-less clocking. Host mode has 8 physical pipes with no pipe size limit, virtual pipes multiplexed on one physical pipe for an unlimited USB tree, and phase-locked SOFs. Endpoint and pipe configuration and data buffers live in internal SRAM at locations software chooses, the space used growing with the endpoints in use; a built-in DMA moves data to and from system RAM on each transaction with no CPU or DMA controller involvement, with multi-packet transfers and dual banks for every endpoint and pipe. Ping-pong operation uses the IN and OUT endpoints of one address in a single direction as two buffers, so software handles one while the USB uses the other. Multi-packet transfer sends a payload larger than the endpoint's packet size as several packets without software, cutting interrupts. When the bus is idle and suspended the USB can let the device sleep in any mode, and a bus resume can wake it from any sleep mode.

The USB pins and the 1 kHz SOF output (available in device and host mode) are assigned to the USB through the I/O controller before use. The USB keeps working through any sleep mode that leaves its source clock on; its interrupts can wake the device.

The bus clock CLK_USB_AHB is gated in MCLK. A generic clock, GCLK_USB, must be set up and enabled in GCLK; it is asynchronous to CLK_USB_AHB, so some register writes are synchronized. Low-speed and full-speed operation needs GCLK_USB at 48 MHz ± 0.25%. To keep up with 12 Mbit/s in full speed, CLK_USB_AHB should be at least 8 MHz. The DFLL48, locked to a reference clock, generates GCLK_USB; the GCLK feeding that DFLL reference should be turned off while the USB is disabled. Clock recovery is done inside the USB by a digital PLL that meets the USB jitter specification; crystal-less device operation uses the USB clock recovery module.

The built-in DMA reads and writes system RAM without the CPU or DMAC. The interrupt line goes to the NVIC. No events and no analog connections. The USB keeps running in debug halt. Writable registers can be PAC write-protected except the device INTFLAG, EPINTFLAG, host INTFLAG and PINTFLAG registers; not against an external debugger.
Production calibration values for the DP/DM output drivers sit in the NVM software calibration area; software copies them into PADCAL before enabling the USB to reach the specified accuracy.

After a hardware reset the USB is idle: disabled (CTRLA.ENABLE reset), module clock stopped, pad in suspend, device and host states and registers reset. CTRLA.MODE (0 device, 1 host) and CTRLB.SPDCONF may be set before enabling and take effect when CTRLA.ENABLE is written 1, which enters device or host mode; writing 0 disables the USB at any time and returns it to idle. CTRLA.SWRST = 1 resets every register and disables the USB, from any state. PADCAL must hold the calibration values before use.

Writing CTRLB.DETACH = 0 attaches the device and 1 detaches it. After attach the host asks for the device descriptor at default address 0, then sends a bus reset and an address; software writes it to DADD.DADD and sets DADD.ADDEN to answer at that address. A USB reset clears ADDEN. Endpoint data can be anywhere in RAM; the USB reaches it through its AHB host using endpoint descriptors whose base address is written to DESCADD. Before use each endpoint's direction and type are set in EPCFG.EPTYPE0/1, its descriptor is filled with known values so no random RAM is read, PCKSIZE.SIZE is set to the size reported to the host, and ADDR points at the data buffer. INTFLAG.RAMACER sets on a RAM access underflow during an IN data stage. Disabling an endpoint clears its EPINTENCLR/SET, EPINTFLAG and EPSTATUS.STALLRQ0/1.

operation.topic: USB device multi-packet transfers and bus reset
operation.text: For multi-packet transfers software gives the RAM buffer's address and size, and the USB splits it into packets with no software help, otherwise behaving as single IN and OUT transactions. A bus reset comes from the host and is handled in hardware; it clears EPCFG (except endpoint 0), FNUM, DADD, EPINTENCLR/SET, EPINTFLAG, EPSTATUS.STALLRQ0/1, EPINTSMRY and CTRLB.UPRSM, and sets INTFLAG.EORST when done. On each SOF token the frame number goes into FNUM.FNUM and INTFLAG.SOF sets; a CRC or bit-stuff error sets FNUM.FNCERR.

A SETUP token is ignored if its address does not match DADD.DADD, if the endpoint is disabled in EPCFG, or if EPCFG.EPTYPE0 is not control. Otherwise the USB fetches ADDR from the endpoint descriptor and waits for DATA0; a PID error or any other PID returns it to idle. If EPINTFLAG.RXSTP = 0 the data is written to the buffer whatever EPSTATUS.BK0RDY says; bytes beyond PCKSIZE.SIZE are discarded though the packet is still checked for bit-stuff and CRC errors, and software must never report an endpoint size to the host larger than PCKSIZE.SIZE. A bit-stuff or CRC error returns it to idle. On success an ACK is returned and the byte count without CRC goes to PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT; a full-size packet stores no CRC bytes in the buffer, one byte short stores the first CRC byte, two or more short stores both. Then EPSTATUS.DTGLOUT, DTGLIN, CURRBK and BK0RDY are set, BK1RDY and STALLRQ0/1 cleared, and RXSTP sets (interrupting if enabled in EPINTENSET).

An OUT token is ignored if its address does not match DADD.DADD, if the endpoint is disabled, or if EPCFG.EPTYPE0 is not OUT. The USB fetches ADDR and waits for DATA0 or DATA1; a PID error or other PID returns it to idle. With EPSTATUS.STALLRQ0 set the data is discarded and, unless isochronous, a STALL is returned and EPINTFLAG.STALL0 sets. Isochronous endpoints accept DATA0 and DATA1; others check the PID against EPSTATUS.DTGLOUT and on a mismatch discard the data and return ACK. With EPSTATUS.BK0RDY set the data is discarded, EPINTFLAG.TRFAIL0 and STATUS_BK.ERRORFLOW set, and a non-isochronous endpoint returns NAK. Otherwise data goes to the buffer at ADDR, bytes beyond PCKSIZE.SIZE discarded, the packet still checked; a bit-stuff or CRC error returns to idle, except that on an isochronous endpoint the byte count is written and EPINTFLAG.TRFAIL0 and STATUS_BK.CRCERR set. On success a non-isochronous endpoint returns ACK, the byte count without CRC goes to PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT with CRC bytes stored as for SETUP, BK0RDY sets, DTGLOUT toggles (non-isochronous) and EPINTFLAG.TRCPT0 sets.

BYTE_COUNT counts received bytes and is updated after each transaction, so it is zeroed when a transfer is set up. The total to receive goes in PCKSIZE.MULTI_PACKET_SIZE and must be a multiple of PCKSIZE.SIZE, or excess data may land in SRAM used by other parts of the application. Data toggle and bank-ready handling are as for single transfers. Each full-size packet adds PCKSIZE.SIZE to BYTE_COUNT and toggles DTGLOUT (non-isochronous); when BYTE_COUNT reaches MULTI_PACKET_SIZE, BK0RDY/BK1RDY and TRCPT0/TRCPT1 set.

An IN token is ignored if its address does not match DADD.DADD, if the endpoint is disabled, or if EPCFG.EPTYPE1 is not IN. With EPSTATUS.STALLRQ1 set a non-isochronous endpoint returns STALL and EPINTFLAG.STALL1 sets. With EPSTATUS.BK1RDY clear, EPINTFLAG.TRFAIL1 sets and a non-isochronous endpoint returns NAK. Otherwise the data at ADDR is sent, in DATA0 for isochronous endpoints or DATA0/DATA1 by EPSTATUS.DTGLIN otherwise, PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT bytes followed by the CRC. Isochronous: BK1RDY clears and TRCPT1 sets. Non-isochronous: the USB waits 16 bit times for an ACK, returning to idle without one; with an ACK, BK1RDY clears, TRCPT1 sets and DTGLIN toggles.

operation.topic: USB device multi-packet IN, ping-pong and feedback
operation.text: Multi-packet IN: the total to send goes in PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT, and MULTI_PACKET_SIZE, which counts bytes sent, is zeroed at set-up. On each IN token, if BYTE_COUNT − MULTI_PACKET_SIZE is less than PCKSIZE.SIZE that remainder is sent, otherwise SIZE bytes; if BYTE_COUNT is a multiple of SIZE and AUTOZLP is set, a zero-length packet ends the transfer. A full packet adds SIZE to MULTI_PACKET_SIZE and toggles DTGLIN (non-isochronous); the short last packet adds its length, clears BK0/1RDY and sets TRCPT0/1. Ping-pong: one direction is enabled in EPCFG.EPTYPE0/1 and the opposite is set to dual bank; the enabled endpoint's buffer, address pointer and byte counter are bank 0 and the other's bank 1. EPSTATUS.CURBK names the bank for the next transaction and updates after each; the matching TRCPT/TRFAIL flags and BK0RDY/BK1RDY are set, and DTGLOUT/DTGLIN update only for the enabled direction. Feedback endpoints share an address in opposite directions, as in USB Audio explicit feedback, the feedback endpoint taking the number of the first (lower) data endpoint; they are made by giving IN and OUT different PCKSIZE.SIZE and EPCFG.EPTYPE, for example endpoint n IN as interrupt IN with SIZE 64 and endpoint n OUT as isochronous OUT with SIZE 512.

The pad is in low-power idle while CTRLA.ENABLE = 0, CTRLB.DETACH = 1 or INTFLAG.SUSPEND = 1, and active when ENABLE = 1, DETACH = 0 and SUSPEND = 0. A suspend on the bus sets INTFLAG.SUSPEND and idles the pad automatically; a non-idle bus state sets INTFLAG.WAKEUP and wakes the pad. The pad also idles when the USB is disabled or DETACH is written 1, and becomes active again when ENABLE is written 1 and DETACH 0.

Upstream resume is the only request a device sends unprompted, and the host should first have sent DEVICE_REMOTE_WAKEUP. It can be sent only after INTFLAG.SUSPEND has set: writing CTRLB.UPRSM = 1 sends it, which the controller does after 5 ms of bus inactivity. Sending it sets INTFLAG.WAKEUP and clears INTFLAG.SUSPEND, and UPRSM clears when the resume ends. INTFLAG.EORSM sets when a host-rebroadcast resume completes. If UPRSM is set while a host downstream resume has already begun, UPRSM clears and the request is ignored.

CTRLB.LPMHDSK sets how LPM transactions are answered. When one arrives on an enabled endpoint (usually endpoint 0) and is answered, the EXTREG field in bank 0 of that endpoint's descriptor is updated with BESL (best effort service latency), bRemoteWake and bLinkState. After an ACK, INTFLAG.LPMSUSP sets and the transceiver suspends 9 µs after the transaction; stopping the USB clock while suspended saves more, and the MCU may sleep in a mode whose wake-up latency meets the host's BESL. Leaving L1 works as from ordinary suspend, but a USB-initiated remote wakeup is shorter, as LPM requires. A NYET answer sets INTFLAG.LPMNYET (interrupting if enabled); a STALL or no handshake sets nothing and the transaction is ignored.

Per endpoint, EPINTFLAGn holds STALL0/STALL1, TRFAIL0, TRFAIL1, RXSTP, TRCPT0 and TRCPT1, each enabled in EPINTENSETn; EPINTSMRY collects one bit per endpoint into the endpoint interrupt. Device-wide INTFLAG sources are LPMSUSP, LPMNYET, RAMACER, UPRSM, EORSM, WAKEUP, EORST, SOF and SUSPEND, each enabled in INTENSET. All combine into the one USB interrupt. WAKEUP is asynchronous and can wake the device from any sleep mode.

operation.topic: USB host device detection and reset
operation.text: Software sets CTRLB.VBUSOK once VBUS is present; while VBUSOK = 0 host operation is halted even if the host is configured and enabled. Software watches STATUS.LINESTATE: a device is connected when DP or DM is pulled high (which one depends on the device's speed), setting INTFLAG.DCONN, and disconnected when both are pulled down, setting INTFLAG.DDISC. In host mode an endpoint of a device is reached through a pipe. Writing CTRLB.BUSRESET = 1 sends a bus reset; when it is sent INTFLAG.RST sets and all pipes are disabled. From a suspended bus (CTRLB.SOFE = 0) the USB first goes to resume, asynchronously setting INTFLAG.WAKEUP, and sets SOFE so SOFs start right after the reset. A bus reset clears every PCFG, FNUM, BINTERVAL, HSOFC, PINTENCLR/SET, PINTFLAG and PSTATUS.FREEZE; STATUS.SPEED then gives the speed the device supports.

Pipe data can be anywhere in RAM, reached by the USB's AHB host through pipe descriptors whose base goes in DESCADD. Before use: PCFG.PTYPE sets direction and type, the descriptor gets known values, PCKSIZE.SIZE matches the size the device reports for the endpoint, ADDR points at the buffer, and PCFG.BK = 1 selects dual bank (not for control pipes). INTFLAG.RAMACER sets on a RAM access underflow during an OUT stage. A disabled pipe is inactive and its registers reset; disabling clears BINTERVAL, PINTENCLR/SET, PINTFLAG and PSTATUS.FREEZE. Writing PCFG.PTYPE to a non-zero value enables the pipe and sets PSTATUS.FREEZE, so set-up can finish before any transfer. At enumeration the device descriptor from GET_DESCRIPTOR gives bMaxPacketSize0, to which the default control pipe is resized. After the device answers at address 0, the host sends a bus reset and SET_ADDRESS; once that completes, software writes the new address into CTRL_PIPE.PDADDR in the pipe descriptor.

operation.topic: USB host suspend, wakeup and phase-locked SOFs
operation.text: Writing CTRLB.SOFE = 0 stops SOFs and suspends the bus; the device suspends 3 ms later. First the active pipes are frozen with PSTATUS.FREEZE (a pipe in progress completes its transaction), and at least one full frame should pass before suspending to avoid data loss. A non-idle bus sets INTFLAG.WAKEUP; if it is an upstream resume (K state) INTFLAG.UPRSM sets and software must answer with a downstream resume within 1 ms lasting at least 20 ms, by writing CTRLB.RESUME = 1. The host may also resume on its own with CTRLB.RESUME = 1. When the downstream resume ends SOFE sets automatically and the host is active again. For synchronous endpoints the SOF period is held through the active, idle, suspend and resume states (not disconnected, connected or reset): 1 ms while active and a whole number of milliseconds otherwise. This needs GCLK_USB kept running, or the SOF period becomes erratic.

operation.topic: USB host IN and OUT pipes
operation.text: IN pipe: the device sends IN data on request and the host stores it in an empty bank. Clearing PSTATUS.BK0/1RDY marks a bank free; IN requests run while the pipe is unfrozen (PSTATUS.PFREEZE = 0). When the current bank fills, PINTFLAG.TRCPT0/1 sets (interrupting if enabled) and BK0/1RDY sets; software clears TRCPT0/1 by writing 1, reads PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT bytes from ADDR and clears BK0/1RDY to free the bank. With several banks, each successful IN moves to the next; PSTATUS.CURBK and PSTATUS.DTGLIN track the bank and toggle. Single bank (PCFG.BK = 0) uses only TRCPT0 and BK0; dual bank (PCFG.BK = 1) uses both. OUT pipe: a filled bank is sent to the device once the pipe is unfrozen; software writes data at ADDR and sets PSTATUS.BK0/1RDY to send it, which in dual bank also moves to the next bank. PINTFLAG.TRCPT0/1 must be cleared before setting BK0/1RDY so no TRCPT event is missed.

operation.topic: USB host alternate pipes and errors
operation.text: Several logical pipes can run in turn on one physical pipe, reaching any endpoint of any device; software saves the pipe context (pipe registers and descriptor) before switching and restores it, notably PCFG and PSTATUS, after. Data flow error (isochronous and interrupt pipes, either direction): PINTFLAG.TRFAIL sets (interrupting if enabled); PINTSMRY gives the pipe and STATUS_BK.ERRORFLOW the bank. On OUT it is an underflow, the host sending from an empty bank; on IN an overflow, the device sending while the bank is full, typically a CPU too slow, and the packet is lost. A later successful transaction clears ERRORFLOW. CRC error (isochronous IN only): TRFAIL sets and STATUS_BK.CRCERR marks the bank; the corrupted packet stays in the bank and TRCPT0/1 sets. PERR (all pipes): PINTFLAG.PERR sets when an error field of STATUS_PIPE in the pipe descriptor is set and STATUS_PIPE.ERCNT exceeds CTRL_PIPE.PERMAX; while ERCNT is below PERMAX each error increments it.

Any enabled pipe can send an EXTENDED LPM transaction with PCFGn.PTYPE = EXTENDED (PTOKEN, BK and PCKSIZE.SIZE do not matter) and EXTREG.VARIABLE set in the descriptor. An EXTENDED token and an LPM token go out and the device answers with a valid, corrupted or no handshake. ACK: the host enters L1 sleep at once, PINTFLAG.TRCPT0 sets, CTRLB.SOFE clears to stop SOFs, and L1 lasts at least TL1RetryAndResidency of the USB 2.0 LPM addendum. NYET sets PINTFLAG.TRFAIL; STALL sets PINTFLAG.STALL. A corrupted or missing handshake repeats the token pair up to CTRL_PIPE.PERMAX times, after which PINTFLAGn.PERR sets and STATUS_BK updates. Every LPM outcome (ACK, NYET, STALL, PERR) sets PSTATUS.PFREEZE, and the pipe must be unfrozen for another. To leave L1 software sends a downstream resume (CTRLB.RESUME) or an L1 resume (CTRLB.L1RESUME), whose K-state length comes from BESL in EXTREG.VARIABLE. A device upstream resume during L1 sets INTFLAG.UPRSM and the host then does an L1 resume. After L1, CTRLB.SOFE sets and SOFs resume.

Per pipe, PINTFLAGn holds STALL, PERR, TRFAIL, TXSTP, TRCPT1 and TRCPT0, each enabled in PINTENSET; PINTSMRY collects one bit per pipe into the pipe interrupt. Host-wide INTFLAG sources are DDISC, DCONN, RAMACER, UPRSM, DNRSM, WAKEUP, RST and HSOF, each enabled in INTENSET; DDISC, DCONN and WAKEUP are asynchronous. All combine into the one USB interrupt. WAKEUP can wake the device from any sleep mode.

Up to two CAN controllers implementing ISO 11898-1:2015: Classic CAN 2.0 (A and B), and CAN FD with data fields up to 64 bytes. Each has two configurable receive FIFOs, a separate signal for high-priority received messages, as many as 64 receive buffers and 32 transmit buffers that are dedicated to single messages, a configurable transmit FIFO, transmit queue and transmit event FIFO, error logging, a programmable loop-back test mode, maskable interrupts, power-down support and debug-on-CAN support. It is optimized for AUTOSAR and SAE J1939. Messages and filters live in a Message RAM in system SRAM, outside the controller, which the CPU reads and writes directly. Transfer rates reach 1 Mb/s in CAN 2.0 mode and 10 Mb/s in CAN FD mode.

CAN_TX and CAN_RX are assigned to the CAN in the I/O pin controller before use. The CAN keeps running in any Idle sleep mode whose source clock is on, and its interrupts can wake the device. While the CAN is enabled its clocks may only be stopped through the CAN's own low-power (clock stop) mode.

Two clocks run the CAN: the AHB clock CLK_CAN_AHB, gated in MCLK (its reset state is in MCLK.AHBMASK), and the generic clock GCLK_CAN, which must be set up and enabled in GCLK. The two are asynchronous, so some register writes are synchronized; the only write-synchronized bit is CCCR.INIT, whose read-back updates once synchronization completes. A built-in DMA moves message data between the CAN and system RAM on each transaction with no CPU or DMAC involvement; the DMAC is used only for the debug-message function. The interrupt lines go to the NVIC. Events, debug operation, PAC protection and analog connections do not apply.

Message handling is done by an Rx handler and a Tx handler. The Rx handler runs acceptance filtering, moves received messages from the CAN core into the Message RAM and keeps receive status; the Tx handler moves transmit messages from the Message RAM into the CAN core and keeps transmit status. The Message RAM, single- or dual-ported, is reached over AHB. Acceptance filtering uses up to 128 filter elements, each set up as a range, a bit mask or a dedicated-ID filter.

Initialization begins when CCCR.INIT is set: by software, by a hardware reset, by an uncorrected Message RAM bit error, or on entering Bus_Off. While INIT is set, bus traffic stops, CAN_TX sits recessive (high) and the error counters keep their values; setting INIT changes no configuration register. Clearing INIT ends initialization; the bit stream processor then waits for 11 consecutive recessive bits (Bus_Idle) before joining the bus.
