Configuration registers can be written only while both CCCR.INIT and CCCR.CCE are set; CCE can be changed only while INIT = 1 and clears itself when INIT clears. Setting CCE resets HPMS, RXF0S, RXF1S, TXFQS, TXBRP, TXBTO, TXBCF and TXEFS, presets TOCV.TOC to TOCC.TOP, and holds the Tx and Rx handler state machines idle. TXBAR and TXBCR can be written only while CCE = 0. CCCR.TEST and CCCR.MON can be set only while INIT = 1 and CCE = 1 and can be cleared at any time; CCCR.DAR can be changed only while INIT = 1 and CCE = 1.

With initialization done and CCCR.INIT cleared, the CAN synchronizes to the bus and is ready. Messages that pass acceptance filtering, with their ID and DLC, go to a dedicated Rx buffer or to Rx FIFO 0 or Rx FIFO 1. Transmit messages are placed in dedicated Tx buffers, a Tx FIFO or a Tx queue. Automatic transmission in answer to remote frames is not implemented.

CAN FD frames come in two forms: a longer data field (more than 8 bytes) at one bit rate, and a frame whose control, data and CRC fields run at a higher bit rate than the rest. The FDF bit (formerly a reserved bit) is recessive for CAN FD and dominant for Classic CAN; in an FD frame res dominant with BRS recessive selects bit-rate switching. A received frame with FDF and res both recessive sets PSR.PXE (protocol exception); with protocol exception handling on (CCCR.PXHD = 0) the CAN moves from receiver (PSR.ACT = 10) to synchronizing (PSR.ACT = 00) at the next sample point, and with it off (PXHD = 1) the recessive res is a form error answered by an error frame. CCCR.FDOE = 1 enables sending and receiving FD frames; Classic frames always work. With FDOE = 0 received frames are read as Classic, so an FD frame draws an error frame, and FDF and BRS in Tx buffers are ignored. With FDOE = 1 and CCCR.BRSE = 0 only FDF is used; with both set, buffers with FDF and BRS set go out as FD with bit-rate switching. FDOE and BRSE can be changed only while INIT and CCE are both set. Changing mode during operation is recommended only for: turning off bit-rate switching when data-phase errors are much more frequent than arbitration-phase errors; start-up, where all nodes send Classic frames until every node is known to handle FD; CAN partial-networking wake-up messages, which must be Classic; and end-of-line programming with non-FD nodes held silent until done.

In an FD frame the nominal bit timing (NBTP) applies through arbitration up to the BRS bit; if BRS is recessive the fast data bit timing (DBTP) applies from there until the CRC delimiter or the first detected error, whichever comes first. The highest data-phase bit rate depends on GCLK_CAN: at 20 MHz with the shortest bit time of 4 tq it is 5 Mbit/s. In both FD formats the ESI bit carries the transmitter's error state at the start of transmission: recessive if error passive, otherwise dominant.

In the FD data phase a transmitter reads its own bits back through the transceiver on CAN_RX, delayed by the transceiver loop delay; a delay longer than TSEG1 would show as a bit error, so without compensation the data bit rate is limited by that delay. With compensation enabled (DBTP.TDC = 1, data phase only, never in arbitration), the received bit is checked at a secondary sample point (SSP) placed at the measured CAN_TX-to-CAN_RX delay plus the offset TDCR.TDCO (for example half a data bit), rounded down to whole mtq; a bit error found there is acted on at the next regular sample point. PSR.TDCV shows the value in use; it clears when CCCR.INIT is set and updates on each FD frame sent while TDC is set. Limits: measured delay plus TDCO must be under 6 data bit times and at most 127 mtq (a larger sum is clamped to 127 mtq); the data phase, and with it SSP checking, ends at the CRC delimiter's sample point. The delay is measured in each FD frame sent, from the falling edge between FDF and res until that edge is seen on the receive input, at one-mtq resolution. A filter window, TDCR.TDCF, sets a minimum SSP position so that a short dominant spike during the FDF bit as received cannot stop the measurement too soon; the measurement stops only once the SSP position is at least TDCF and CAN_RX is low.

In restricted operation the node receives data and remote frames and acknowledges valid frames, but sends no data, remote, active error or overload frames; on an error or overload condition it sends no dominant bits and waits for bus idle to resynchronize. The error counters ECR.REC and ECR.TEC hold still, but the error log count ECR.CEL still increments. Software enters it by setting CCCR.ASM (only while CCE and INIT are both 1) and can clear ASM at any time. The CAN also enters it by itself when the Tx handler cannot read the Message RAM in time; software clears ASM to leave. It suits bit-rate detection: the application tries bit rates and leaves the mode after receiving a valid frame.

CCCR.MON = 1 puts the CAN in bus monitoring mode (ISO 11898-1, 10.12): it receives valid data and remote frames but cannot start a transmission and drives only recessive bits; a dominant bit it would have to send (ACK, overload flag, active error flag) is looped back internally so the CAN sees it while the bus stays recessive. TXBRP is held reset. It lets bus traffic be watched without disturbing it.

Frames that lose arbitration or are hit by errors are retransmitted automatically by default (ISO 11898-1, 6.3.3). For time-triggered communication (ISO 11898-1, 9.2) CCCR.DAR turns this off. In DAR mode every transmission is cancelled once started; TXBRP.TRPx clears after a successful transmission, when the transmission had not yet started at cancellation, on lost arbitration, or on an error. Outcomes: success sets TXBTO.TOx and leaves TXBCF.CFx clear; success despite cancellation sets both TOx and CFx; lost arbitration or a disturbed frame sets CFx only. A successful frame, with Tx event storage enabled, stores a Tx Event FIFO element whose ET field is 10, meaning sent although cancelled.

Setting CCCR.TEST opens the TEST register. TEST.TX gives CAN_TX four functions: the normal serial output, the CAN sample point signal for checking bit timing, constant dominant, or constant recessive; TEST.RX reads the CAN_RX pin. Because of the GCLK_CAN to AHB clock synchronization, a TEST.TX write reaches the pin, and a pin change reaches TEST.RX, several AHB clock periods later. Test modes are for production test and self-test only; software control of CAN_TX interferes with all protocol functions. External loop-back (TEST.LBCK = 1): messages the CAN sends are also taken in as received ones, and stored if they pass acceptance filtering; acknowledge errors are ignored, the Tx output is fed back internally to the Rx input, the CAN_RX pin is ignored and transmitted messages can be watched on CAN_TX. Internal loop-back (TEST.LBCK = 1 and CCCR.MON = 1): CAN_RX is disconnected and CAN_TX held recessive, so the CAN can be self-tested while connected to a running bus.

A 16-bit wrap-around timestamp counter is clocked in multiples of 1 to 16 CAN bit times set by the prescaler TSCC.TCP and read in TSCV.TSC; writing TSCV clears it, and a wrap sets IR.TSW. At the start of each frame received or sent its value is stored in the Rx buffer or Rx FIFO element (RXTS[15:0]) or Tx Event FIFO element (TXTS[15:0]). The timestamp counter cannot be used in CAN FD mode with bit-rate switching on (CCCR.BRSE = 1). A 16-bit down-counting timeout counter, using the same prescaler, signals timeouts on either Rx FIFO or on the Tx Event FIFO; it is set up in TOCC and read in TOCV.TOC, runs only while CCCR.INIT = 0 and stops when INIT is set (as on Bus_Off). TOCC.TOS selects the mode. In continuous mode it starts when INIT clears, a write to TOCV reloads TOCC.TOP, and on reaching zero it restarts at TOP. When a FIFO controls it, an empty FIFO reloads TOP, counting starts with the first element stored, and TOCV writes do nothing. Reaching zero sets IR.TOO. It is clocked from the CAN core's sample point, so its decrement moves with resynchronization, and with FD bit-rate switching it runs at different rates in the arbitration and data fields.

Two filter lists, one for standard (11-bit) and one for extended (29-bit) IDs, send accepted frames to an Rx buffer or Rx FIFO 0 or 1. Each list runs from element 0 and stops at the first match. Each element can be a range filter, a filter for one or two dedicated IDs, or a classic bit mask filter; can accept or reject; and can be enabled on its own. Configuration registers are GFC, SIDFC, XIDFC and XIDAM. A match, by the element's SFEC/EFEC setting, stores the frame in FIFO 0 or FIFO 1, stores it in an Rx buffer, stores it in an Rx buffer and pulses the filter event pin, rejects it, sets the high-priority flag IR.HPM, or sets IR.HPM and stores it in FIFO 0 or 1. Filtering starts once the whole identifier is in; after a match the message is written to the target buffer or FIFO in 32-bit pieces. A frame then found faulty (a CRC error, for example) is discarded: an Rx buffer's New Data flag is not set but the buffer may be partly overwritten, and a FIFO's put index is not advanced but the element may be partly overwritten; PSR.LEC or PSR.FLEC gives the error type. The stored identifier is always the received one, unchanged by the filters, and the outcome depends strongly on the order of filter elements.

Range filter: matches IDs from SF1ID to SF2ID (standard) or EF1ID to EF2ID (extended); for extended frames EFT = 00 ANDs the received ID with XIDAM first and EFT = 11 does not use XIDAM. Dedicated-ID filter: one or two specific IDs; for one ID set SF1ID = SF2ID or EF1ID = EF2ID. Classic bit mask: SF1ID/EF1ID is the ID and SF2ID/EF2ID the mask; a mask bit of 0 makes that ID bit don't-care and only bits whose mask bit is 1 are compared, so an all-ones mask needs an exact match and an all-zeros mask passes every ID.

operation.topic: CAN standard and extended ID filtering flow
operation.text: For a valid received frame, its ID, RTR and IDE bits are compared against the configured list. Standard frames: remote frames are rejected if GFC.RRFS = 1; with SIDFC.LSS = 0 the list is skipped; otherwise elements 0 to LSS are tried. Extended frames: the same with GFC.RRFE and XIDFC.LSE, and the received ID is ANDed with XIDAM before the list runs. A matching accept element, or a non-matching frame when GFC.ANFS[1] / GFC.ANFE[1] = 0, leads to storage; a reject element or ANFS[1] / ANFE[1] = 1 for non-matching frames discards it. The frame is also not stored when the target FIFO is full in blocking mode or the target Rx buffer's ND flag is 1.

Rx FIFO 0 and Rx FIFO 1, configured in RXF0C and RXF1C, hold up to 64 elements each. When a FIFO's fill level reaches its watermark RXFnC.FnWM, IR.RFnW is set; when the put index reaches the get index, RXFnS.FnF and IR.RFnF signal full. An element is read at RXFnC.FnSA plus RXFnS.FnGI times the element size. Blocking mode (RXFnC.FnOM = 0, the default): when full (FnPI = FnGI) nothing more is written until a message is read and the get index advances; a message arriving while full is dropped and RXFnS.RFnL and IR.RFnL are set. Overwrite mode (FnOM = 1): when full the next accepted message overwrites the oldest and both indexes advance; reading should start at least at get index + 1, since a new message may be written at the put index while the CPU reads at the get index, the offset needed depending on how fast the CPU reads (with an offset of two, the messages in the two skipped elements are lost). After reading, software writes the last element number read to RXFnA.FnA, which moves the get index there and clears the full flag if the put index has not reached it.

Up to 64 dedicated Rx buffers start at RXBC.RBSA. Each needs a standard or extended filter element with SFEC/EFEC = 111 and SFID2/EFID2[10:9] = 00, whose SFID2/EFID2[5:0] gives the buffer number. An accepted message goes to that buffer in the same format as an Rx FIFO element and sets IR.DRX. Once its last word is written, the buffer's New Data flag in NDAT1 or NDAT2 sets and locks the buffer against further matching frames until the CPU clears the flag by writing 1; while it is set, filter elements pointing at that buffer do not match and filtering continues, so the message may go to another buffer or a FIFO, or be rejected. Handling order: clear IR.DRX, read the New Data registers, read the messages from the Message RAM, clear the New Data flags of those processed.

Debug messages A, B and C are stored in three consecutive Rx buffers (for example 61, 62 and 63), in the Rx buffer element format, giving a fixed DMA start address relative to RXBC.RBSA with no further setup. One filter element per debug message is set with SFEC/EFEC = 111; then SFID2/EFID2[10:9] drives the debug state machine and SFID2/EFID2[5:0] gives the storage buffer. Storing a debug message sets neither a New Data flag nor IR.DRX; RXF1S.DMS shows progress. Only when A, B and C have arrived in order does the DMA request go active, and the three can be read by DMA; the CAN leaves those RAM words alone while the request is active, as for an Rx buffer with its New Data flag set. The DMA acknowledge clears the request and the CAN is ready for the next set. A missing message restarts the sequence.

The Tx handler takes transmit requests from dedicated buffers, the FIFO and the queue, passes the messages to the CAN core, keeps the put and get indexes and fills the Tx Event FIFO. There are at most 32 Tx buffers, and each Tx buffer element chooses Classic CAN or CAN FD on its own. A Tx scan for the highest-priority pending request (the buffer with the lowest message ID) runs whenever TXBRP is updated or a transmission starts. AUTOSAR needs at least three Tx queue buffers and transmit cancellation.

For systems whose message IDs are fixed and whose arbitration priorities run against what the application needs, CCCR.TXP = 1 makes the CAN wait two CAN bit times of bus idle after each successful transmission before starting the next, so other nodes' pending messages can start in that gap without arbitrating against it. After receiving a message the node may send as soon as the bus is released. It breaks up bursts from one node and guards against a node requesting too many transmissions by mistake. It is off by default (TXP = 0).

Dedicated Tx buffers are fully under CPU control, each set up with a specific message ID; of several with the same ID the lowest-numbered goes first. After the data is updated, an add request in TXBAR.ARn requests transmission; the message then arbitrates internally against any Tx FIFO or queue messages and on the bus by ID. Each buffer takes element-size 32-bit words of Message RAM.

TXBC.TFQM = 0 selects Tx FIFO operation. Messages go out starting at the get index TXFQS.TFGI, which advances cyclically until the FIFO is empty, so messages with the same ID from different buffers leave in the order written. TXFQS.TFFL gives the free level (the difference between get and put index). New messages go into the element the put index TXFQS.TFQPI points at, and each add request steps it on to the next free element, and when it reaches the get index TXFQS.TFQF signals full, after which nothing more should be written until a message has gone and the get index has moved. One message is requested by writing 1 to the TXBAR bit of the buffer at the put index; n messages are written to n consecutive buffers from the put index, requested through TXBAR, and the put index moves on by n, n not exceeding the free level. Cancelling the buffer at the get index moves the get index to the next pending buffer and recalculates the free level; cancelling any other buffer changes neither. The next free element is at TXBC.TBSA plus TXFQS.TFQPI (0 to 31) times the element size.

TXBC.TFQM = 1 selects Tx queue operation: queued messages go out lowest ID (highest priority) first, and of equal IDs the lowest buffer number first. New messages are written at the put index TXFQS.TFQPI and an add request moves it cyclically to the next free buffer. A full queue, flagged by TXFQS.TFQF = 1, leaves the put index invalid and nothing more should be written until a message has been sent or a request cancelled. Software may instead use TXBRP and place messages in any buffer with no pending request. The next free buffer is at TXBC.TBSA plus TFQPI (0 to 31) times the element size.

operation.topic: CAN mixed dedicated Tx buffers with Tx FIFO or Tx queue
operation.text: The Tx buffer section can be split into dedicated Tx buffers (count in TXBC.NDTB) and a Tx FIFO or Tx queue (count in TXBC.TFQS); with TFQS = 0 only dedicated buffers are used. With a FIFO, the dedicated buffers and the oldest pending FIFO buffer (at the get index) are scanned and the lowest ID goes next. With a queue, all buffers with a pending request are scanned and the lowest ID goes next.

Meant for gateway and AUTOSAR applications, and not for Tx FIFO operation: writing 1 to a buffer's bit in TXBCR cancels a request from a dedicated Tx buffer or queue buffer, and success sets that bit in TXBCF. If the buffer is already transmitting, its TXBRP bit stays set until the transmission ends; success then sets TXBTO and TXBCF, failure sets only TXBCF and the frame is not retried. Cancelling a request just before it would have started leaves a short window in which no transmission starts even with another message pending, which may let another node send a lower-priority message.

After each message sent, its ID and timestamp are written to a Tx Event FIFO element, with the message marker copied from the Tx buffer to tie the event to the message. The FIFO holds up to 32 elements. When full (IR.TEFF) nothing more is written until an element is read and the get index advances; an event arriving while full is lost and sets IR.TEFL. When the fill level reaches the watermark TXEFC.EFWM, IR.TEFW is set. An element is read at TXEFC.EFSA plus twice the get index TXEFS.EFGI.

Each of the three FIFOs with a get index (both Rx FIFOs and the Tx Event FIFO) advances it when software writes its acknowledge index register (RXF0A, RXF1A, TXEFA): the get index becomes the written value plus one and the fill level updates. After reading one element, its index is written; after reading a run, writing the last index once is enough. When elements are read out of order (a high-priority message from an Rx FIFO, for example), the acknowledge index should not be written, as that would put the get index in the wrong place, change the fill level and lose older elements. The CAN does not check the values written.

What can raise an interrupt: a reserved address being accessed; a protocol error (arbitration or data phase); the watchdog; entering Bus_Off; reaching error warning or error passive; overflow of the error log; corrected or uncorrected bit errors in the Message RAM; a message landing in a dedicated Rx buffer; a timeout; a failed Message RAM access; wrap of the timestamp counter; the Tx Event FIFO (new entry, watermark, full, element lost); an empty Tx FIFO; finished cancellation; timestamp completed; a high-priority message; and, per Rx FIFO, new message, watermark, full and message lost. Every source has a flag in IR and an enable in IE, and is routed to either of two interrupt lines. A request is raised while the flag, its enable and its line's enable are all set, and is held until one of these happens: the flag clears, the interrupt or its line gets disabled, or a CAN reset. Requests go to the NVIC; software reads IR to find the cause. Interrupts must also be enabled globally.

The CAN works in any Idle sleep mode but not in Standby. Its own low-power mode can be used at any time without disabling it, and must be used before Standby so pending transfers finish: software writes CCCR.CSR = 1; once pending transfers are done and the bus is idle the CAN sets CCCR.CSA = 1 and returns to CCCR.INIT = 1, blocking transfers, after which CLK_CAN_AHB and GCLK_CAN can be stopped and the device may enter Standby. To leave, both clocks must run before CSR is written 0; the CAN clears CSA, and software restarts communication by clearing INIT.

Rx and Tx messages and the filter configuration are kept in a single- or dual-ported Message RAM, 32 bits wide (plus parity or ECC bits where used), of which the CAN can be set to use up to 4352 words. Any section can be left out and the sections can be in any order. In CAN FD mode the RAM needed depends strongly on the element sizes chosen for Rx FIFO 0, Rx FIFO 1, the Rx buffers and the Tx buffers (RXESC.F0DS, RXESC.F1DS, RXESC.RBDS, TXESC.TBDS). The CAN addresses 32-bit words: start addresses are word addresses with only bits 15 to 2 used and the two low bits ignored. The Message RAM must lie in the first 64 KB of system RAM. The CAN does not check the Message RAM configuration, so the section start addresses and element counts must be set with care to avoid corrupted or lost data.

operation.topic: CAN Rx buffer and FIFO element
operation.text: The Message RAM can hold as many as 64 Rx buffers plus both Rx FIFOs, each FIFO taking at most 64 messages; RXESC sets the element size for data fields up to 64 bytes. Word R0 holds ESI (bit 31), XTD (bit 30), RTR (bit 29) and ID[28:0]; word R1 holds ANMF (bit 31), FIDX[6:0] (bits 30:24), FDF (bit 21), BRS (bit 20), DLC[3:0] (bits 19:16) and RXTS[15:0]; words R2 onward hold the data bytes, four per word with DB0 in the low byte of R2. ESI = 0 means the sending node was error active, 1 error passive.

Two SD/MMC host controllers, SDHC0 and SDHC1, supporting e.MMC, SD memory cards and SDIO, compliant with the SD Host Controller Standard: the register set of SD Host Controller Simplified Specification V3.00 plus registers for e.MMC and extra features. Each runs on as many as three clocks (bus, core, and a slow clock used by some functions); both MCLK and GCLK must be set up first. Features: 1-bit and 4-bit SD/SDIO and e.MMC devices; SD/SDIO default speed (SDCLK up to 25 MHz) and high speed (SDCLK up to 50 MHz); e.MMC default speed (SDCLK up to 26 MHz); e.MMC boot operation mode; block sizes from 1 to 512 bytes; stream, block and multi-block reads and writes with advanced DMA and SDMA; an internal 1024-byte dual-port RAM; synchronous and asynchronous abort; SDIO card interrupt.

The SDHC pins are assigned in the I/O pin controller (PORT) before use. The SDHC keeps working in any sleep mode whose source clock runs. It uses one bus clock and two generic clocks: CLK_AHB_SDHC, gated in MCLK; the core clock GCLK_SDHCx, always needed; and the slow clock GCLK_SDHCx_SLOW, needed only for some functions and only with GCLK_SDHCx enabled. The generic clocks are set up and enabled in GCLK before use and are asynchronous to the bus clock. The interrupt line goes to the NVIC. DMA and events do not apply.

For SD and SDIO devices the controller follows SD Host Controller Simplified Specification V3.00, and cards are managed as the SDIO Simplified Specification V3.00 and the Physical Layer Simplified Specification V3.01 set out. That specification does not cover e.MMC, so most of its registers are used for e.MMC as well and the e.MMC-specific features are handled in two added registers, MC1R and MC2R.

The configurable custom logic is a programmable logic block linked to pins, events and other peripherals, replacing simple glue-logic gates on the board. It has up to four lookup tables (LUTs). Each LUT takes three inputs, each of which can be masked, through a truth table, then an optional synchronizer or filter and an optional edge detector, and can produce any logic function of its inputs: AND, NAND, OR, NOR, XOR, XNOR, NOT. Each pair of adjacent LUTs (LUT0/LUT1, LUT2/LUT3) can feed a sequential block acting as a flip-flop (gated D or JK) or a latch (gated D or RS). Inputs can come from pins, events, internal peripherals or the next LUT's output; outputs go to pins or the event system.

Pins used as LUT inputs or outputs are assigned to the LUT in PORT. The CCL keeps working in any sleep mode whose source clock runs, and its events can trigger other peripherals without waking the CPU. The bus clock CLK_CCL_APB is gated in MCLK. The generic clock GCLK_CCL, asynchronous to the bus clock, is needed only when a LUT uses events as inputs, or its filter, edge detector or sequential block, and must then be set up and enabled in GCLK first. The CCL takes and generates events through the event system; DMA, interrupts and analog connections do not apply. It keeps running, and cannot be halted, while the CPU is halted in debug. All writable registers can be PAC write-protected, except against an external debugger.

SEQCTRLx.SEQSEL can be written only while the matching even LUT is disabled, and LUTCTRLx (apart from ENABLE) only while that LUT is disabled; enable-protected LUTCTRLx bits may be written together with ENABLE = 1 but not with ENABLE = 0. CTRL.ENABLE = 1 enables the CCL and 0 disables it; LUTCTRLx.ENABLE enables each LUT. CTRL.SWRST = 1 resets every CCL register and disables the CCL.

Each LUT produces OUT as any function of its three inputs IN[2:0], set by the eight bits LUTCTRLx.TRUTH; the input value IN[2:0] read as a binary number picks which TRUTH bit is output. Any input can be masked.

Each input y of LUT x is chosen in LUTCTRLx.INSELy: masked, a peripheral (AC output, TC or TCC waveform output, SERCOM transmit output), an internal event, or another CCL block. MASK ties the input to 0. FEEDBACK takes the output of the LUT pair's sequential block: inputs of LUT 2N and LUT 2N+1 take SEQ N. LINK takes the next LUT's output (LUT2 feeds LUT1, for example). EVENT takes the LUT's one asynchronous event input line, which any of its inputs can select; an edge detector makes a strobe one GCLK_CCL cycle long on a rising edge of the event. IO connects the input to its pin. AC: comparator 0's output goes to the even LUTs (LUT0, LUT2) and comparator 1's to the odd LUTs (LUT1, LUT3). TC: WO[0] of TC N is the default source of LUT N and WO[0] of TC N+1 the alternative (TC0 and TC1 for LUT0, TC1 and TC2 for LUT1), wrapping at the number of TC instances, with TC4 as a second alternative for LUT0. TCC: only WO[2:0] of TCC N, with IN0 from WO0, IN1 from WO1 and IN2 from WO2, wrapping at the number of TCC instances. SERCOM: the transmitter output (TxD for USART, MOSI for SPI) of SERCOM N, wrapping at the number of SERCOM instances; the SERCOM must output TX on its PAD[0], which is the CCL's input pad. Peripherals and the event system must be configured before being selected.

To use an event as a LUT input: enable GCLK_CCL; route the event asynchronously in the event system; select the event input in LUTCTRLx.INSEL; to strobe on the falling edge instead, set LUTCTRLx.INVEI; then enable the event input with LUTCTRLx.LUTEI = 1.

The LUT output is combinational by default and can glitch when inputs change. LUTCTRLx.FILTSEL selects a synchronizer or a digital filter clocked by GCLK_CCL; with one enabled the output is delayed by two to five GCLK cycles, and events used as inputs are filtered too. The filter logic is cleared one APB clock after the LUT is disabled. The edge detector, enabled by LUTCTRLx.EDGESEL = 1, outputs a pulse on a rising edge of its input; a falling edge is detected by inverting the truth table. The filter or synchronizer must be on when the edge detector is used. Disabling the LUT also clears the edge detector, one APB clock later.

Each LUT pair can drive a sequential block chosen in SEQCTRLx.SEQSEL: a gated D or JK flip-flop, or a gated D or RS latch. GCLK_CCL must be enabled first, and optionally each LUT's filter or edge detector. The even LUT must be disabled while the block is configured and enabled afterwards. The even LUT (LUT0, LUT2) drives D, J or S; the odd LUT (LUT1, LUT3) drives G, K or R. Disabling the even LUT clears the block: the flip-flops asynchronously, with reset held for one APB clock; the D latch with G forced on and D forced 0 for one more APB clock; the RS latch with R forced on and S forced 0 for one more APB clock. Otherwise the flip-flops update on the rising edge of GCLK_CCL and the latches update from their inputs (characteristic tables below).
Each LUT can output its value OUTx as an event, enabled by LUTCTRL.LUTEO, and can take an input event as a truth table input, enabled by LUTCTRL.LUTEI.

With CTRL.RUNSTDBY = 1, GCLK_CCL stays on in Standby. With RUNSTDBY = 0 it stops in Standby, and any LUT using its filter, edge detector or sequential logic outputs 0; otherwise the truth table keeps working and its output follows the inputs.

A symmetric-key AES engine for 128-bit blocks, compliant with FIPS Publication 197, using one key for encryption and decryption. Keys of 128, 192 and 256 bits take 10, 12 and 14 rounds, and an encryption takes 57, 67 and 77 cycles respectively. It offers the five NIST SP 800-38A confidentiality modes, ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB and CTR, plus CCM/CCM* authenticated encryption and GCM encryption and authentication. CFB works on 8, 16, 32, 64 or 128-bit data sizes.

The AES has no pins. It keeps working in Standby if its source clock runs, and its interrupts, all synchronous wake-up sources, can wake the device from Standby. It is clocked only while DMA is enabled, during an APB read or write of its registers (not in Standby), or while enabled with an encryption or decryption running. It runs entirely on the bus clock CLK_AES_APB, gated in MCLK. It raises two DMA requests to the DMAC, for data in and for data out, which the DMAC acknowledges. The interrupt line goes to the NVIC. It keeps running while the CPU is halted in debug and can be forced to halt then. All writable registers except INTFLAG can be PAC write-protected, except against an external debugger. Events and analog connections do not apply.

Round keys are derived from the cipher key by the Rijndael key schedule. An initial AddRoundKey XORs each state byte with the round key; each following round applies SubBytes (byte substitution from a lookup table), ShiftRows (cyclic shift of each row), MixColumns (mixing the four bytes of each column) and AddRoundKey; the final round leaves out MixColumns. Decryption uses the inverse steps in reverse order.

CTRLA is enable-protected. CTRLA.ENABLE = 1 enables the AES, 0 disables it, and CTRLA.SWRST = 1 resets it. CTRLA.CIPHER chooses encryption or decryption, CTRLA.KEYSIZE the key size, and the key goes in the KEYWORD registers; with CTRLA.XORKEY set, a key write stores the XOR of the new and previous key words. Input data goes through the INDATA address into a buffer of four 32-bit registers shared by input and output; DATABUFPTR shows which register the next access reaches, advancing and wrapping on each INDATA access, and can be written directly. CBC, CFB and OFB also take a 128-bit initialization vector in INTVECT, which in counter mode holds the counter; GCM also needs its 128-bit authentication data. CTRLB.NEWMSG = 1 marks the next block as the start of a new message. CTRLA.AESMODE selects the mode and CTRLA.CFBS the CFB data size (8, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits). The counter-mode block counter is 16 bits, so it rolls over after 1 megabyte. Pre- and post-processing and chaining are done in hardware. When a block is done INTFLAG.ENCCMP sets (interrupting if enabled) and the result is read through INDATA; ENCCMP clears once the relevant output registers have been read. In CFB with a segment under 128 bits only the first one or two buffer registers are used.

CTRLA.STARTMODE selects how processing starts. Manual: write the key to KEYWORD, the initialization vector or counter to INTVECT (all modes except ECB), enable interrupts in INTENSET if wanted, write the data to INDATA, then set CTRLB.START; INTFLAG.ENCCMP sets when done, raising the interrupt if enabled, and clears when an output register is read. Auto: processing starts as soon as the right number of input registers has been written, with no START bit; DMA uses this mode. Last output data (LOD): for the MAC in CCM mode, which combines counter-mode encryption with CBC-MAC authentication. With LOD off in CCM, counter-mode encryption runs on the input; with it on, CBC-MAC runs with a zero block as initialization vector, and ENCCMP clears on the next INDATA write rather than on a read, so only the last result of a run of blocks need be read. Building the message for the CCM* security level is done in software.

The expanded key has 4(Nr + 1) 32-bit words, the first Nk (4, 6 or 8 for 128, 192 or 256-bit keys) being the user key. Encryption uses it forward from the first four words; decryption uses it backward, starting with the last four. The AES does not store the expanded key but computes each round's four words on the fly from Nk words of earlier rounds, so decryption needs the last Nk words first. Setting CTRLA.KEYGEN computes them in advance in Nr clock cycles; otherwise they are computed when a decryption starts, if not already valid, adding Nr cycles of latency to the first decryption.

operation.topic: AES countermeasures against differential power analysis
operation.text: Four hardware countermeasures: type 1 randomly adds one cycle to processing; type 2 randomly adds one cycle in another way; type 3 adds a random number of cycles, at most 11, 13 or 15 for 128, 192 or 256-bit keys; type 4 adds random spurious power consumption. All are on by default but take effect only after a write to the DRNGSEED register; CTRLA.CTYPE turns them off individually. They draw on a deterministic random number generator seeded through the RANDSEED register, which must be reseeded whenever the key size changes. Countermeasures lower throughput: fastest with all off, best protected and slowest with all on.

GCM combines CTR-mode encryption for confidentiality with a GHASH universal hash over a binary Galois field, run on the data after the AES, which produces an authentication tag (NIST SP 800-38D). It works on 128-bit input fields with no unaligned data, with any supported key length. Hash key: with CTRLA set to manual start (auto for DMAC), encryption, the key size, ECB and the chosen countermeasures, set ENABLE, write 0 to CIPLEN, write the key to KEYWORD and zeros to INDATA, set CTRLB.START and wait for ENCCMP; the hash subkey appears in HASHKEY. Authentication header: with CTRLA set to manual, encryption, key size, GCM and countermeasures, set ENABLE, write the key, set CTRLB.GFMUL, write the authentication data to INDATA, set START and wait for INTFLAG.GFMCMP; the result is in GHASH; repeat for the rest of the header, zero-padding a final block shorter than 128 bits.

operation.topic: AES GCM plaintext processing and tag generation
operation.text: Plaintext: set CTRLB.NEWMSG, load CIPLEN, load J0 + 1 into INTVECT, where J0 = IV || 0^31 || 1 for a 96-bit IV and otherwise J0 = GHASH_H(IV || 0^(s+64) || [len(IV)]64), s being the zero padding that brings the IV to a multiple of 128 bits. Load plaintext into INDATA, set START, wait for ENCCMP; the ciphertext is in INDATA and the running hash in GHASH; repeat for each block. For the last block set CTRLB.EOM, write it, set START and wait for ENCCMP; the final hash is in GHASH. Then load [len(A)]64 || [len(C)]64 into INDATA, set GFMUL and START, wait for GFMCMP, and GHASH holds the final value. With the DMAC the sequence is the same without setting START for each data block. Tag: disable the AES, set AESMODE to CTR, enable it, load J0 into the initialization vector register and GHASH into INDATA, set NEWMSG and START, wait for ENCCMP; the GCM tag is in INDATA.

The Public Key Cryptography Controller accelerates public-key arithmetic over prime fields GF(p) and binary fields GF(2^n). Its software interface, the Public Key Cryptography Library (PUKCL), sits in a ROM inside the device and implements: RSA and DSA, with modular exponentiation up to 7168 bits using the Chinese Remainder Theorem and up to 5376 bits without it, prime generation, and utilities (GCD and modular inverse, division, modular reduction, multiplication); elliptic curves, with ECDSA over GF(p) handling common curves of 521 bits and less (with room to 1120 bits for future use) and over GF(2^n) common curves of 571 bits and less (room to 1440 bits for future use), curve parameters chosen freely for NIST or other Weierstrass curves, point multiply and point add/doubling, from which other algorithms such as ECDH can be built; and a deterministic random number generator to ANSI X9.31 for DSA.
The PUKCC has no I/O lines, DMA, interrupts or events. It runs in all sleep modes provided its clock source keeps running. Its bus clock CLK_PUKCC_AHB is gated in the Main Clock Controller (MCLK).

The library's services fall into four groups: basic arithmetic and cryptographic services (self-test, GCD, integral division and others); modular arithmetic (modular reduction, modular exponentiation with and without CRT, probable prime generation); elliptic curves over GF(p) (point addition and doubling, ECDSA signature generation and verification); and elliptic curves over GF(2^n) (the same set). It can sit under an SSL software stack to speed it up and cut RAM use. A PUKCC driver for it is offered in Atmel START under Drivers > Cryptography.

After a power-on reset, enabling the PUKCC clock starts a clear of the Crypto RAM; the library must not be used until it ends, which is seen as the CLRRAM_BUSY bit of PUKCCSR returning to 0. The SelfTest service must then be run before any other service, and its outputs compared with the known values: u4Version equal to PUKCL_VERSION, u4CheckNum1 = 0x6E70DDD2 and u4CheckNum2 = 0x25C8D64F, with status PUKCL_OK. Some services use the device's random number generator, which must then be initialized, seeded where required and started before they are called.

Every service is called through the macro vPUKCL_Process(service, pointer), with the service name and a pointer to a parameter block, for example vPUKCL_Process(SelfTest, pvPUKCLParam). The parameter block (PUKCL_PARAM) holds a common header, PUKCL_HEADER, and a union P of service-specific structures: ClearFlags, Comp, CondCopy, CRT, Div, ExpMod, FastCopy, Fill, Fmult, GCD, PrimeGen, RedMod, Rng, SelfTest, Smult, Square, Swap; for GF(p) curves ZpEccAdd, ZpEccDbl, ZpEccAddSub, ZpEccMul, ZpEcDsaGenerate, ZpEcDsaVerify, ZpEcDsaQuickVerify, ZpEccQuickDualMul, ZpEcConvProjToAffine, ZpEcConvAffineToProjective, ZpEcRandomiseCoordinate, ZpEcPointIsOnCurve; and for GF(2^n) curves GF2NEccAdd, GF2NEccDbl, GF2NEccMul, GF2NEcDsaGenerate, GF2NEcDsaVerify, GF2NEcConvProjToAffine, GF2NEcConvAffineToProjective, GF2NEcRandomiseCoordinate, GF2NEcPointIsOnCurve. Each service has an accessor macro of the form PUKCL_<Service>(field), and PUKCL(field) reaches the header. For each parameter, Type is the data type from CryptoLib_typedef_pb.h, Direction is I when the application passes data in and O when the library passes it back, Location says whether the data must be in Crypto RAM or may be in device SRAM, and Data Length is the size of the data a pointer addresses.

Most services take memory areas, each given as a base pointer and a length in bytes; the pointers and lengths are normally left unchanged while the areas are read or written. For most services the areas must lie in Crypto RAM, the PUKCC's own 4-Kbyte area for exchanging parameters with the library; some may be in system SRAM, as each parameter's Location states. The last two 32-bit words of Crypto RAM must not be used. Unless a service says otherwise, areas hold GF(p) integers or GF(2^n) polynomials least significant byte first, lengths must be multiples of four and pointers 32-bit aligned. A GF(2^n) polynomial is stored with no transformation, one bit per coefficient, least significant byte first, with zero padding in the most significant bytes when the area is larger than the polynomial.

A parameter of any byte length is brought to the multiple of four the library needs by padding zero to three zero bytes on its most significant side; it then meets the aligned significant length requirement.

Where a service does not apply to a field, the field is not named and the Specific.GF2n bit has no effect. Where a service supports both GF(p) and GF(2^n), Specific.GF2n selects the field. Where it supports only one, that field is named and Specific.GF2n has no effect.

Each service returns a 16-bit status in u2Status. Bits 15-14 are the severity indicator and bits 13-0 the reason code. A severe status means the operation was not done or was corrupted and its result must not be used; a warning means the result's correctness cannot be guaranteed and needs a close look; an informative status means the result is correct; zero means no error. Services check their parameter placement constraints, and these must be respected during development and test for the library to work correctly.

SelfTest initializes the library: it puts the PUKCC through a reset, wipes the Crypto RAM, runs internal tests and reports the version numbers of the library and of the PUKCC. No other service may run before it, and its status has to be checked. It is also reached through the PUKCL_SelfTest() macro. u4Version depends on the PUKCL version and u4PUKCCVersion on the PUKCC version; the expected u4CheckNum1 is 0x6e70ddd2, u4CheckNum2 is 0x25c8d64f, and the final u1Step is 3.
ClearFlags clears the CarryOut, CarryIn, Zero and Violation flags of the Specific field and leaves Gf2n as it is. Macro PUKCL_ClearFlags().

Swap exchanges two buffers X and Y of equal size. Macro PUKCL_Swap(). It fails if nu1XBase or nu1YBase is not 32-bit aligned; if u2XLength is under 4, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; if either area is not wholly in Crypto RAM; or if the two areas overlap.

Fill writes a 32-bit constant repeatedly through an area R of Crypto RAM. Macro PUKCL_Fill(). It fails if nu1RBase is not 32-bit aligned, if u2RLength is under 4, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4, or if the area is not wholly in Crypto RAM.

FastCopy sets R = X. With equal lengths it is a straight copy; with R longer than X, X fills the low bytes of R and the high bytes are zeroed; with the X pointer equal to zero, R is cleared (as Fill can also do). R must be at least as long as X. Macro PUKCL_FastCopy(). With nu1XBase zero, nu1XBase and u2XLength are not checked. It fails if nu1XBase or nu1RBase is not 32-bit aligned; if u2XLength or u2RLength is under 4, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4, or u2XLength exceeds u2RLength; if either area is not wholly in Crypto RAM; or if the areas overlap.

CondCopy does the FastCopy operation (R = X, zero-padded, or R cleared when the X pointer is zero) only when the condition chosen in u2Options holds; two of the four conditions test Specific.CarryIn. When the condition holds, R must be at least as long as X. Macros PUKCL_CondCopy() and PUKCL(). When the option and CarryIn mean no copy is made, nothing is checked; with nu1XBase zero, nu1XBase and u2XLength are not checked. Otherwise it fails on the same alignment, length, Crypto RAM and overlap faults as FastCopy.

Smult multiplies a long number X by a one-word value MulValue, adds a carry operand and optionally adds the result to, or subtracts it from, a long number Z, giving R; the result can then be reduced modulo N. It works in GF(p) or GF(2^n), and operands may overlap within limits. With MulValue = 1 it copies a block (as FastCopy does), adds or subtracts two numbers, or, in GF(2^n), XORs two blocks. The result is stored on u2RLength bytes, so it is truncated if too large and zero-padded if smaller; R must be at least as long as X. nu1ZBase must always point to Crypto RAM, even with no accumulation or subtraction, and may then equal nu1RBase. With reduction, N is at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4} and the constant Cns at {nu1CnsBase, 64 bytes} for a big reduction or {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 8} for a fast or normalized one; R must first be zero-padded to 2 × u2ModLength + 8 bytes, the reduced result is written to X at {nu1XBase, u2ModLength + 4}, and R is corrupted. For example, with u2ModLength and u2XLength both 0x80, R takes 2 × (u2ModLength + 4) = 0x108 bytes and, for a fast or normalized reduction, X at least 0x84 bytes. A result larger than twice the modulus plus one word must be reduced separately with a Euclidean division.

u2Options is the inclusive OR of a required operation option (multiply only, add or subtract), a required carry option, and, only when reduction is wanted, a modular reduction option. nu1ZBase need not be filled when neither addition nor subtraction is chosen. Smult fails if nu1XBase, nu1RBase or nu1ZBase is not 32-bit aligned; if X, Z or R is not wholly in Crypto RAM; if u2XLength or u2RLength is under 4, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4, or u2XLength exceeds u2RLength; if R overlaps X; or if nu1R is below nu1Z and R overlaps Z (R may overlap Z when nu1R is at or above nu1Z). A reduction option brings the Modular Reduction constraints and codes with it. With accumulation or subtraction R = (Z ± (MulValue × X + CarryOperand)) mod B^RLength; without, R = (MulValue × X + CarryOperand) mod B^RLength.

Comp compares two integers (GF(p) only) by subtracting X + CarryIn from Y without storing the difference: X and Y are left unchanged and only CarryOut and Zero are set. If Y is longer than X, X is treated as zero-padded; Y must be at least as long as X. It fails if nu1XBase or nu1YBase is not 32-bit aligned, if either area is not in Crypto RAM, or if u2XLength or u2YLength is under 4, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4, or u2XLength exceeds u2YLength.

Fmult multiplies two long numbers X and Y, adds a carry operand and optionally adds the product to, or subtracts it from, a long number Z, giving R on u2XLength + u2YLength bytes; the result can then be reduced modulo N. It works in GF(p) or GF(2^n), and operands may overlap within limits. nu1ZBase must always point to Crypto RAM and may equal nu1RBase when Z is not used. With reduction, N is at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4} and Cns at {nu1CnsBase, 64 bytes} for a big reduction or {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 8} for a fast or normalized one; R must be zero-padded to 2 × u2ModLength + 8 bytes, the reduced result goes to X at {nu1XBase, u2ModLength + 4}, and R is corrupted. For example, with u2ModLength, u2XLength and u2YLength all 0x80, R takes 0x108 bytes, X at least 0x84 bytes for a fast or normalized reduction, and since the product fills 0x100 bytes the 8 bytes at offsets 0x100 to 0x107 must be zeroed first. A product larger than twice the modulus plus one word must be reduced separately with a Euclidean division.

u2Options is the inclusive OR of a required operation option, a required carry option and, only when wanted, a modular reduction option. nu1ZBase need not be filled without addition or subtraction. Where the product is one word short of twice the modulus plus one word, a zero padding word must be added before reduction, or uninitialized high words are taken as part of the number. Fmult fails if nu1XBase, nu1YBase, nu1RBase or nu1ZBase is not 32-bit aligned; if X, Y, Z or R is not in Crypto RAM; if u2XLength or u2YLength is under 4, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; if R overlaps X or Y; or if R overlaps Z with nu1RBase above nu1ZBase. A reduction option brings the Modular Reduction constraints and codes with it. With accumulation or subtraction R = (Z ± (X × Y + CarryOperand)) mod B^(XLength + YLength); without, R = (X × Y + CarryOperand) mod B^(XLength + YLength).

Square squares a long number X, adds a carry operand and optionally adds the result to, or subtracts it from, a long number Z, giving R on 2 × u2XLength bytes; the result can then be reduced modulo N. It uses an optimized squaring, faster than a general multiplication, and faster still with the GF(2^n) flag set. Operands may overlap within limits. nu1ZBase must always point to Crypto RAM and may equal nu1RBase when Z is not used. With reduction, N is at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4} and Cns at {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 8}, or 64 bytes for a big reduction; R must be zero-padded to 2 × u2ModLength + 8 bytes and the reduced result goes to X at {nu1XBase, u2ModLength + 4}, R being corrupted. With u2ModLength and u2XLength 0x80, R takes 0x108 bytes, X at least 0x84 bytes for a fast or normalized reduction, and the 8 bytes at offsets 0x100 to 0x107 must be zeroed first. A result one word short of twice the modulus plus one word needs a zero padding word; one larger than that must be reduced separately with a Euclidean division.

u2Options is the inclusive OR of a required operation option, a required carry option and, only when wanted, a modular reduction option. nu1ZBase need not be filled without addition or subtraction, and for a square alone the constraints on it are not checked. Square fails if nu1XBase, nu1RBase or nu1ZBase is not 32-bit aligned; if {nu1XBase, u2XLength}, {nu1ZBase, 2 × u2XLength} or {nu1RBase, 2 × u2XLength} is not in Crypto RAM; if u2XLength is under 4, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; if R overlaps X; or if R overlaps Z with nu1RBase above nu1ZBase. A reduction option brings the Modular Reduction constraints and codes with it. With accumulation or subtraction R = (Z ± (X² + CarryOperand)) mod B^(2 × XLength); without, R = (X² + CarryOperand) mod B^(2 × XLength).

Div performs Euclidean division of multiple-precision numbers in GF(p) or polynomials in GF(2^n): the numerator Num divided by the divisor Mod gives quotient Quo and remainder R. The remainder overwrites Num and is copied to the R area; with nu1RBase equal to nu1NumBase the copy is skipped. With nu1QuoBase zero (NULL) the quotient is not stored; otherwise it takes u2NumLength - u2ModLength + 4 bytes. The top 32-bit word of Num must be zero, and u2NumLength counts it. The library also uses one word below Num, restored afterwards, so nu1NumBase must be at least the Crypto RAM base + 4, and one word above it, not corrupted, so nu1NumBase + u2NumLength must not exceed the Crypto RAM end - 4. u2ModLength must be the true modulus length (its top word non-zero) and not under 8 bytes, which also sets 8 bytes as the least significant length of Num; a 32-bit divisor is handled by scaling divisor and numerator by 2^32, which leaves the quotient exact and the remainder to be scaled back down by 2^32. Div fails if any of nu1ModBase, nu1RBase, nu1QuoBase, nu1WorkSpace or nu1NumBase is not 32-bit aligned; if Mod, R, the 64-byte workspace or Num is not in Crypto RAM; if u2ModLength or u2NumLength is under 4, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; or if any two of Mod, R, Num and the workspace overlap; and, with a quotient, if Quo is not in Crypto RAM or overlaps any of them. R may not overlap Num, but nu1RBase may equal nu1NumBase.

GCD computes the greatest common divisor D of X and Y (multiple-precision numbers in GF(p) or polynomials in GF(2^n)) by the extended Euclidean algorithm, together with A of the Bezout identity; when X and Y are co-prime (D = 1), A is the inverse of X modulo Y. When D is non-zero it also returns Z = Y / D. Afterwards X holds D, Y is cleared, and A and Z (if D is non-zero) are stored. X and Y must each have their top 32-bit word zero, and u2Length is the length of the longer of them including that word; X, Y, A and Z all take u2Length bytes (Z one zero word more), and the workspace 32 bytes. For example, with X of 8 bytes and Y of 12, u2Length is 16: Y gets 4 zero bytes on its high side and X 8, both written least significant byte first. GCD fails if nu1XBase, nu1YBase, nu1ABase or nu1ZBase is not 32-bit aligned; if any of the X, Y, A or Z areas is not in Crypto RAM; if u2Length is under 4, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; or if any two of those areas overlap.

Rng supplies random numbers either from the hardware random number generator (the TRNG), option PUKCL_RNG_GET, or from a deterministic generator, option PUKCL_RNG_X931_GET; two further options are reserved. It does not initialize, seed or start the hardware generator, which must be set up and started as that peripheral requires, and it has no continuous or entropy testing, so applications needing these (FIPS 140, ZKA) must provide their own. The deterministic generator follows ANSI X9.31 (1998, the rDSA document, algorithm B.2.1 for computing m values of x) and FIPS 186-2 Appendix 3.1 as changed by Change Notice 1 of October 2001; for FIPS 186-2 behaviour XSeed[0] and XSeed[1] must be equal. The hardware option fills R at {nu1RBase, u2RLength}, which may be in Crypto RAM or device RAM. The deterministic option takes key XKey at {nu1XKeyBase, u2XKeyLength}, seed XSeed at {nu1XSeedBase} of length max(2 × u2XKeyLength, 44 bytes), prime Q at {nu1QBase, 20 bytes} and gives R at {nu1RBase, 20 bytes}, updating XKey. Macros PUKCL_Rng() and PUKCL(). The hardware option fails if R is not in RAM or not writable. The deterministic option fails if any of its pointers is not 32-bit aligned; if XKey, the 64-byte workspace, Workspace2 (2 × u1XKeyLength + 4), XSeed, Q (24 bytes) or R (20 bytes) is not in PUKCC RAM; if u2XKeyLength is under 20, over 64 or not a multiple of 4; if nu1Workspace2 is not a multiple of 256; or if any of those areas overlap, except that R may overlap the workspace or Q and nu1RBase may equal nu1XSeedBase.

Two sets: modular reductions, used alone or as the last step of Smult, Fmult and Square; and modular operations, modular exponentiation with and without CRT and probable prime generation. The modulus may have any form. Reductions come in a fast form (the result may be a congruent value, usually but not always the normalized one), a normalized form and a Euclidean form (both exact and below the modulus). Except for the Euclidean form, the setup must first be run with the modulus and a free area for the constant that speeds up reduction. Most services (not exponentiation) keep the quotient in the high bytes of the number being reduced, using eight bytes more than its largest size. A number to be reduced may have any significant length up to 2 × u2ModLength + 4 bytes. The modulus must have a significant length of u2ModLength bytes and be supplied as u2ModLength + 4 bytes with a zero 32-bit word on its high side, or results are wrong. Normalization always includes a reduction step and uses the same memory. A modular setup must come before any modular operation.

RedMod works on GF(p) numbers or GF(2^n) polynomials and does one of: setup (computing the reduction constant Cns for the fast and normalize forms), fast modular reduction, big modular reduction by Euclidean division, or normalization. In every form u2ModLength gives the modulus length counted as an aligned significant length, not in plain bytes. Setup computes Cns = SetupConstant(N) and must precede any fast reduction or normalization; it takes N at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4}, writes Cns to {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 12}, and uses X at {nu1XBase, 2 × u2ModLength + 8} and R at {nu1RBase, 64 or 68 bytes} as workspace. The fast reduction gives a result congruent to X mod N that may exceed N by up to 4N; it reduces inputs up to 2 × u2ModLength + 4 bytes, such as the product of two (u2ModLength + 4)-byte numbers, X being treated as a (2 × u2ModLength + 8)-byte number. Its result is u2ModLength + 4 bytes long but has u2ModLength + 2 significant bytes, of which the top two can carry at most two low bits set. Normalize gives the exact X mod N from an input no longer than u2ModLength + 4 bytes, such as a fast reduction's result; it cannot take a raw product of two NLength numbers, which must first be fast-reduced, and it clears the top u2ModLength + 4 bytes of the X area first. Both take X at {nu1XBase, 2 × u2ModLength + 8}, R at {nu1RBase, u2ModLength + 4}, N at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4} and Cns at {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 12}, and save and restore extra bytes just above the X area, which must be counted in the memory map so they overlap nothing. The big reduction gives the exact X mod N for inputs below 2 × NLength + 4 bytes, with X at {nu1XBase, 2 × u2ModLength + 8}, R and N at u2ModLength + 4 bytes, and a 64 or 68-byte workspace at nu1CnsBase.

u2Options is one of three exclusive operations, PUKCL_REDMOD_SETUP, PUKCL_REDMOD_REDUCTION or PUKCL_REDMOD_NORMALIZE, with PUKCL_REDMOD_REDUCTION ORed with one sub-option, PUKCL_REDMOD_USING_DIVISION or PUKCL_REDMOD_USING_FASTRED. CarryIn must be 0. The R and Cns areas differ by operation: setup R 64 bytes and Cns u2ModLength + 12; fast reduction and normalize R u2ModLength + 4 and Cns u2ModLength + 8; big reduction R u2ModLength + 4 and Cns 64. Run alone (not as an option of another service), RedMod fails if nu1ModBase, nu1CnsBase, nu1RBase or nu1XBase is not 32-bit aligned; if the modulus, Cns, X (2 × u2XLength + 8 plus the extra saved bytes) or R area is not in Crypto RAM; if u2ModLength is under 4, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; or if any of those areas overlap. R may not overlap X, but for the fast, normalized and big reductions nu1RBase may equal nu1XBase.

ExpMod computes a modular exponentiation without the CRT, on GF(p) integers only, in a fast or a regular implementation, with the exponent in Crypto RAM or elsewhere and a choice of exponent window size. The constant Cns must first be computed with the RedMod setup. It takes X at {nu1XBase, u2ModLength + 16}, which also serves as workspace (four words longer than the number) and receives the result; N at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4}; the exponent at {pfu1ExpBase, u2ExpLength + 4}; Cns at {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 8}; a precomputation workspace at {nu1PrecompBase, PrecompLen}; and an exponent blinding value u1Blinding. u2ModLength must be at least 12 bytes, so N has at least three significant 32-bit words. The exponent carries an extra zero word on its low-address side, which u2ExpLength does not count. Unless PUKCL_EXPMOD_EXPINPUKCCRAM is set, no part of the exponent may be in Crypto RAM; if any word of it is, that option must be set. The exponent, extra word included, may be masked in memory with an 8-bit XOR value in u1Blinding; 0 means no mask.

u2Options is the inclusive OR of a required calculus mode (fast or regular, exactly one), a required window size, and PUKCL_EXPMOD_EXPINPUKCCRAM when any exponent word lies in Crypto RAM. The options do not change the result; they trade RAM, time and security level. A larger window needs a larger precomputation workspace and shortens computation, except perhaps for very small exponents. ExpMod fails if nu1ModBase, nu1CnsBase, nu1XBase, nu1PrecompBase or the exponent base is not 32-bit aligned; if the N, Cns, X or Precomp area is not in Crypto RAM; if PUKCL_EXPMOD_EXPINPUKCCRAM is given while no part of the exponent is in Crypto RAM; if u2ModLength or u2ExpLength is under 4, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; if neither or both calculus modes are given; if Precomp overlaps N, Cns, X or the exponent; if X overlaps N, Cns or the exponent; or if N overlaps Cns.

PrimeGen tests a number for probable primality, or generates a probable prime, by the Rabin-Miller test on GF(p) integers, with a chosen number of Rabin-Miller iterations (T), fast or regular exponentiation and a window size. Being probabilistic, it cannot guarantee primality; the probability of a composite result depends on the number's size and on T (Menezes, van Oorschot and Vanstone, Handbook of Applied Cryptography, sections 4.2.3 and 4.4). The hardware random number generator must be initialized, seeded and started first. N at {nu1NBase, u2NLength + 4} carries a zero word on its high side and holds the number to test, which is left unchanged, or the seed for generation. Generation adds to the seed until a probable prime is found, then leaves it in N; it stops without a useful N if the number would outgrow u2NLength bytes or the increase passes u2MaxIncrement, and the seed plus the maximum increment must not exceed u2NLength bytes. Workspaces are Cns at {nu1CnsBase, u2NLength + 12}, Rnd at {nu1RndBase, max(u2NLength + 16, 64)}, Precomp at {nu1PrecompBase, PrecompLen} and Exp at {nu1ExpBase, u2NLength + 4}, wholly in Crypto RAM. The library also uses one word below N, restored afterwards, and one word above it, not corrupted, so N must be at least one word from either end of Crypto RAM. The service neither tests nor generates primes shorter than 96 bits, that is three 32-bit words.

u2Options is the inclusive OR of the operation (PUKCL_PRIMEGEN_TEST for a test; without it, generation from the seed), the calculus mode (fast or regular) and the window size. For long exponents a larger window is faster but needs a larger precomputation table. The result is the status PUKCL_NUMBER_IS_PRIME or PUKCL_NUMBER_IS_NOT_PRIME. PrimeGen fails if nu1NBase, nu1CnsBase, nu1RndBase, nu1PrecompBase or nu1ExpBase is not 32-bit aligned; if the N, Cns, Rnd or Precomp area is not in Crypto RAM; if u2NLength is under 12, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; if both calculus modes are given; if Precomp overlaps N, Cns, Rnd or Exp; if {nu1RndBase, 3 × u2NLength + 24} overlaps N, Cns, X or Exp; or if N overlaps Cns.

CRT computes a modular exponentiation using the Chinese Remainder Theorem, on GF(p) integers only, with fast or regular exponentiation, the exponent area in Crypto RAM or not, and a choice of window size; the RSA directives for the chip apply. The modulus N must be the product of co-primes P and Q, and the private exponent D co-prime with (P - 1)(Q - 1). Inputs are P and Q at {nu1ModBase, 2 × u2ModLength + 8}, X at {nu1XBase, 2 × u2ModLength + 16}, which is also workspace (four words longer than the number) and receives the result, the reduced exponents EP and EQ at {pfu1ExpBase, 2 × u2ExpLength + 8}, Rval with the precomputation workspace at {nu1PrecompBase, RandPrecompLen}, and a blinding value u1Blinding. u2ModLength must be at least 12 bytes, so P and Q each have at least three significant 32-bit words. Without PUKCL_EXPMOD_EXPINPUKCCRAM the exponent area must not be in Crypto RAM, even partly; if any part of it is, the option must be set. The exponents, spill word included, may be masked with a 32-bit XOR value in u1Blinding; 0 means no mask.

u2Options is the inclusive OR of a required calculus mode (fast or regular), a required window size and PUKCL_EXPMOD_EXPINPUKCCRAM when any part of the EP/EQ area is in Crypto RAM. A larger window needs more precomputation space and shortens computation, except perhaps for very small exponents. CRT fails if nu1ModBase, nu1XBase, nu1PrecompBase or pfu1ExpBase is not 32-bit aligned; if X, P/Q or Precomp is not in Crypto RAM; if the exponent area is not in Crypto RAM while PUKCL_EXPMOD_EXPINPUKCCRAM is given; if u2ModLength or u2ExpLength is under 4, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; if neither or both calculus modes are given; or if any two of X, P/Q, Precomp and the exponent area overlap.

The GF(p) curve services work on integers in GF(p) only and cover point addition, doubling, multiplication by an integer, conversion between projective and affine coordinates, and testing whether a point lies on the curve, plus ECDSA signature generation and verification compliant with FIPS 186-2. Curves have the short Weierstrass form Y² = X³ + aX + b. Two coordinate systems are handled: affine (X, Y) and projective (X, Y, Z). Affine converts to projective by setting Z = 1; the library converts projective to affine as (X / Z², Y / Z³).

A point is stored as consecutive coordinates from low to high address: X, then Y, then (projective only) Z. Each coordinate takes the modulus length plus one 32-bit word and is stored least significant byte first, the extra word being zero. In both representations every coordinate must be below P × 2^15. u2ModLength must be at least 12 bytes, so the modulus has at least three significant 32-bit words. The point at infinity is a point whose Z coordinate is zero or congruent to zero. Most services take the modulus P, the prime defining the field, at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4}, u2ModLength bytes long with a zero 32-bit word on its high side, and its modular constant Cns at {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 12}. Most curve arithmetic is reduced modulo P, in many services by the fast reduction. Cns must first be computed by the RedMod setup with the GF(p) option.

ZpEccAddFast adds two points A and B, both in projective coordinates and either possibly the point at infinity, on a curve over GF(p); it is not meant for adding a point to itself, for which the doubling service is used. The result C, in projective coordinates and possibly the point at infinity, overwrites A. It takes A and B at {nu1PointABase} and {nu1PointBBase}, 3 × u2ModLength + 12 bytes each, Cns at {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 8}, P at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4} and an uninitialized workspace of 5 × u2ModLength + 32 bytes. It uses the fast mode and fast reduction, so Cns must first be set up. No overlap between inputs and output is allowed. It fails if any of nu1ModBase, nu1CnsBase, nu1PointABase, nu1PointBBase or nu1Workspace is not 32-bit aligned; if any of those areas is not in Crypto RAM; if u2ModLength is under 12, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; or if any of them overlap.

ZpEccAddSubFast adds point B to, or subtracts it from, point A on a curve over GF(p), as chosen by u2Operator (PUKCL_ZPECCADD or PUKCL_ZPECCSUB); it is not meant for adding a point to itself. Points, result, areas, workspace (5 × u2ModLength + 32 bytes) and constraints are those of ZpEccAddFast; C overwrites A. It uses the fast mode and fast reduction, so Cns must first be set up.

ZpEccDblFast doubles a point A, in projective coordinates and possibly the point at infinity, on a curve over GF(p); the result C, possibly the point at infinity, overwrites A. It takes A at {nu1PointABase, 3 × u2ModLength + 12}, Cns at {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 8}, P at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4}, the curve parameter a at {nu1ABase, u2ModLength + 4} and an uninitialized workspace of 4 × u2ModLength + 28 bytes. It uses the fast mode and fast reduction, so Cns must first be set up. No overlap between inputs and output is allowed. It fails if nu1ModBase, nu1CnsBase, nu1PointABase, nu1ABase or nu1Workspace is not 32-bit aligned; if any of those areas is not in Crypto RAM; if u2ModLength is under 12, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; or if any of them overlap.

ZpEccMulFast multiplies a point A, in projective coordinates and possibly the point at infinity, by an integer K on a curve over GF(p); the result C, possibly the point at infinity, overwrites A. It takes A at {nu1PointABase, 3 × u2ModLength + 12}, Cns at {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 8}, P at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4}, the curve parameter a at {nu1ABase, u2ModLength + 4}, K at {nu1KBase} of u2KLength bytes and an uninitialized workspace of 8 × u2ModLength + 44 bytes. It uses the fast mode and fast reduction, so Cns must first be set up. No overlap between inputs and output is allowed. It fails if any of those pointers is not 32-bit aligned; if any of the areas is not in Crypto RAM; if u2ModLength is under 12, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; or if any of them overlap.

ZpEccQuickDualMulFast computes K1 × A + K2 × B on a curve over GF(p) in one call, a quick implementation with no additional security. Points A and B, in projective coordinates and possibly the point at infinity, sit at {pu1PointABase} and {pu1PointBBase}, each followed by its precomputation table, of (3 × (u2ModLength + 4)) × 2^(WA-2) and (3 × (u2ModLength + 4)) × 2^(WB-2) bytes; P and Cns share {pu1ModCnsBase, 2 × u2ModLength + 16}; the curve parameter a and the workspace share {pu1AWorkBase, 9 × u2ModLength + 48}; and the scalars KA and KB share {pu1KABBase, 2 × u2KLength + 8}, which may be in any RAM. The result C, in projective coordinates and possibly the point at infinity, is written at pu1AWorkBase + u2ModLength + 4. Cns must first be set up. Pointers of type pu1 are 4-byte pointers holding the full address. u2Options is the inclusive OR of the window sizes WA and WB (each 2 to 15, set with the macros PUKCL_ZPECCMUL_WINSIZE_A_VAL_TO_OPT and PUKCL_ZPECCMUL_WINSIZE_B_VAL_TO_OPT) and PUKCL_ZPECCMUL_SCAL_IN_CLASSIC_RAM, which may be set only when both scalars lie entirely outside Crypto RAM, in system RAM. A larger window enlarges the precomputation table, and a window raised to the optimum shortens computation. No overlap between inputs and output is allowed. It fails if pu1ModCnsBase, pu1PointABase, pu1PointBBase, pu1AWorkBase or pu1KABBase is not 32-bit aligned; if the P/Cns, A, B or a/workspace area is not in PUKCC RAM; if u2ModLength is under 12, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; or if any of those areas overlap.

ZpEcConvProjToAffine converts a point A from projective to affine coordinates on a curve over GF(p): A, given in projective coordinates or as affine X and Y with Z = 1 at {nu1PointABase, 3 × u2ModLength + 12}, is left with affine X and Y and Z set to 1. For the point at infinity the status is PUKCL_POINT_AT_INFINITY. It also takes Cns at {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 8}, P at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4} and an uninitialized workspace of 4 × u2ModLength + 48 bytes. Cns must first be set up. No overlap between inputs and output is allowed. It fails if nu1ModBase, nu1CnsBase, nu1PointABase or nu1Workspace is not 32-bit aligned; if any of those areas is not in Crypto RAM; if u2ModLength is under 12, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; or if any of them overlap.

ZpEcConvAffineToProjective converts a point A from affine to projective coordinates on a curve over GF(p): A is given as affine X and Y with Z set to 1 and is left in projective (X, Y, Z) coordinates. It also takes Cns at {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 8}, P at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4} and an uninitialized workspace of 2 × u2ModLength + 16 bytes. Cns must first be set up. No overlap between inputs and output is allowed. It fails on the same alignment, Crypto RAM, length (under 12, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4) and overlap faults as the projective-to-affine conversion.

ZpEcRandomiseCoordinate replaces the projective coordinates (X1, Y1, Z1) of a point with another projective representation (X2, Y2, Z2) of the same point, using a random number. The point at {nu1PointBase, 3 × u2ModLength + 12} must not be the point at infinity. It also takes Cns at {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 8}, P at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4}, the random number at {nu1RandomBase, u2ModLength + 4}, which is corrupted, and an uninitialized workspace of 3 × u2ModLength + 28 bytes. Cns must first be set up, and the hardware random number generator initialized, seeded and started. No overlap between inputs and output is allowed. It fails if any of the pointers is not 32-bit aligned; if any area is not in Crypto RAM; if u2ModLength is under 12, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; or if any of the areas overlap.

ZpEcPointIsOnCurve tests whether a point, in projective coordinates and possibly the point at infinity, satisfies the curve equation over GF(p), and reports the answer in the status. It takes the point at {nu1PointBase, 3 × u2ModLength + 12}, the curve parameters a and b at {nu1AParam} and {nu1BParam}, u2ModLength + 4 bytes each, Cns at {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 8}, P at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4} and an uninitialized workspace of 4 × u2ModLength + 28 bytes. Cns must first be set up. No overlap between inputs and output is allowed. It fails if any of the pointers is not 32-bit aligned; if any area is not in Crypto RAM; if u2ModLength is under 12, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; or if any of the areas overlap.

ZpEcDsaGenerateFast performs the second step of ECDSA signature generation to FIPS 186-2 over GF(p): from a hash of the message, computed beforehand by any secure hash algorithm (not only SHA-1), and a scalar k chosen at random, it computes the signature (R, S): R from the base point A and k, S from R, k, the private key and the hash. The hardware random number generator must be initialized, seeded and started, and k generated with it before the call. If k is outside [1, order - 1], or R or S comes out zero, it stops with PUKCL_WRONG_SELECT_NUMBER. Inputs: A in mixed coordinates (affine X, Y with Z = 1) at {nu1PointABase, 3 × u2ModLength + 12}; an uninitialized Cns workspace at {nu1CnsBase, u2ScalarLength + 8}; P at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4}; an uninitialized workspace of 8 × u2ModLength + 44 bytes; the curve parameter a at {nu1ABase, u2ModLength + 4}; and, each u2ScalarLength + 4 bytes, the order of A at nu1OrderPointBase, k at nu1ScalarNumber, the hash at nu1HashBase (its top 4 bytes zero) and the private key at nu1PrivateKey. u2ScalarLength is usually u2ModLength or u2ModLength + 4. The signature overwrites A: R at offset 0 and S at offset u2ScalarLength + 4, each u2ScalarLength + 4 bytes, whose top four zero bytes can be dropped to give u2ScalarLength-byte values. It uses the fast mode and fast reduction. No overlap between inputs and output is allowed. It fails if any of the pointers is not 32-bit aligned; if any area is not in Crypto RAM; if u2ModLength is under 12, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; or if any of the areas overlap.

ZpEcDsaVerifyFast performs the second step of ECDSA signature verification to FIPS 186-2 over GF(p): from the hash of the message (computed beforehand by a secure hash algorithm) and the signature (R, S), it computes a value V and compares it with R, setting PUKCL_OK for a good signature and PUKCL_WRONG_SIGNATURE for a wrong one. The hardware random number generator must be initialized, seeded and started. Inputs: the base point A as affine X, Y with Z = 1 at {nu1PointABase, 3 × u2ModLength + 12}; an uninitialized Cns workspace at {nu1CnsBase, u2ScalarLength + 8}; P at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4}; an uninitialized workspace of 8 × u2ModLength + 44 bytes; the curve parameter a at {nu1ABase, u2ModLength + 4}; the order of A at {nu1OrderPointBase, u2ScalarLength + 4}; the hash at {nu1HashBase, u2ScalarLength + 4} with its top 4 bytes zero; the public key as affine X, Y with Z = 1 at {nu1PointPublicKeyGen, 3 × u2ModLength + 12}; and the signature, stored like an affine point (R then S), at {nu1PointSignature, 2 × u2ScalarLength + 8}. A, the public key, the signature and the hash are corrupted. It uses the fast mode and fast reduction. No overlap between inputs and output is allowed. It fails if any of the pointers is not 32-bit aligned; if any area is not in Crypto RAM; if u2ModLength is under 12, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; or if any of the areas overlap.

ZpEcDsaQuickVerify verifies an ECDSA signature to FIPS 186-2 over GF(p) like ZpEcDsaVerifyFast but computes with the quick dual multiplication, a quick implementation with no additional security. With u2MaxLength = max(u2ModLength, u2ScalarLength), it takes the base point A (affine X, Y, Z = 1) with its precomputation table at {pu1PointABase, (3 × (u2ModLength + 4)) × 2^(WA-2)}; P with an uninitialized Cns workspace at {pu1ModCnsBase, u2ModLength + u2MaxLength + 16}; the curve parameter a with the workspace at {pu1AWorkBase, 8 × u2MaxLength + u2ModLength + 48}; the order of A at {pu1OrderPointBase, u2ScalarLength + 4}; the hash at {pu1HashBase, u2MaxLength + 4} with its top 4 bytes zero; the public key (affine, Z = 1) with its table at {pu1PointPublicKeyGen, (3 × (u2ModLength + 4)) × 2^(WB-2)}; and the signature at {pu1PointSignature, 2 × u2ScalarLength + 8}, which may be in any RAM. The status is PUKCL_OK for a good signature and PUKCL_WRONG_SIGNATURE for a wrong one. Pointers of type pu1 are 4-byte pointers holding the full address. A suggested order in Crypto RAM is ModCns, OrderPoint, Signature (or in system RAM), Hash, PointA, PointPublicKeyGen, AWork. u2Options ORs together the window sizes WA (point A) and WB (public key), each 2 to 15, and PUKCL_ZPECCMUL_SCAL_IN_CLASSIC_RAM, set only when the signature lies entirely in system RAM. A larger window enlarges the precomputation table, and a window raised to the optimum shortens computation. No overlap between inputs and output is allowed. It fails if any pointer is not 32-bit aligned; if any area except the signature is not in Crypto RAM; if u2ModLength is under 12, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; or if any of the areas overlap.

The GF(2^n) curve services work on binary polynomials only and cover point addition, doubling, multiplication by an integer, conversion between projective and affine coordinates and the point-on-curve test, plus ECDSA signature generation and verification compliant with FIPS 186-2. Curves have the form Y² + XY = X³ + aX + b. Polynomials are reduced modulo the field polynomial P[X], the modulus P, and stored as in the aligned significant length rules; comparing polynomials with < or > compares their degrees. A fully reduced polynomial has degree below that of P[X]; the library often keeps polynomials only partly reduced, of degree at least that of P[X] but always below degree(P[X]) + 15. Affine (X, Y) converts to projective (X, Y, Z) by setting Z = 1; the library converts projective to affine as (X / Z, Y / Z²).

operation.topic: PUKCL GF(2^n) point and parameter representation
operation.text: A point is stored as consecutive coordinates from low to high address: X, Y and (projective only) Z, each the modulus length plus one 32-bit word, least significant byte first. Every coordinate must be below P × X^15. u2ModLength must be at least 12 bytes, so the modulus has at least three significant 32-bit words. The point at infinity has Z equal or congruent to zero. Most services take the modulus polynomial P[X] at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4}, u2ModLength bytes with a zero 32-bit word on its high side, and its modular constant Cns at {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 12}. Most curve arithmetic is reduced modulo P, in many services by the fast reduction. Cns must first be computed by the RedMod setup with the GF(2^n) option. Where a service needs the curve parameter a alone it is at {nu1ABase, u2ModLength + 4}, u2ModLength bytes plus a zero word; where it needs a and b they share {nu1ABBase, 2 × u2ModLength + 8}, a first and b at offset u2ModLength + 4, each u2ModLength bytes plus a zero word.

GF2NEccAddFast adds two points A and B, both in projective coordinates and either possibly the point at infinity, on a curve over GF(2^n); it is not meant for adding a point to itself, for which doubling is used. The result C, in projective coordinates and possibly the point at infinity, overwrites A. It takes A and B at 3 × u2ModLength + 12 bytes each, Cns at {nu1CnsBase, u2ModLength + 12}, P at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4}, the curve parameter a at {nu1ABBase, u2ModLength + 4} and an uninitialized workspace of 7 × u2ModLength + 40 bytes. It uses the fast mode and fast reduction, so Cns must first be set up. No overlap between inputs and output is allowed. It fails if any of the pointers is not 32-bit aligned; if any area is not in Crypto RAM; if u2ModLength is under 12, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; or if any of the areas overlap.

GF2NEccDblFast doubles a point A, in projective coordinates and possibly the point at infinity, on a curve over GF(2^n); the result C, possibly the point at infinity, overwrites A. It takes A at {nu1PointABase, 3 × u2ModLength + 12}, Cns, P at {nu1ModBase, u2ModLength + 4}, the curve parameters a and b at {nu1ABBase, 2 × u2ModLength + 8} and an uninitialized workspace of 4 × u2ModLength + 28 bytes. It uses the fast mode and fast reduction, so Cns must first be set up. No overlap between inputs and output is allowed. It fails if any of the pointers is not 32-bit aligned; if any area is not in Crypto RAM; if u2ModLength is under 12, over 0xffc or not a multiple of 4; or if any of the areas overlap.

GF2NEccMulFast multiplies a point A, in projective coordinates and possibly the point at infinity, by an integer K on a curve over GF(2^n); the result C, possibly the point at infinity, overwrites A.
